div.head: Wettry.
div.p: Wettry.

BYGONES. When we went bilb'rry picking On the hill side, you and I, In the golden summer weather, 'Mong tile honey-scented heather 'Neath the blue, just cloud-fieckl sky; How we clamour'd and made merry When our dngers, purple stained, Met above the dewy berry, Fought for it till none remained. Was there ever such heart laughter In those happy summer days? Our spirits loosed to madness, With wild unthinking gladness, That can never come hereafter In life's wind-swept wild'ring ways. Once again I climb the hill top, Sink my knees among the fern, See theyellow tented wheat crop In the golden sunset burn. Other boys and girls are roaming Thro' the bilb'rry bushes by, Plucking berries with stain'd fingers Whilst the dying sunlight lingers, Just as we did—you and I. Comes their laughter from the distance Wafted to me, where I stand Thinking of a past existence In my boyhood's fairy land. Gently gliding comes the twilight, Blinks a star from out the blue— Ah—how bounded is my insight, Here am I—but where are you? —English Illustrated Magazine. H. A. H. -------

THE MISSES WE MEET WITH. The dear little Misses we met with in life, What hopes and what fears they awaken; For when a man chooses a Miss for a wits, He may be Miss-led or Mi-s-taken. When I courted Miss Kid, an i secured the kiss, I thought, in the warmth of my passion, That I'd made a great Hit in thus gaining a Miss; But 'twas only a Miss-calculation. For so many Misses surrounded Miss Yid, With me and my love interfering, A jealous Miss-trust put it into her head That she ought not to give me a hearing. Then a certain Miss-chance that I met with one day Almost sent all my hopes to destruction, For she felt a suspicion of what I would say, All owing to one Miss-construction. Deceived by one Miss-information, I wrote, The cause of her anger demanding; Miss-direction prevented her getting the note, And introduced Miss-understanding; When to make her my wife I exultingly swore, Miss-belief made her doubt my intention, And I nearly got wed to Miss-fortune before I could wean her from Miss-apprehension. But when she no longer would yield to Miss-doubt, Nor be led by Miss-representation, She had with Miss-like a most serious fall out, And to wed felt no more hesitation. But when to the church to be married we went, Miss-take made the parson to linger, And I got so annoyed by an awkward Miss-fit, That I put the ring on the wrong finger. Having been so Miss-used, I kept a strict watch, For I still felt a fear of Miss-leading; And I found, when too late, an unlucky Miss-match Interfered with the joys of our wedding. Miss-rule in our dwelling pat everything wrong, Miss-management there took her station, Till my cash, like the time taken reading this song, Was all wasted by Miss-application. —Leeds Mercury Sup.

div.head: Warteto.
div.p: Warteto.

Which is the best of the four seasons for arithmetic? The summer. Storms generally are a mystery, but you can always see the drift of a snowstorm. 'What is wisdom," asked a teacher of a class of small girls. A bright-eyed little creature rose and answered, "In- formation of the brain." WISDOM AT FAULT.—The Melbourne Argus states that Messrs. Buchanan and Wisdom, two members of the Assent- bly of New South Wales, recently came to blows in the pre- cincts of the House, in consequence of a previous verbal encounter in the Chamber. Mr. Wisdom, being the assail- ant, had to apologise. The following notes of a speech recently delivered in Dublin are not without interest. Speaking on the much vexed Irish land question, the speaker said: "The counthry Is overrun by absentee landlords," and after a magnificent peroration, delivered from the tub on which he was stand- ing, he said," I tell you the cup of old Ireland's misery in overflowing; aye, and it's not full yet." A Mayor of one of the communes in France lately made the following entry upon the register :—" I, Mayor of —, found yesterday in the forest of a man by the name of Rollin committing an act against the laws. I commanded him to surrender, whereupon he set upon me, heaping me with much insult and contumely, calling me a ragamuffin, an ass, a precious dolt, and a scarecrow—all of which I cer- tify to be true." A STORY OF ANTHONY TROLLOPH AND NORMAN MAC- LEOO.—They were both with Mr. John Burns (the well- known chairman of the Cunard Line) at a little Highland inn, when, after supper, stories were told, and the laughter became loud and long, lasting far into the night. In the morning an old gentleman, who slept in a bedroom above where they were, complained to the landlord of the manner in which his night's rest had been disturbed, and presumed to exrress his astonishment that such men should have taken more than was good for them. "Well," replied the landlord, "I am bound to confess there was much loud talk- ing and laughter; but they had nothing stronger than tea and fresh herrinfs." "Bless me," rejoined the old gentle- man, "if that is se, what would they be after dinner 1" 'Good Words Or April. Theodore Hook, at a dinner party one day, was charged with stealing from a farce, written by one of his friends, the expression, "You are down upon me, as the candle said to the extinguisher." He immediately proceeded to show how little he was under the necessity of stealing by supplying the same species of witicism to everything that was said to him for the next half-hour, e g., "You are very pressing, Dean, as the filberts said to the nutcrackers. Pray pass the wine," he continued," though I'm sorry to trouble you, as the pin said to the periwinkle." "Bravo, Hookens!" shouted the Dean, "you must give up your plan of going abroad; we can't afford to loose you." "Oh! it will be all the same one hundred years hence, as the American aloe said when it came into bloom." "But your song, Hook; only a few verses." "You really reduce me to extremities, as the rat said to the trap when it cut its tail off. I've a ,bad cold, but will try my best, and hope to come off with -flying colour', as the English general said when he ordered Lie niggers to retreat. If I attempt a stave don't make a -butt of me." WHY Do Yon &Usti 7—After that night I subjected my unbearable condition to a very searching examination. Bit:tailing and general bashfulness were carefully scrutinised. Why did I blush in church? Why did I blush before girls? Why did I blush when commended? Why did I blush be- fore everybody? Why did I blush when alone? All this was made a matter for deliberate and minute inquiry. And, In course of time, the knowledge gradually dawned upon sue, as it will under similar circumstances to nineteen- twentieths of those who have a kindred weakness, that the feeling does not spring from any inherent physical trouble, but rather from an intense development of a mental affec- tion, known as self-consciousness. To find a remedy let us look upon the world as it unquestionably looks upon us— with indifference. Every man and every woman has plenty to think about in connection with themselves without troubling about other people's blushes. A blusher is im- portant only in his own eyes. It is quite an error to imagine that society is hanging upon our words, or watching, with bated breath, our actions. A grand lesson to learn is how *utterly lost our insignificant lives are in the mightiness of .the universe, or even in the trifling circles of the social -world. Although at first I had no slight difficulty in giv- eing practical effect to the outcome of my reflections on 'blushing, I ultimately did succeed in banishing the trouble. Instead of avoiding company I began to go freely into little coteries of friends, and felt myself consciously being drawn Into having an interest in their conversation and pastimes. At fisst I used to blush very frequently; but then I remem- bered that nobody cared whether I blushed or not. The flush was a cause of discomfort to myself alone. At church, and other public places, I might be frequently seen, but on such occasions I steadfastly endeavoured to concentrate every attention upon the proceedings, and not upon my per- sonal aspect. Blushing people may sometimes find a diffi- culty in this. I especially tried to keep in the good graces Of agreeable and chatty members of the fair sex. I can truthfully say from experience that I know of no better . company tor bashful men. For non-blushing members of the masculine fraternity such a remark would go without saying. --/t took me some time to get ea of the evil, but it has been thoroughly accomplished at last. Company and innocent amusement have done it. I can now walk into any gathering in the most unblushing manner- and can talk with perfect ease to both mammas and daughters. To such ex extent, indeed, did I go with the latter that I actually found myself, one day, proposing to pretty Susan Joy. No, Madero the isn't looking over my right shoulder last now and whispering, a You darling, stupid, old donkey, what nonsenstiS that you're writing ?" She refused me point, Nash and naatTied Blithers, of the Horse Artillery, who has two thousand st year and a place called Blitherly Hall. Ns. body knew why Susan took Blithers, if it wasn't for his Morley. He was as ugly as a Hottentot, and in manners a thorough Yahoo.- Susan must have been a mercenary Creature, and now that .I think of it, the jilt wasn't so pretty as she WU said to be. I am almost sure she had a slight squint and a turn-up nose. But it doesn't at all matter, for I soon found a sweeter girl who "hadn't got neither! " From' Why do you Blush?" in " Cassell's Saturday Journal." When , you ask fur Cadbury's Cocoa Essence be sure that you got it. ; as shopkeepers often push Imitations for the sake of extra profits. Makers to the,Queen. NOTES ON AGRICULTURE, HOi CULTURE, &c,

ADULTERATED Brrrran.—Reports as to mixing old with new butter in this part of the country, and 'selling it as fresh butter, require, attention. Farmers who sell the genuine article complain that they are unfairly handicapped, Just as the honest butter makers are in America. The ser- vices of the public analyst might be invoked to test batter occasionally, as well as milk, with advantage. MAIZE GROWING.—A Manchester Guardian correspondent says:—" I made some remarks last season upon the system of maize growing which I saw in France, and I stated that Professor Leconteux believed it could be almost as well grown in England. At that very time a large crop was growing on Lord Walsingham's property at Merton, and so 11110e...agful was it that it equalled in quantity the enormous Crop I saw at 7,1. Leconteux's farm—namely, 25 tons to the acre. And this, too, was grown from common flat maize bought in the nearest market. As it was converted into en- silage' and given to the milking cows, inducing them to yield 40 per cent, more milk than upon nearly twice the weight of turnips it should be worth the while of dairy farmers in every district to think the matter over, for they might do worse than grow it for their cattle." Cunions EXPERIMENT IN WINTERING Bross.—Some of our beekeepers may be interested in a novel experiment in bee culture made by Mr. William Walker, manufacturer, West Burnside, Laarencekirk, N.B. That gentleman, having informed himself as to the Swiss mode of bee wintering, about the Ist of October last covered up eight hives of bees in two rows, first with a layer of straw about 6in, in depth, on the top of that 6in. to 81n. of earth, and covered the whole over with roofing tiles. They were allowed to remain in this position till a few days ago, when they were disin- terred. Five of the hives were in a healthy and lively state, and on Tuesday week were out working. The other three had succumbed. One of them had evidently been destroyed by mice; the other two were very weakly when earthed up. Mr. Walker says they have lost very little in weight since they were immured in their winter quarters. A DAIRY CONFERENCE will take place at Gloucester next month. Experts and others interested in the milk question from different parts of the country will meet together, and addresses will be given and discussions take place upon the different phases of one of the most popular of questions, and one which, in fact, will have much to do with the future of farming. There will also be a small exhibition in connec- tion with the conference, sufficient, in fact, to enable the public to understand what takes place and to appreciate the explanations and instruction they will receive upon modern appliances and scientific instruments relating to milk. Con- sidering how much has been done in America and other countries by means of such meetings, it is mach to be hoped that this the first in England, will not only be an entire success, but the pioneer of many others to be held in differ- ent parts of the country. Any person interested in the question will do well to communicate with Dr. Bond, of Gloucester. FARMERS AND TUB CATTLE RESTRICTIONS.—Last week, a meeting of farmers at Broughton-in-Furness protested against the oppressive and unequal incidence of the re- strictisns upon the movement of live stock. It was pointe, Out that great pecuniary loss had resulted to the farmers in that division in purchasing and disposing of their live stock. There was not a case of disease within 50 miles I distance and yet, because foot and mouth disease existed in I South Lancashire, the border farmers of North Lancashire I and Cumberland were unable to move their stocks. Even I if a sheep strayed from one field to another across the bor- der, it entailed almost its value in time and money to get it back. Farmers were a long-suffering raco ; but their patience was now thoroughly exhausted. It was resolved—, " That in the opinion of this meeting one general order should be issued by the Privy Council, providing for draw- ing a radius of about half a mile around all affected places, strictly prohibiting any egress of stocks, skins, or other matters that might carry the infection from within such circle, and that the parts outside such circle ehall remain free from any restrictions whatever." ERGOT.—Of late, Messrs. Webb and Sons, the Queen's Seedsmen, Wordsley, Stourbridge, have been issuing a series of original articles upon the pest of farm and garden crops, and the most recent contribution is an interesting and in- structive treatise on Ergot, published in Webbs' Catalogue of Special Manures for 1884, which we have just received. The article fully describes the different phases in the life- history of this fungus, and the illustrations, which are taken from nature, render it clearly comprehensible. The catalogue referred to also contains descriptions of Webbs' Special Manures for all crops, manufactured at Messrs. Webbs' Manure Works, Widnes, Lancashire, which have lately been considerably enlarged owing to the great in- crease in the demand for these high-class fertilisers. Webbs' Special Manures evidently maintain their high position in public favour, as the opinions of the leading agriculturists published in the Catalogue are reliable records of the results obtained from their use in all parts of the kingdom. In preparing their Manures, Messrs. Webb state that they have been guided by the results of a series of carefully conducted trials made at the %haver Seed Farms, and by combining practical experience with scientific investigation they have succeeded in producing manures that are pre. eminently adapted to stimulate both plants and roots in every stage of their formation. Webbs' Catalogue of Special Manures is sent gratis, and post free to all appli- cants. CHESHIRE DAIRY FARMERS' ASSOCIATION.—A large meeting of members of the Cheshire Dairy Farmers' Asso- ciation was held at Nantwich on Saturday, under the presi- dency of Captain Cotton. Mr. G. Willis, the secretary of the association, read a paper on the production of milk. He pointed out that Cheshire farmers might be said to live by the production of milk, but he confessed that their know- ledge either of the product itself or the conditions affecting its production, preservation, and management, was not such as they had any reason to be proud of.—After the paper had been read, the Chairman said that the condition of the pas- tures upon which their cows fed must materially affect the production of milk, and he hoped that one result of their turning attention to this subjeet would be that the landlords of the country would turn their attention more to the drain- ing and manuring of the land. (Applause.)—ln the coarse of a discussion, some doubt was expressed by several memr bers as to the capabilities of cows to give milk sufficient fOi 7 cwt. of cheese per annum, Mr. John Porter stating that It was as much as farmers could do to get 4 cwt. of cheese froni the produce of each animal; but Mr. Dalton and Mr. Willii both gave instances where 7 cwt and 71 cwt. had been got from dairy cows. Mr. Willis, however, stated that in 1 large dairy there were sure to be a few poor animals; but urged them to exercise every care in the selection of their cows, so as to secure good milkers, for these were the most profitable. FARMERS KEEPING UP STOCKS—There is a proverb in England that a farmer had better be over-rented than over- stocked, but it is questionable whether this is altogether I right. The National Live Stock Journal recently published a sensible letter on this question, for it certainly does not II follow that because a man has less pasture than will carry his stock he is over-stocked. The writer put two questions: 1. Can you make cattle pay you a profit, whether by means of the dairy or the fatting stall? 2. Do you sell grain or fodder off the farm? Thus if a farmer can make it pay to feed on grass, it is certain that it will pay him to keep more cattle and to sell less grain and fodder; and with regard to this there is no doubt that farmers do not take sufficient account of the quantity of grape they grew, and that many continue fields in pasture when they have ceased to yield a profitable quantity. It often happens that an individual admits, when too late, that his mistake was in selling what he ought to have consumed upon his land, not only because steck would have paid him better, but because he has thus failed to return to the land what he took from it. The writer submits that when stock do pay the farm should be heavily stocked, and that if cattle pay a profit upon home- grown corn they would also pay a profit upon purchased corn or hay at the same prices, in which case a man might carry such a stock as to be largely over-stocked. The fact Is that if stock pay at all well a farm cannot be easily over- stocked, therefore over-stocking means in reality that a man is farming badly, and not growing such crops as he might be able to consume. Many men handle their cattle so badly that they are generally compelled to sell at wrong periods, and it is then that the sensible farmer buys and profits. MR. Already the g, - trees are too forward, and the bloom of the pear and atone fruit trees is beginning to come out. The horse chestnut trees are breaking through their gummy buds, the common poplar is throwing out its pale green leaf, the hawthorn is fast developing into foliage, and all the earlier sorts of forest trees and bushes have made a remark- able stride. The eellandine is very gay in many places. The blue iris, which had shot up too far, were nipped by the frosts of a fortnight ago. On Monday I found at Cottam ground ivy in flower, also heliborus virida, a very poisonous plant. On Monday I found on the banks of the Yarrow at Eccleston that shy plant the sweet violet in flower, and near the mill, within flood range, is a very fine bed of wild gar- lick, and amongst it were arum, dog's mercury, and cow parsley ; in front of the rectory the roadside " cop " has the best show of the barren strawberry plant in bloom that I have seen for a long time past. The hazel bushes are gay with catkin and "nut bloom," and the palm willow is very gay with its " goslings " or catkins. In the orchard ad- joining the water mill at Croston I saw several plum trees in bloom, and in various places, especially about Cottam, where the blackthorn abounds, that beautiful blooming shrub was showing for flower. On the Leyland Moss Side I saw pear tree bloom more than half developed. The flower of the wych elm is just now very pretty. I noticed a great many yews, extending over something like a dozen miles running from north to south, and found them all strongly marked on the westerly side with the salt spray thrown by the great storms some time ago. Within the same distance the hawthorns are unusually bright and clean on the bark, all tendency to moss having been destroyed. Apple trees also have benefited in the same manner, and their boles and branches are very bright. SOWING.—SEED POTATOES.—LAMBS.—An agricultural correspondent writes to the Manchester Guardian :—ln a few places beans and oats have been sown in Lancashire. I have heard of a farmer at St. Michaels-on-the-Wyre, another at Thurnham, and one or two over Lune, having sown a little last week; but there is no great quantity done, though it is expected that in the course of another week oat sowing will be general on the north side of the Lune. On the freer soils it will be time, and the ground, if no more rain comes, will be ready; but there is much heavy ley ground that is in too crude a state to receive seed, and it will take mach favourable weather to bring it into a condi- tion to be pulverised with an ordinary amount of harrowing. In some of the heavier potato growing districts there are still many " hoggs" to be removed, and spritting, cleaning, and sorting is being pushed forward. In the neighbourhood of Winmarleigh Moss a few days ago there was a consider- able quantity of potatoes on the land, and large quantities have been got away from that district within the last few weeks. Farmers are anticipating a slight advance upon the low figures which their fine potato crops are bringing them in. Those who have had large quantities regard the closing season as a most unfortunate one. Those farmers who grew grain and had good crops of straw are considered to be more fortunate. The favourite plant for seed north of the Wyre, as on the south of the Ribble, is the Reading Hero, and already one large grower has sold his coming crop at 14e. a load. This has some significance for both grower and buyer. Why don't our local agricultural societies, as well as the larger ones, give more attention to the encouragement of raising new sorts? It is plain from the short time that it takes to bring almost any kind of potato into ill repute, and from the belief in the nelessity of frequently changing the seed, that there is muclrto be made by raising new sorts, and it is not Bo costly an experiment or so very diffi- cult as to be practicable only for men with well-filled purses. I have visited the neighbourhood of Garstang during the last few days, and found on the low lands a con- siderable number of very young lambs, and In many cases the ewes had brought forth twins, all of which seemed to be healthy. The little spring in the grass on the richer soils is a help to the ewes, as the herbage is good. The better class grass land in the immediate vicinity of Garstang fetches as much as £5 per statute acre. From the milk producing district immediately north of Preston, taking Falwood and Grimsargh and that locality, I learn that slipping" the calf has been rather frequent, but not so bad as in some seasons.

RURAL NOTES.—A North-East Lancashire correspondent writes :—Birds have lately been most lively and vocal, even during the spells of stormy and snowy weather. Song thrushes, missel thrushes, blackbirds larks, robins, and other birds have rarely been so plentiful, or have sung more freely than daring the present month of March. The meadows and uplands are quite vocal with the song of larks, and in the dough, and woodlands the throstles and black- birds have been piping every day, and almost all day long, since the commencement of March, though many of these birds were in song in January and Fabruary. Several throstles' nests have recently been found containing eggs; and even so early as the middle of January, so mild was the weather, a brown linnet's nest, with eggs, was found in a gentleman's shrubbery. The lapwings are now numerous and noisy ix their breeding haunts on the uplands, and some have already commenced to nest. On Saturday, the 22nd inst., I heard of a nest having been found, not robbed, containing two eggs. Common snipes are fairly numerous on the moors, and they have evidently commenced to nest, as they have been piping, or "drumming," and gyrating about in their nesting haunts since the commencement of March. Some of our earliest summer visitors have arrived, and at rather early dates, at least for this upland part of Lancashire. The twites, or mountain linnets, and meadow pipits, the former usually late breeders, commenced to ar- rive about a fortnight ago. The latter are not yet in song, but the pipits have been singing freely for ten days past. The wheatear, as a rule our earliest spring arrival, is occa- sionally noticed early in March on the southern coast, im- mediately after its sea voyage; yet, in this part of Lanca- shire, for several seasons at least, I have noticed these birds on the moorlands here before their arrival on the southern and eastern coasts. The same has occurred this year, as I was informed on Saturday by a practical natural- ist, that he saw two pairs of wheatears on the moors near the source of the Irwell on Saturday, the 15th instant. The males almost invariably arrive a day or two before the females and when two are seen together it is usually found that they have paired. Some naturalists are of opinion that there are two varieties of the wheatear—the smaller, which arrives first and nests on the higher moorlands, and a larger variety, which arrives later, and frequents lower grounds. Of two male wheatears the reputed larger variety Is nearly one-third bulkier than the other. The males, on their arrival, are always found to be in full breeding plumage. The rooks commenced nesting operations in earnest about the let of the month, or perhaps a day or two earlier. Their labour in the rookeries has been heavy, as all the old nests were completely blown out of the trees by the previous storms. In one large rookery, on the Bth, nothing could be seen beyond a few twigs, but on Saturday, the 22nd, I counted sixty-five evidently completed nests in the same rookery; and in an adjoining dough two pairs of magpies were also busy nesting on the same day. On the Towneley and adjaeent moors there are good heads of grouse; the old cocks have commenced to "bark," and if the weather continues favonrable the nesting season will evidently be early. In the lower part of the valley of Roe- sendale we have still a few pairs of kingfishers and dippers, and these handsome and interesting birds would be more numerous if they were not so persecuted by specimen hunters. Several kingfishers, lam sorry to say, were shot during the winter, but there is reason to believe that the survivors will be preserved as far as practicable. The dip- per, a water crow or water ouzel (Cinclus Europaus), is an early breeder, and I have found its nest and eggs, highly incubated, in Cumberland in the second week of February. I mention this, as on Saturday last I saw a mounted dipper, a female, which was taken from the nest in Cliviger, close to the source of the Lancashire Calder, a month ago. I also saw the nest and eggs, and was informed that the latter were partially incubated. Even specimen-hunters should have some mercy on birds in the nesting season.

ee, A certain old Borderer, on being complimented by a divine on the strength of his memory, replied, "No, sir, I have no command of my memory. It only retains what hits my fancy; and probably, sir, if you were to preach to me for two hours, I would not be able when you finished to remember a word you had been saying." It is related of an assistant to a quack doctor that he was once sent into the woods to get some of the inner bark of a certain tree. "Tom," said the doctor, as he departed," I want you to scrape this bark downward. It is for a cathartic. Don't scrape it upward, or it will be an emetic. And whatever you do, Thomas, don't scrape it both ways. If you do, nobody on earth can tell how it will act." Don't you think she's pretty ?" said the fond mother to the father, as she stroked the baby's silken hair. The father was in a sulking mood—something had disagreed with him—and he replied, somowhat curtly—" Oh, all babies are about alike. They look like little monkeys." Just then a neighbour entered, and, taking the baby on her lap, said—" Mercy on us! how like its father that child is V' A number of persons were discussing telescopes, each pro- fessing to have looked through the "largest one in the world." One after another dilated on the powerful effects of his particular telescope. At last a quiet man said mildly, "I once looked through a telescope. I don't know that it was the largest one in the world. I hope it wasn't. Bat it brought the moon so near that we could see the man in it gesticulating wildly, and crying ont, 'Don't shoot ! Don't shoot!' The old duffer thought it was a big cannon that we were pointing at him." A Wks Nunsw.—A "nursing-sister !" I wonder how many who read that word realise all that it means, the strict discipline and the total abnegation of self which such a vocation involves. I have the very highest respect for all the sisterhood ; especially do I sympathise with those who have known, not better—for that would be impossible —but brighter days. They have the most interesting of all work, I think, to perform, and are encouraged by the knowledge that they are doing immense good in the relief of suffering humanity. Still, in the lonely watches of the night, during the long weary vigils of an anxious case, the tears must sometimes unbidden flow, as memory recalls the days that are no more, and thoughts "retrace their hurried footsteps" to the time when existence was more pleasurable, but not so noble as at present.—Lady ltrassey, in "Good Words" for _April. the London Gazette contains the folk Lng .4noemeol :—" On Friday, the 28th instant, at two o'clock in the morning, His Royal Highness, Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany, fourth son of Her Majesty the Queen, departed this life at Cannes, to the great grief of Her Majesty and of all the Royal Family." Telegrams of condolence have been received from royal personages abroad. Princess Christian, who is staying at Claremont, broke the news to the Duchess of Albany, who was terribly affected at her bereavement, and, as the Duchess is near her confinement, it was feared the shock would per- manently injure her health.

Prince Leopold, the youngest son of the Queen, was born I at Buckingham Palace, April 7th, 1853. He was named after Her Majesty's uncle, the late King of the Belgians. The education of the Prince, whose health has always been delicate, was directed by private tutors until he was of age te go to Oxford. At that university he had the reputation of , being an able and earnest student. He attended the lectures of Professor Ruskin, for whom he testified his admiration in some felicitious words spoken at the Mansion House in February, UM The Prince matriculated at Christ Chinch in 1872, and in 1878 received the degree of D.C.L. In I addition to that of Professor Ruskin, he had the friendship of Professor Max Muller and other distinguished members of the University, who gladly recognised in him one whom nature and circumstances alike ?seemed to point out as the representative in a special sense in the Royal family of literature and learning. He had, indeed, so early evinced a love of literature and art that there was a general hope , and expectation that he would inherit, not only the scholarly tastes of his lamented father, but, like him, would take an Active part in the diffusion of educational and beneficent agencies throughout the nation. This hope was well ex- pressed in the House of Lords in 1874, when the question of making suitable provision for him was under discussion. The Duke of Richmond testified to the assiduity with which his studies had been prosecuted, and Earl Granville—cer- tainly ne mean judge of character—said, "From some per- sonal acquaintance with the illustrious Prince, I am able to say that there are few young men of his years who have cultivated their natural abilities with greater assiduity and success than Prince Leopold has done." The annuity granted by Parliament was the usual one of £15,000, which, it will be recollected, was augmented to £25,000 in March, 1882, in view of his approaching marriage with the Princess Helen. Prince Leopold was in December, 1881, created Duke of Albany, Earl of Clarence, and Baron Arklow, in the peerage of the United Kingdom. He was also a Duke of Saxony and Prince of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha. He had the Orders of the Garter, the Thistle, the Star of India, St. Michael and St. George, gt. Andrew, St. Alexander Newski, the White Eagle of Poland, the Southern Cross of Brazil, St. George of Hanover, the Osmanli, the Redeemer, the Black Eagle of Prussia, Louis of Hesse, the Ernestine Family Order, and the Order of Philip of Hesse. Princess Helen, te whom ha was married on April 27th, 1882, is the daughter of Prince Henry of Waldeck, an ancient kingdom in Germany, subject to Uaited Germany. The Princess is learned for her years, and she and her husband were blessed with a unanimity of taste. The Queen, before she learned of the proposed alliance, which was a genuine love match, had heard of Princess Helen's good qualities from her brother-in-law, the King of the Netherlands, when on his last visit to England, and she allowed no delay to take place before she gave her conaent. The issue of this mar- riage is a daughter, Alice Mary Victoria Augusta Pauline. born 25th February, 1883. The Prince, as already intimated, was of„a very studious disposition, and was regarded as the literary member of the Royal family. On his marriage, in 1882, an additional grant of £lO 000 was made to him by Parliament, the Prima Minister urging it partly, as he stated, on account "of the Duke's intellectual attainments." His Royal Highness took great interest in music, and was an enthusiastic promoter, along with his Royal brothers, of the Royal College of Music. It will be remembered that he attended a meeting at Manchester, in furtherance of the object, and delivered an address which was regarded as showing a thorough mastery of the subject, while he expressed himself vary happily throughout. With regard to the Duchess of Albany, it may be stated that in voting an annuity of £lO,OOO to the Duke, in addition to the income of £15,000 which he then enjoyed, the House of Commons provided (March 23,1882), that the Duchess should receive £B,OOO per annum if she survived her husband.

LAST MOMENTS. It appears that the Prince was present at the celebration if the Naval Club, at Cannes, on Thursday evening, and there sustained a fall on the polished oak floor of the danc- ing salon which necessitated his removal to the house where he was staying. The ultimate cause of death was net directly traceable to this mishap, but to an attack of syn- cope or a similar affection of the heart, the effects of which were instantaneously mortal. It is singular that the fall which His Royal Highness sustained was similar to that which he experienced at Meatone. The Duke was visiting in the Riviera at that time, just prior to his marriage with the Princess Helen, and about the 7th of April he slipped ' and fell on the stones of the Grand Parade, sustaining a severe shock which kept him in his room for several daye. Another singular coincidence connected with his death is the fact that it was while staving at Cannes that he first received the news of the death of his father. One telegram from Cannes says :—" The Duke fell on the steps of the club at Cannes at half-past six on Thurs- day evening, but he was well enough subsequently to tele- graph to the Duchess to say that he had had a fall, and to warn her that he might not be able to fulfil his intention of returning next day to England. Shortly after this he be- came unconscious, and he remained In this condition until he died. The Duke fell on his head, and the doctors cannot quite make out whether death was eaused by concussion Cr was merely accelerated thereby. His Royal Highness had in previous years been subject to attacks of faintness, but lat- terly these had been much rarer."

The AS'Eandard Cannes correspondent supplies the follow- ing interesting particulars o' the Duke's end :—His Royal Highness had left the balcony with Captain Percival, Dr. Royle, and Mr. Usher, when, at the foot of the staircase leading to his own private room at the club, he suddenly fell heavily to the ground. He did not trip, nor did he fall down stairs; but it was, on the contrary, when about to as- send the first step that he fell. The Prince was immediately raised by Captain Perceval, Dr. Hoyle, and M. Paul, the manager of the club, and carried into the large saloon, where it was found that he had hurt his knee. Dr. Hoyle bathed aid dressed It, as he had often done on previous oc- casions. The Prince, who was to have returned to England on the following morning, did lot seem to suffer much pain, and in a comparatively short time appeared to have quite recovered his good spirits. He was, however, annoyed at the accident, and conscious that the fall would prevent his eturn home. He exclaimed, "Well, here I sin for at least ,rhree weeks." While his knee was being dressed he called 'for some note paper, aid after writing a few short telegrams to other members of his family he penned the last loving letter his hand was destined to write to his wife. He feared that on the receipt of the news of the accident she would feel anxious, unless it was accompanied with a letter from him. The Prince, who could not put his foot to the ground, was then carried to a carriage and transported to the Villa Nevada. This villa is situated at a considerable distance from the Cercle Nautique, at the top of an eminence overlooking the town and sea. It is a pretty little house, with a small garden in front. It is of two storeys only. The Duke's room was on the first floor, and he was carried from the carriage and placed on his bed. At that moment he did not feel quite so well, but nevertheless he ate some dinner and chatted some time afterwards with Captain Perceval and Dr. Roy'.. Miss Perceval, the captain's aunt, a most ami- able lady, was also with the'Prince. His conversation was of a depressing and melancholy nature. As if conscious that his end was approaching, he spoke of his own funeral, an 1 of the Royal tombs in Windsor Castle. His friends tried to change the tenor of his ideas, and at last Dr. Boyle read him to sleep. 'lt was then elevek o'clock, but the Prince's faithful friend and diedical attendant did net retire to rest. He threw himself for a few minutes on abed which had been prepared for him in the same room, but was con- stantly on the watch. Until about three o'clock in the morning the Prince seemed to be in a sound sleep. Then, however, he was seized with convulsions. Dr. Boyle was at the Prince's side In an instant, and Captain Percival, whom he called to his assistance, was not long in coming. They endeavoured to administer a little brandy, but in vain, and in a few minutes the Prince had ceased to live. Dr. Russell Reynolds and another medical man were sent for. It was broad daylight when they arrived, and they could only listen to what was told them and give their opiaien as to the cause of death. That opinion is that the Duke of Albany died from an effusion of blood upon the brain.

Writing at the time of one ef Prince Leopold's serious illnesses, a medical contemporary said :—Haamophilia is a very learned-looking word, and, as it should do, it bespeaks a disease of which we know very little. The malady, which from time to time so unhappily incapacitates H.R.H. Prince Leopold, is one which most unprofessional people think to be due be some abnormal condition of the skin. A Person who bleeds easily is said to have only one skin, in the place of the proper number which it must puree many to tell. It is not, however, any such malfor- mation, but what it Is is much less certain. Such persons bleed easily from not only the skin when wounded, but from the gums and the mouth, and mucous membranes. They also bruise easily, and in the same way it is probable that the troubles in the joints from whick they antraq are to be explained by supposing some slight injury to the synovial membrane, and a subsequent escape of fluid to the cavity of the joint. We do not know what is the malformation or disease which predisposes to such an easy escape of the blood from its proper channels. The chemical constitution of the blood has been thought by some to be at fault, the smaller blood-vessels by others; but no chemical or micros- copical investigations that have been conducted as yet have been anything but contradictory, and, therefore, have been without result. One curious fact, however, ham been elicited from various observations that have been made; and this is, that it is hereditary to a marked degree, and that it is trans- mitted along the male much oftener than along the female tine. A special correspondent says had a long conversation with Captain Perceval and Dr. Royle, at the Villa Nevada. Both gentlemen are overwhelmed with grief. Captain Per- cent said the Prince had greatly benefited by his stay at Villa Nevada. "When he came here," continued the cap- tain, "it was merely for a five days' visit—but he stayed five weeks. His great fault was, wanting to do too much in

state of health; he Pia never quiet for leng He would sometimes take a cruise in the bay on .ae coast in our little boat, or, failing that, would .in in some picnic excursion to which he had been invited. He made himself agreeable in all directions, and with all with whom he came in contact. The result was that, al- though he appeared in splendid health, his tissues were weakened and an excess of blood was produced. He made himself in five weeks as popular as many men who have resided in Cannes for twenty years. He was universally popular and is universally regretted." Captain Perceval then related the circumstances in con- nection with the fall of His Royal Highness., "The duke," continued Captain Perceval, "although suffering acute I momentary pain after his fall en the steps of the Cercle Nantique, was not rendered unconscious, and almost his first words to me when he saw that he would be unable to meet those whom he expected were, 'Please entertain my guests for me.' I did as he recptested. After being attended to at the Villa Nevada, the duke rallied completely. He wrote some letters, dined, and was in bright spirits. But I feared the shock, and got Dr. Hoyle to lie in the same room with the duke. About midnight there was a sadden col- lapse. A few minutes after the hour I heard Dr. Boyle cal- ling for brandy. I fetched some, and hurried into the room with it. The duke was then in geat pain, but this subsided under Dr. Royle's care and attention. He grew marvel- lously calm as death approached, and pawed away from earth lying in my arms peacefully and tranquilly. There was but one faint shudder at the close and all was over. A few moments afterwards, and he looked exactly as though asleep. His Royal Highness died on the day he was to have left Cannes, and just five weeks and one day after his arrival here."

M2IIIY pathetic incidents are now related of the late Nuke by the two or three constant friends who were rarely absent from his side during his stay at Cannes. The Duke was at times sad. He felt that he had not a robust strength, and the thought at times depressed him. At rare intervals, too, he complained of his ill-luck. It happened that on the flrst day after his arrival he met with an accident in Captain I PercevaPs boat, the little craft being wrecked. The matter was by no means serious, but the Duke despondingly ex- claimed, "My usual fate! Disaster to friends as well an to I myself!" On another occasion, when Ma Royal Highness was in a serious and reverential mood, he rose and gazed long and wistfully over the luxurious grounds before him to the deep blue sea beyond. Turning at length to Captain Perceval, he said quietly, "Perceval, I would rather die here than anywhere else in the world." He died in that very room. I was shown the apartment to-day. It is a most pleasant room, and one that Captain Perceval himself formerly used, but gave up to his distinguished guest on his arrival. The walls are hung with sporting and military pictures, a shield bearing the coat of arms of some dis- tinguished foreigner forming a noteworthy feature. The bed which the Duke occupied is a small one, and is placed in the centre of the room. From the windows a magnifi- cent view of the town, the bay, and the mountains is obtained.

----- FUNERAL ARRANGEMENTS AT CANNES. CiNNES, SATURDAY, 6 P.M —The remains ef the Duke of Albany were placed in the coffin towards noon to-day. The coffin is enclosed with a glass cover, so that the body re- mains visible. The Prince is dressed in a violet robe, and wears some decorations. The face has a peaceful look, the lips being slightly parted. At the foot of the coffin, which is covered with black velvet, and has silver-plated handles, is a magnificent wreath of white (manilas sent by Mr. Webb, of the Villa des Fayeres ; and at the head is laid another beautiful wreath presented by Lord Kilmorey. Be- sides these, numerous crosses of white roses and other lowers, the gifts of different residents in Cannes, are dis- posed about the bier. Yesterday evening, the sculptor, M. de Paoli, made a plaster cast of the face of the deceased Prince. All through to-day there has been a constant stream of sympathetic visitors to the Villa Nevada, where the re- mains of the Prince lie, and on all sides, but especially among the English colony, the warmest expressions of re- gret continue to be heard.

- Camas, SIINDAY.—The members of the Orleans family, headed by the Comte de Paris, on Friday visited the mor- tuary chamber. The Comte de Paris was much affected. The Prefect of Nice has had a company of infantry sent to render military honours at the funeral. General du Plat, aide de camp to the Queen, arrived here at a quarter to three this afternoon. The Mayor of Cannes met the General at the railway station and accompanied him to the Villa Nevada. No visitors are now allowed to enter the villa, which is guarded by police. A picket of French Infantry arrived this morning from Antibes in order to render military honours at the departure of the remains of the de- ceased Prince for England, but have left again owing to the time of the departure not being fixed. Cameos, March 31, 7-20 a m.—The Prince of Wales arrived here at seven o'clock this morning. His Royal Highness was received at the railway station by General Du Plat, Captain Percival, the Mayor of Cannes, the British Consul, the Comte de Paris, the Duke of Saxe-Coburg, Sir Charles Murray, and other prominent members of the Eng- lish colony. The Prince embraced the Comte de Paris and the Duke of Saxe-Coburg, and shook hands with the other persons assembled to greet him. He then drove immediately to the Villa Nevada. His Royal Highness will reside at Villa Saville, which has been placed at his disposal. CANNES, TITESDAY.—The Duke of Saxe Cobourg Gotha, the Comte and Comtesse de Paris,the Countess of Caserta,the Duke and Duchess of Vallombrosa, the Duchess de Luynes. Prince de Penthievle, the Prefect, the general in command of the district, and the Mayor of Cannes, arrived at the Villa Nevada at 10 o'clock this morning, and visited the mortuary chamber. The coffin was completely covered by a number of wreaths sent as tokens of respect for the memory of the late Duke. At half-past tenl a short funeral service was held in the mortuary chamber in the Villa Nevada, in the presence of about 40 persons. The Comte de Paris did not attend per- sonally, but sent a gentleman to represent him. The Prince of Wales entered at the hour named, and, taking his place at the head of the coffin, gave a sign for the service to be- gin. The officiating clergyman, the Rev. William Brookes, then read some appropriate prayers from the English liturgy. The brief but impressive service was over by eleven o'clock. At 20 minutes past twelve the signal for the departure of the cortege was given by the firing of a gun in Fort Sainte Marguerite, and the procession began to move forward. At its head rode four mounted gendarmes, followed by six policemen, and a small detachment of troops. Then came several carriages, one of which was filled with wreaths and crosses. The funeral car was escorted by a detachment et troops. Twenty-four carriages, containing the principal residents and visitors, followed. As the carriages drove through the crowded streets the Prince of Wales bowed ini recognition of the respectful salutations with which he was received. The station WAX reached about 1-30. There was some slight confusion when the cortege arrived, but after some delay, the coffin, which was covered with flowers, was taken from the car and placed in a van, draped in black, with a single white cross. VISIT OF THE QUEEN TO CLAREMONT. At Windsor, the movements of the Royal Family, whs are frequently seen in the town, seldom excite so much in- terest as in less favoured parts of the country, but on such a sad emergency as the present every item of news regard- ing them is discussed with peculiar interest. The towns- people, like loyal subjects everywhere, are relieved to learn that the Queen bears up as well as cart be expected under the trying circumstances. Her Majesty rested fairly well OD Friday night, and was up betimes on Saturday morning arranging for a visit which she purposed paying to her widowed daughter-in-law.

At eleven o'clock her Majesty, accompanied by the Marchioness of Ely, left Windsor Castle in a carriage and four, preceded by an outrider, the Princess Beatrice folloW- ing in another carriage, with her lady-in-waiting. They travelled through the private drives in the slopes to old Windsor, thence over Runnymede, along Egham Cause- way, to Chertsey, where the horses were changed, a relit"! having been sent on in advance from the Royal mews. After a drive of eighteen miles, Her Majesty arrived at Claremont House, near Esher, about half-past twelve o'clock, and there the interview between herself and the Duchess of Albany was, as may well be supposed, of a most, affecting character. It is stated that on enteriag the pm she was unable to restrain her tears at the sight of her de- parted sen's desolate home. After spending the entire after - loon at Claremoat, the Queen and Princess Beatrice drove back by the RAMA rOlltG la the evening to winds., Castle, where they arrived about seven o'clock. Her Majesty looked somewhat fatigued after the sorrowful journey, tut feels rather better although naturally still much downcast and distressed at the bereavement which has so quickly overtaken her home circle. There was some expectation that the Duchess of Albany might return with the tttleel to Windsor, but, upon consultation the widowed duchess in her present state did not feel herself quite able for the ohmage so soon after the shock of her husband's death.

B.- EitruroN.— COTTAGE A correspondent WATER CRESS.—Thia is a native of Bri shall have to Pay 1 it is said that it possesses .. rbutic properties to we '-- had. y some of its virtues may be attributed. It is also supposed to contain iodine. Its culture is carried on exten- sively in Kent, Esaex, Herts, Oxford, and Backs, and from the two latter counties quantities are sent to Manchester, Liverpool, and probably other northern towns. This can- not be because there are not sufficient suitable streams in Lancashire to grow cress for its population, for there are miles of water channels in the neighbourhood of Preston alone , that are admirably adapted for its culture. But it is not our intention at present to enter into details of its culture as an aquatic, as that is more likely to concern the farmer than the cottager, though we heard the other day of a cot- tager utilising a stream that passed through his garden, and Increasing his income 3s. to ss. per week by the sale of the cress. It may seem anomalous in any case to introduce its culture into a column devoted to cottage gardening, but it may not be generally known that it is not necessary for the cress to be always submerged in water. We have grown excellent cress during the summer on a moist shady border under a wall with a northern aspect. In our first attempt we sowed the seed in a box and placed it on a slight hotbed, and kept it well shaded. The seed soon germinated, and they were ready for planting out in May, which was done on a well prepared border. The ground was covered with 4in. of manure, and this was dug in as many inches below the surface. The plants were placed 6in. distant, which we found was too near, as everything was favourable to their well-being, including a wet season, and beyond a watering as soon as they were planted, they received very little from us after. They made rapid progress, and some must have been cut two or three times during the season, or till they were destroyed by frost. We did not keep any record of what was cut, but our impression at the time was that from two to three dozen bunches must have been taken from everyjesquare yard. We dial not deem it necessary to sow the following year, and as the corner was almost useless we merely raked it over and left it. The following April to our surprise our bed was covered with young seedlings which we thought at first to be the common land cress, as there were several about during the previous season. Time re- vealed to us that our seedlings were water cress, and another bed was prepared to receive them, and as they became suffi- ciently large to handle they were plaited Sin, distant, and they soon filled that space. The plants will lot seed if cut at all. Some odd plants of ours from careless cutting, were left till they came in flower, and were then rejected by everyone who helped themselves. Now is a good time to sow the cress either in boxes or in the open, or both ways in case of failure in the one case or the other. It was alleged that our land grown water cress was more pungent than that grown in water, and was preferred on that account. From inquiries we are convinced that there are three sorts Of water cress—one has very dark brown leaves, the other is a pale green, and the third intermediate. THE FRONT Gamma—We always endeavour to sow a patch of Mignonette the last week in March or early in April. The ground should be made moderately firm, and the seed evenly distributed over its surface, and slightly pressed with the back of the spade, or, if not too wet, pressed with the feet. Raking seeds, if they have been de- posited where they ought to be, is a mistake, because the teeth of the rake moves them in the direction it is drawn. Our earliest and best plants of Mignonette are those from self•sown seeds, which have escaped the attacks of vermin and the severity of the winter. Purple and WhiteXandy- tuft may be sown in circular patches. The best way is to mark the outline of the patch, which may be indicated by a blunt pointed stick, which will make a channel sufficiently deep for the seeds. The centre will not require any, as each plant should have at least fin, of space, and we have seen one plant when isolated and in good ground grow one foot in diameter. Hardy Ferns that are divisible may now be taken in hand, and in doing so the knife, which should be a strong one, should be carefully placed amongst the rising fronds and forced downwards. With strong roots, it may be necessary to use a sharp spade. If it is not desirable to increase the stock, Ferns are best left alone if they are doing fairly. Mach may be done to improve them by top- dressing with leaf mould and loam, with an addition of sand. Peat or bog earth will also snit many of the finer rooting ones. • THE WlNDOW.—Mesers. Sendell and Sharpies made a Judicious choice when they selected Aspidistra Lnrida Variegate for their exhibits as ornamental foliage window plant, and which gained for them the first and second prize respectively at the Preston and Falwood Horticultural So- ciety's Show, on the 19th inst. The variegation was as well brought out as if they had been grown in a well-constructed greenhouse. The plant has but few rivals in its clam on the exhibition table, and they may be found in Draccena Indviea and Dracaena Congesta. The variegated Aloe which takes years to make a decent sized plant, is another, and there are very few plants that will stand the arid atmo- sphere of a room better than it. In the class for flowering plants, anyone introducing a well-grown plant of Primula Cortusoides or Echeveria Retusa would find them formid- able opponents to a Chinese Primula or a Dentzia Gracilis. When the schedule of the next spring show is being drawn we would advise a class or twa for those cottagers who have not taken a first prize in 1884, so that the success of the competitors of the present year may not deter them from coming forward with their productions. We shall be glad to subscribe, through the proprietors of The Guardian, the sum of ss. towards such prizes. SCIENTIFIC NOTES. The latest return of the number of volumes in the British Museum is just over 1,300,000. There are 160 miles of shelves, and about 20 more 'miles to be filled. It is calcu- lated that about one ton of literature a day is sent into that institution. Professor W. F. Barrett states in a letter to this week's Nature that he is putting to the test the idea that the lower organisms may have a special "magnetic sense." It is well known that the mysterious "sense of direction" observed in many animals has been attributed to possible magnetic Influences. Professor Barrett is engaged on a systematic series of investigations from minute structures up to man, though he frankly confesses that he hardly anticipates any affirmative results. M. Alphonse Milne-Edwards gave at the last meeting of the French Academy of Sciences an account of some inter- esting experiments with sediments, and water collected at great ocean depths (3,000 to 4,000 metres) daring the Talis- man dredging expedition. The object was apparently to see if germs capable of producing fermentation existed at these depths. The samples of sediment and water were col- lected with great care so as to avoid contact with atmo- spheric germs. Added to various infusions, they gave rise to fermentation, from which, of course, it must be inferred that they contained living germs. The curious thing was, however, that if atmospheric oxygen was excluded from the "culture" infusions no fermentation took place, from which it would appear that the germs belong to the " aerobie" rather than the "anaerobic" species. THE FLOODING OF TEE NORTHERN SAHARA.—A neat little volume, entitled "The Chotts of Tunis," by Edward Dumergne hi.R.A.S. (London: W. H. Allen and Co.) gives a brief and interesting account of Commander Roudaire's project for flooding the Northern Sahara by means of a cut- ting from the Gulf of Gabes. Mr. Damergue reviews the history of the project, and adds a short account of the his- tory of North Africa from the earliest times of which any record is extant. English readers will find Mr. Damergue's little book an interesting statement of the case for the pro- ject and of the remarkable evidence in support of the hypothesis that the region of the Chotts was formerly the Bay of Tritonitis mentioned by Herodotus and other writers. He does not, however, give the arguments of geologists and naturalists like lianbree and Coeson, who deny that the basin in question has ever been beneath the sea, at least slice the Tertiary epoch; though he points out, in conclusion, that if the region has been slowly elevated, the proms may still be going on, a circumstance which might prove fatal to the scheme, which has the approval of M. de Lesseps. A NEW METHOD OF BLEACH/NC-4 correspondent of the Standard telegraphs from New York on Tuesday night: —Many scientists and millowners assembled at Salem, Mas- sachusetts, to hear Professor Rickie, of Harvard University, illustrate Charles Tappan's discovery of a new method of bleaching. They saw flax fibre made perfectly white in 27 minutes. 'The inventor claims that one day is long enough for any material; hitherto 10 days have been re- quired, and in the process the fabric was injured. Tappan's process is said to strengthen the fibre, and jet only decreases the weight 5 per cent. Instead of 25 as at present. The chief commercial importance of this discovery lies in the enormous increase which it renders available as textiles of cotton and cornstalks, which are said to be scarcely in- ferior to the cotton bolls for weaving. Even cotton roots may be made available for threads, and flax waste can be woven withie four hours. Cocoa husks and pineneedlee can be converted into good paper, and Bromelia and Ramie yield readily to Tappan's earlier patents. A streng syndi- cate has been formed in New York and Baton to test theft diseoveries on a large scale. div.head: WIDOWED DUCHESS.
div.p: THE WIDOWED DUCHESS.

CL/REMONT, %WILLY Monnume.—Before retiring to rest on Friday night, the Duchess of Albany desired Mr. Collins, the master of the house, to give instructions to the gardener to cut a quantity of the choicest flowers in his conserva- tories. This having heen done, the blossoms were made into a wreath, which was sent to Windsor soon after mid- night by special mounted messenger, and intrusted to the care of the Hon. A. G. Yorke, who yesterday morning Pro' seeded to Cannes. It was the wish of the Duchess that this wreath should be placed in the coffin of her late husband before the homeward journey was commenced. The widowed Princess retired to rest about ten o'clock. She was completely worn out with grief and anxiety, and slept comfortably for about a couple of hours. Soon after two o'clock she awoke, but, a composing draught having been administered by Dr. hod, who remained in attendance with her Royal Highness, she dozed off again, and slept until nearly nine o'clock, when she arose apparently con- siderably refreshed. After breakfast, which was served in her own apartment, the Duchess was visited by Dr. hod, and at the dc cc of the interview the following bulletin was issued The Duchess of Albany has posted a fair night, is tran- quil, and as well as can be expected.—Cnis. W. bon. March 29, 10 a.m.

Durinithe morning the Duchess saw no one but Princess Christian. Instructions were given by her medical at tendant that she must have as much quiet as possible and all visitors were forbidden audience, save those connected with the invalid by family ties. Her Majesty the Queen arrived at Claremont in an open carriage drawn by font greys at 12-35, having driven from Windsor. PrinoesS eatrice, with whom was Lady Biddulph, arrived in 3 brougham a few minutes after her Majesty. The ' meeting between the Queen and her widowed daughter-in-law was very tduching, and the interview was protracted considerably beyond the length originally in- tended. Luncheon was served in the Duchess's apartment, and the Royal relatives remained in conversation for nearly two hours afterwards. Her Majesty was eager to induce the Duchess to accom- pany her back to Windsor, but this coarse was absolutely forbidden by Dr hod, who paid a visit to his patient shortly' after the Queen's arrival. He informed Her Majesty that although, under the present conditions, no anprehensiorts need be entertained respecting the Duchess, yet if the pro. posed step was taken he would net be answerable for tbe consequences in his patient's then delicate state of health. Her Majesty was, therefore, reluctantly compelled toabandou the idea.

The Royal party left Claremont at five minutes to five. I Ten minutes later the Prince and Princess of Wales ar- rived, having travelled to Esher by the 4-20 train train Waterloo. It had been understood that their Royal High' noises would not reach Claremont until somewhat later in the evening, and, in the absence of any provision to convey them from the station to the Royal residence, they were obliged to hire a public conveyance. Mrs. Gladstone drove over frorn Coombe Warren in the afternoon, and expressed a wish to see the Duchess, but on being informed that the bereaved lady was closeted with the Queen she contented herself with leaving a written met' sage. Her Royal Highness has expressed a strong desire to see her hisband again before his remains are laid in their final resting place, and her Majesty is also anxious that the young widow should join her at Windsor, but Dr. Izod, Princess Helene's medical attendant, is entirely opposed to the proposal. Although her Royal Highness bears her af— fliction as well as can reasonably be expected, there is no doubt she is in a very weak condition, and to expose her to the certainty of the renewal of the intense excitement of the last week would be, in Dr. Izod's opinion, suicidal. It may be taken for granted, therefore, that, with so power- ful a voice against her departure, the Duchess will remain at Claremont, at any rate until after the funeral. Princess Christian recognises the necessity of this, and has intimated that she will return to Claremont at the end of the week. The Queen ef the Netherlanels, the sister of the Mohan, arrived at Esher by special train on Monday morning. On Sunday the Duchess was in a very depressed state, but she improved towards night, and awoke next morning, after some hours of refreshing sleep, better bath in health and spirits.
LOCAL REFERENCES. AT TRI WARRINGTON POUCH COURT.

At the sitting of the Warrington Borough magistrates, on Monday, the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) made allusion to the death of the Duke. He said: "Sitting here as.l am in her Majesty's name to administer justice, and in that sense as her representative, I think a brief reference to the melancholy death of her yonngest son, Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany, should have precedence over anr other business of the court this morning, for there are features of peculiar sadness in the fearfully sadden collapse of this young and promising life. By his, to us, as it appears, un- timely death, or rather untimely removal, from the exalted sphere which he already so worthily adorned (for he wag good and wise beyond his years), our beloved Queen has sus- tained another crushing blow—perhaps only exceeded in severity by the death of the Prince Consort more than 20 years ago—and who, with the young widow and her little fatherless child, in their great afkiction, have the highest claim to the nation's Christian love and sympathy, and if that could assuage their grief,l.am sure it would be loyally bestowed. We are all, I am sure, deeply moved bY this visitation which has befallen our Royal family. All the incidents surrounding the Prince's death point in a re- markable manner to the truth of what the Bible nye-- " That death borders upon our birth, and our cradle stands in the grave." I thought it was only right that this sad ChM should be noticed in this court this morning. AT • TIMPIHANCII AtZITINO. Speaking at a temperance raeeting held on Illenday even- ing, at Wycliffe Hall, Warrington, Mr. J. B. Anderson, of Liverpool, referred to the death of the Duke of Albany. The duke, he said, was dead, but being dead yet spoke, and he hoped the words that the deka on one occasion made use of would be sounded throughout the land in which he lived, and which was hollowed by his presence so abort a time, that they would be remembered by temperance workers and thought over by all who had dealings with the sale of in' toxicating drinks, "that the most terrible enemy England had talear was strong dunk." AT NIIRTON 51SSIONS.

The death of theliui-e-aii-lb-an;l;s-foresed the princi- pal theme of conversation throughout the Barlestewn dis- trict and many warm-hearted expressions-of sympathy for the bereaved Duchess and Her Majesty the Queen have been heard among all classes of the community. A fitting anll. sion to the sad event was made at the Newton Petty BessienS' su,Saturday last, when the magistrates on the Bench were Colonel George MuCorquodale, R. Houghton, T. J. Gilles- pie; C. Pilkington, and A. C. MeCorquodele. Eerie- When these gentlemen had taken their seats, Colonel McCorrine- dale said: Before commencing the business of the court this morning, I feel I cannot refrain from making a little alltr mon to the sad mews that has come upon the country this morning; and Lam sure that we all deeply sympathise with the Queen on the occasion of the loss of her youngest son. as well as with the Doles and newly-widowed lady. I feel also certain that the country at large will mourn the leas it has sustained very much. - _ - circumstances, almost, OM might say, "(vaginal, id, Way from home, in a foreign land, seeking, and ',aced enjeTing, health and pleasure, and yet in the Without a moment's notice 1 d ..et of It he was eu.t off almost A death so Melancno y so isolated would in the distressing to con' ..amblest sphere of life be painful and to the irnagir- ...tinplate, but it was intensely impressive gifted as ' ...otion when it befell a prince of royal lineage, no was with great intellectual talents, highly cut. a patriot, and an orator almost by instinct, full of eight and hopeful promise, with a perspicuous wisdom far in advance of his years. Such a death was a loss to the nation, a loss to science, a loss to literature, and to his young Widow and infant child a loss unspeakably great, whilst it had added another sorrow to the Queen's heavy burdens,— whose life had already been darkened by many shadows. Only a few weess ago the dead prince's words were heard on the public platform in St. George's Hall on subjects ot a local and national character when he delivered himself in SO sterling, patriotic, and discriminate a manner, that the recollection of him wood tend to elevate the thoughts, temper the feelings, and undoubtedly for many a day to come, touch the heart. He did not think it was necessary to say more, and would move the resolution which he hoped and believed would meet with the unanimous support of the Council. It was to the effect that the Council received With deep, regret the announcement of the death of his Hopi Highness the Duke of Albany, fourth son of her Majesty the Queen, and desiretj most humbly to offer to her Majesty and tto her Royal Eighneee the Princes& Helen of Waldeck, Dachau of Albany, and the other members of the Royal Family, a loyal and sincere expression of their sympathy and condo- lence on this melancholy occasion, and that addresses of condolence be forwarded to the Queen and to Her Royal Highness the Duchess of Albany.—Alderman Holmes seconded the resolution.—Alderman Pickmere said that it Was useless for anyone to add to what the Mayor had al- ready so well said on this sad subject. He was sure that the members of the Corporation would heartily agree with the reselution.—Alderman Webster said that he cordially agreed with the expression of sympathy. It was a melan- choly task that they had on all occasions when the Royal Family suffered bereavement, and he was sure that the feel- ing of sympathy was spread throughout the country. It was not a feeling of a transient character, but was deeply and truly felt. The loss sustained was really a national loss. The late Duke very early recognised the necessity of a Person in his position leading a life that would not be one of luxurious ease, and devoted himself largely to objects of a Philanthropic character, and that tended to improve the con- dition of the subjects of the Queen, his mother—just the Objects that interested his illustrious father. They all felt that his loss would not easily be replaced, and he was sure that they would all express their sympathy, not only with Her Majesty the Queen, but with the young widow, in this moment of bereavemeut.—The Town Clerk then read the address as follows: To the Queen's most Excellent Majesty.—May it please your Majesty, We, the Mayor, aldermen, and burgesses of the borough of Warrington in Council assembled. beg to approach imit Majesty in deep sorrow at the announcement of the death si His Royal Highness Prince Leopold George Duncan Albert, Duke of Albany, and desire most humbly to offer to your Majesty the loyal and dutiful expreasion of our sympathy and condolence with your Majesty and the members of the Royal ffamily on this melancholy occasion. We also desire most tenably to express our high sense of the regard and affection 'entertained for lita Royal Highness by all your Majesty's sub- jects for the nobleness of his character, the admirable manner in which he discharged the duties of his exalted station, and the unvarying devotion shown by His Royal B.lghness in the exercise of his brlllisnt talents te the welfare of all classes ot your Majesty's subjects. We beg to assure your Majesty of our loyal and devoted attachment to your Majesty's throne and person, and to declare our ardent wishes for the happiness of your Majesty and your family. Given under the Corporate eommon seal of the borough of Warrington the let day di April, 1884. The resolution was rnanimsusly carried. s. PULPIT REFERENCES. ' WARRINGTON' PARISH CHURCH. Preaching at the Parish Chucch on Sunday morning; the Rev. J. Varley, of t. Paul's, Derby, said that there was no station in life but had its due share of sorrow and trial. If any life in the world might fairly be coveted because of its greatness and privileges, surely it was that of the Queen of England, and,yet who would like at that moment to change Places with her? A few days ago the Queen of 'England was rejoicing that soon she would meet again he favourite SOH restOred to health; but without a sign or word of warn- ing, in one fell moment, as it were, there sped a messenger of death, and she was robbed of all that was dearest to her heart. Without one word of parting, without one farewell cry, a mother's heart had been rent asunder, while she was robbed of the fairest of all her dock. Frail and delicate from his birth, he had above all others been his mother's boys and dearest to her heart. Quick and intelligent he had become the scholar of the family. An ettist, a musician, and a scholar, he had endeared himself to rich and poor alike, and given great promise of a useful life. Few were the interests of the poor which Prince Leopold was not fore- most in, and while the rich had lost a gifted companion, the Poor had lost a faithful friend. .. There's not a flock, however watched and tended, Bat one dead lamb is there; There is no fireside, howsoe'er well defended, But has one vacant chair.
