The Rev. S. Wilkinson (vicar), preaching at St. Paul's Church, on Sunday morning, said that that day many of them had very solemn feeling!. When they opened their newspapers on Saturday morning, they found many of them draped with black, and as they passed by their public buildings they saw the flags floating at half-mast. That day, in numbers of their churches, the solemn peal of the organ would be heard thundering forth the magnificent Dead March" in Saul. They knew the reason. It was • because a prince had passed away—one who had a life of usefulness stretchiag out before him, one who was beloved by all on account of his goodnese and his virtues. But • that promising young man had passed away. Ile had left a beloved Queen to mourn his loss—their gracious Queen whom they all loved, respected and reverenced. She was that day plunged in the deepest grief at the loss of her • youngest son. They also thought about the widow, but they prayed Almighty God to pour His grace into the hearts of the bereaved, because they knew he had given a special Promise that He would be a husband to the widow, and. a father to the fatherless. The "Dead March" was played On the organ at the conclusion of the service.—The Rev. T. P. Williamson, vicar of Thelwall, speaking in the even- ing from the words "Know ye not that there is a prince and, a great man fallen this day in Israel," said that the hearts of all the men of England, were bowed down even as the heart of one man, because a .prinee aid a great man was fallen, and became they knew that the heart of ens—and she the highest in the land, oar anointed monarch—was that day weak ; weak from the natural feelings ef a mother's love, Weak in that she was bereaved of her child, weak from the recollection of bitter grief experienced In days gone by, Past, indeed, but never to be forgotten. It was a end mes- sage that came on Friday to their shores, telling with stern • and pitiless brevity, that the bright young life of Leopold, Duke of Albany, was ended, that ha who was but a few hours before in as strong and good health as his fragile constitution aver knew, was now freed from all pain, healed of all disease, secured against all disaster at the touch of the hand of the !tugs' of death. Duty was the very mainspring of the Duke's life. And where would they find that high quality more developed than among the members of the Royal family? •Fo..;s and all seemed to have as their motto the grand word ioblesse Oblige,"—at least the noble sentiment those Words expressed coald seem to be their ruling idea of life, and well did they act up to it. What each in his station could do for the honour and glory and good of England and for the welfare and happiness of her people, that he did. There were no drones in the hive, all were working bees, and though to the unthinking their life might seem simply constant round of pleasure, believe him it was true that there were no more busier workers and more fully occupied I People among her Majesty's subjects than were to be found t,_ In her own family. From his early birth the Prince had been most fragile and delicate, requiring the most careful WI,: watching and constant tending. He never could indulge in , koyish sports and pastimes; a chance fall or a rough blow I might have proved fatal' His pleasures were perforce quiet tuad.sedate. His path lay along the quiet ways of life, by -'• • the still waters, and suffering was his constant companion. Debarred from outdoor sports and violent exercises, he gave himself up to study and to scientific and artistic parsuits. His whole effort was devoted to the attainment of know- ledge and cultfire, and with notable results; and this not I for his own selfish gratification only, but that he might be the better fitted to fulfil whatever tasks his Almighty Father might lay upon him, And BO as hearrivecht years of maturity, they-found him taking a protntnent lead in all that might add to the real happiness and well-being of his fellow subjects, ever ready, often When his delicate health forbade it, to forward with his per- sonal help.andliniziaany good work; and one of his last acts before leaving England was to sing that Pathetic ;English ballad " The sands of Dee," at a concert at a neighbouring villige to his home, for the benefit of the Village schools. .When just entering upon manhood, such • eminent judges as Lord Beaconsfield and Mr. Gladstone e oeltld speak in the highest terms of the attainments of this xt: scholarly prince; such men as Professor Tyndal could speak to his attainment& in science, while in music, in painting, 41 End modelling, notably in music he took very high rank. '7 these graces add that of a disposition most noble and Sunny; he had almost written holy, for, indeed he believed. 1 that word would not be much too strong. His sufferings
. the

were lifelong, sad were endured with patient resignation I ;Our ADd unflinching fortitude, and it was by suffering they were ')ri, Perfected. He was cast into the furnace, and truly, so far as ittunan eyes could see, and men might judge, there came . ant much that was pare gold.

WINWWE CRIIROII, WARRINGTON. On Sunday mornlng, preaching at Winwick Chuck; ma Rev. James Carson said that of their lost Prince might it be recorded as of his noble father, "He, being Pue perfect in a short tiiiie;fulided a lon % inle Ttat bodily infirm- ity," which watt hie thrOngh taa turned out to hi a profit. Instead of causing bath& indulgence, it spurred him on to many tleefal lintsnits: Thus was he a bright example to sufferers ; and to all young men. For he was one of , those who "scorn delights, and live laborious days." Still, the ' more they remembered all that was noble in his character, 80 much the greater must appear the grief of our Queen, and of all those other dear ones who had lost him. Did it not almost seem as if every family in our land had been bereaved when they were; nay, this sorrow was shared IQ not only by the Queen's own subjects, but by all civilised peoples—for, so widely as the Royal House of England was known, so were they respected, and even loved. IT ST. JOHN'S, EARLESTOWN. Preaching in St. John the Baptist's Church, Earlestown, on Sunday forenoon the vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) impressively referred to the death of the Prince. He selected as his text the words 'lt is appointed unto men oace to die, and after this the judgment" (Hebrews ix., 27th verse), The req. gentleelaa observed that the histories of all great mad, ancient and modern—prophets, priests, monarchs, and apostlea—showed that all came to the same end—that they all died. .Death was indeed a mighty leveller. _lle spared none, he waited for none, he stood on no ceremony, and he was irresistible. That they knew from personal ad well As other experience; that they also knew from the pages of the newspapers which all over the country were at. that moment announcing the death in high quarters. There was not One way into eternity for the rich and another way for the poor; no, death took all alike. One man might roll along the road in the best carriage, and another man toil away scarcely earning sufficient to feed ' himself with, and yet both were sure to meet intthe same house, the same lonely grave, and upon an equality. They had all doubtlessly read the sad news of the death of Prince Leopold, san of our most gracioas Queen. = A prince! Just think for one moment! Why should a prince the? A prince was mortal simply because lie descended from Adam. Though a prince, as moot people had been in- clined to think and as many people had always said, one of the best of Her Majesty's sons, yet he had been taken away. Again, he was a member of the Royal household of our be- loved country, so that they would see the house of royalty was now and then visited by the messenger of death as well as the cottages in their own streets. Then let them think of their different circumstances. He was a prince of Royal blood, a youth comparatively speaking. They should at all times remember in their prayers those who were suffering— and the poor man whose wife might be. passing away gradually into eternity needed an interest in their prayers as well as the mother of the young prince at the head of our nation. In conclusion, he asked them to take care what they were doing when death called them. RUNCORN AND WID/DlB. The Bad death of Prince Leopold has been the subject of regretful comment amongst the inhabitants of Runcorn and Widnes during the past few days, and from the Town Hall, Messrs. C. Hazlehurst's works, Halton Castle, and other places flags have floated at half•mast. On Sunday reference was made to the event in the churches and chapels in the neighbourhood, and the organs peeled forth the solemn strains of the "Dead March" in Saul.

MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL. The House of Lords Committee on the Mancheeter Ship 'Canal Bill met on Monday for the fifteenth time. The Duke of Richmond mod Gordon presided, and the other members of the Committee were present. Mr. &spinall, Q.C., fertile Corporation of Liererpool, said he thought the time had come when the opponents of the bill had a right to ask that the Committee should have laid before them the clauses relating to the making of a subsi- diary chaenel near Ellesmere Port. Mr. Pember, Q.C., said the only point c: difficulty with regard to the Ellesmere channel was as to whether it should be made at once, or whether there should be a discretion in the Mersey Conservators to call upon them to do it at any time whenever they thought it necessary to be made. The Chairman said it must be taken from Mr. Pemba that the clauses had rot been finally agreed to. and counsel might understand that the case of the opponents to the bill would not be prejudiced by day in producing the, clauses. Mr. A. Giles, C.E., M.P., in answer to Mr. Pember, said her had been engineer to the Southampton Docks for 45 years. His view was that the dock propeced to be made in Man- chester was well designed, would give all the accommoda- tion that could be either desired or required, and wouldroarn a large revenue for the company of persons who might take shares in the undertaking. Mr. A. Adamson, shipyard manager to Messrs. Palmer and Co., shipbuilders on the Tyne; Captain Pearson, retired captain in the commercial navy; Mr. F. Edwards, ship- owner, of the firm of Edwards, Robertson, and Co., Cardiff; and Mr. W. H. Raeburn, chairman of the Clyde Steamship Owners' Association, of Glasgow, also gave evidence. The Committee adjourned until Tuesday morning. On Tuesday,Mr.Pember. read the clause which had been agreed to between the Mersey Commissioners and the pre- moterm of the' Bill respecting the execution of the training walls. Evidence was then called with the ebjectcf proving the feasibility of navigating the canal, and of showing that shipowners would prefer to go to Manchester rather than to Liverpool, because, among other reasons, of the probabilities of their getting a better return cargo at the former place. One witness said that London shippers would be very likely to ship Manchester goods at Manchester rather than use the railway frsm Manchester and pat the goods on board at Linden, and a Glasgow underwriter said he ehould be pre- pared to accept the same rates of insurance to 'Manchester as to Liverpool, in which statement he was confirmed by a London Custom House agent, who said he had no doubt that ample return cargoes would be got at Manchester, con. sidering the immense quantities of Manchester goods now to be seen in the London docks. On Wednesday, Mr. Wells, engineer to the Weaver Navi- gation, gave evidence on behalf of the Tremoters of the scheme. He thought it would be a great advantage to the Weaver Navigation and the canals in communication with it to be brought into connection with a deep-water channel. He considered that the estimates for the worts were ample. Mr. Jacob, engineer to the Corporation of-Salford, was next examined' He said he believed the construction of the canal would prove a complete remedy against the floods to which Manchester and Salford and places lower down the valley were now liable. Dr. Burghardt, of Owen'e College, and Mr. Estconrt, the Manchester city analyst, described the water of the Irwell as showing a progressive improvement.—Mr: B. T. Leech, a member of the Manchester Town Council, also gave evi- dence. He said commercial men in Machester were almost unanimously in favour of the Bill. The witness produced a I letter, in which Mr. John Rylands said he was willing, if I the Bill was passed, to subscribe for at least £50,000 worth I of shares. On Thursday evidence was, given by Mr. James Eadee, ,an American witness, who has to return to the States. He ' said if he were asked to make Manchester a port he would bring a canal through the land to Garston, but would do I nothing to the estuary in connection with such a project. IMr. Marshall Stevens, shipping agent, recalled, was I examined relative to his table on the estimated traffic en the canal.

A polite little girl was shown a Bet of plaything and a doll, and was asked which she would have. She looked at the doll, which was a fine one, and then drawing her mo- ther's head down whispered, "I would rather have the playthings, but please don't tell the doll." KEEP Yours. MIST Fon Host.—Keep your best fare for home. You will never have any company that will so much appreciate the choice things as your own family. It is in excellent form to place before visitors the daintiest fare, with all the tasteful furnishings at your command; but a refined influence is wholly wanting in that home where they are put out of sight when company are gone, where coarse diet makes the daily fare, and the refinement that lifts eating and drinking into social enjoyment is omit- ted. It may not be economical or desirable to use the best at all times, but there are many homes whose choice things are kept in the closest seclusion, only brought out on state occasions, when the children gaze in wonder and awe on the fine linen and china, and are in a state of delight at the prospect of "good things," when there is company. There are farm houses where the turkeys and chickens are sold, the money put in the bank, and the children never know what it is to "keep Christmas," and birthdays are unmarked in the family calendar. Children remember such things long, and a happy home with a share in the best the house affords, without regard to company, educates a lad to the ease of polite society, to a loving respect for his early home, that is worth to him more than bank stock accumulated by close economy. Keep the best manners for home. It is in- stinctive with most people to put on the best appearances when in society. There is a woful ignoring of the simplest rules of etiquette and common politeness in the several rela- tions of home life. Members of a family will omit a morn- ing salutation that they accord the humblest servant.; they :Trill contradict and deny the assertions of each other with acrimony they would be ashamed to use to an inferior, and .they refuse favours to one another that they would not deny a stranger. There is no place where good manners and punctilious etiquette is of more value than the home circle. It is the moral agent of good breeding; it is the law that governs the manifestations of kindness and good feeling, and also the law that restrains unkind and ignoble traits of human nature from expression. Keep your best temper for home. In society, in the streets, in business, everywhere, it is easier to control that attribute, if we guard the hasty word, the peevish tone, the irritating action in the home circle, and study toiwound none of its inmates. Keep your best spirits for home. Nowhere do gloomy and depressed spirits tell so disastlnusly as at home. The parents may 'have just cause for anxiety and care, but it is wrong and 'unjust to shadow the young life of children with anxieties they cannot appreciate, and cares they cannot understand. The tendency to brood over trouble or misfortune increases with its indulgence. So, also, does the disposition to be -cheerful and happy at all times increase with cultivation. This is by far the most admirable trait. Those who are sunshiny and cheerful in character always have the most friends, and where are friends so true and loyal, and so de- sirable to perpetuate, as those of home and family? The old coraparison of the bent swig is as true in this case as slay other, and children who grow up in an atmosphere of foreboding of the future, anxieties about the present, and cynical reflections on the motives and actions of people About them, are training a tendency to be miserable and tad, and in their turn cast shadows, instead 9! sunshine, on the path of all about them.—Sefeefed.
FOREIGN NEWS.

THE SOUDAN : FIGHTING AT KHARTOUM. COWARDICE OF EGYPr/AN SOLDIERS. TWO PASHAS EXECUTED. 'Lust/room, Maraca 16ru.—Yesterday's victory has been followed by a rather serious reverse. This morning it was arranged to attack the rebels drawn up opposite the palace on the other side of the Blue Nile. The rebel lines, two miles long, about eight distant, and parallel to the Blue Nile, stretched from Halfiyeh to some wooded sandhills. At an early hour our troops, about 2,000 strong, marched. The Bashi-Bazonks and Egyptian regulars were in a long line facing the enemy, and also parallel to the Blue Nile. On the left gank wile a sale. e of regnier 8911017 Mope with one field gun. On the right front flank was a handful of mounted troops. As our men drew near the rebels, the latter began to file away to the right if our line, disappear- ing behind the sandhills. This supposed retreat commenced at 9-40. At 10-30 all had disappeared behind the sandhills. The enemy's rear was covered by about 60 Arabs, mounted on horses and camels. Our line still advanced, and the artillery fired two shells at the retiring rebels. Our horsemen haying entered the woods at the foot of the sandhills, we saw to our astonlehment the five pan- elpal officers of our own force, who had been riding a little ahead, dash back, breaking through their own ranks. At that moment the rebel cavalry shot out at full gallop from behind the sandhille on our right. Their appearance was the signal of a disgraceful sauve qui peat on the part of our men, who broke up and rushed back without firing a shot. The 60 horsemen, who were only armed with lances anl swords, dashed about, cutting down the flying men. I saw one Arab lancer kill seven Egyptians In as many minutes. He then jumped off his horse to eecure a rifle and ammunition, when a mounted Bashi-Bazouk officer cut him down. The rebel infantry now appeared, and rushed about in all dim- tines, hacking at the men disabled by the cavalry charge. This slaughter continued for nearly two miles, our men not stopping to fire a shot. Then the Arabs halted, and an officer rellied 11100113 of our troops, and they commenced a dropping but harmless fire at the enemy, who seemed con- tent not to advance, . but treated us with the greatest .con- tempt, some riding quietly on camels in front of. our_mnz- ales. This continued till mid-day, some of- our men droppihg from stray bullets fired by the Arabs. The rebels then drew off to their old position, carrying a lot of rifles and cartridges and one mountain piece. The irregulars, in- stead of returning into camp, coolly adjourned to a neigh- bouring friendly village opposite the palace. When they had completely looted this and killed some of the inhabit- ants, they strolled into camp—Times. MARCH 17, MORNING.—The two black Pashas—Hassan and Said-who ,behaved so disgracefully yesterday have been arrested. Notwithstanding yesterday's reverse, the towns- people are as staunch as ever to General Gordon. An Arab has come forward and volunteered to lend General Gordon one thousand guineas, free of interest. This most welcome offer has been accepted, as the Treasury here is exhausted. Another Arab has equipped, armed, and paid 200 blacks for General Gordon's service. All the Arabs in the town who are armed constantly display loyalty to General Gordon Later reports about the two Pashas imply preconceived treachery in their part. Surviving Soudanese say that the two Pashas charged into the square; the soldiers recognis- ing them, opened their ranks, and through this gap the rebel horsemen, following closely behind, entered. This tallies with what I saw, and with the report—a hundred times confirmed—of the Pashas cutting down the gunners.

—Tiaras. Cam, Strem&Y.—General Gordon telegraphs very few details of the fighting, and after announcing the defeat, merely gives warning to any force which may hereafter ad- vance for his relief that the rebels now possess his two guns. He also says a messenger from Obeid reports both the people and the treops in the town to be discontented with the Mandre supremacy, and ready to turn against him should they be encouraged by any show of English force. Two large tribes, the Kahabish and Zuola, are also reported to be ready to join us if serious operations against the Mandi shou:d be undertaken, but for the present therare evidently trimming.—Standard. Otano, MoaroAY.—Despatches have been received here from General Gordon, dated Khartoum, March 23rd, an- 1 nouncing that the two Soudanese Pashas, who were sue- pacted of treachery on the occasion of the defeat near ,Halfiyeh on the lath inst., have been tried. by court-martial,' 'found guilty, and executed. The General adds that ample supplies were coming in from the White Nile, and that it was asserted that the rebels at Halfilyekk were in want CC food, and that a famine was apprehended. Two emissaries ef the Mandi had arrived at Khartoum with drawn swords in their hands, and declared he would,tot recognise his sp- pointment as Sultan of Kordofan. He advised General Gordon to embrace Mahometanism, and added that the European prisoners were beina well cared for. RUMOURED CAPITULATION OF A DARFOIYR GARRISON

Canto, TIIIVIDAY.—A despatch 'received by the French Consul-General from Khartoum states that General cordon has abandoned his termer policy of conciliation, finding it to be utterly useless. Rumours are current at Khartoum that Statin Bey has capitulated k the province of Darfour. Intelligence from Korosko to the 23rd ultimo, announces that the first arrivals from Khartoum, consisting mostly of Egyptian civil servants and women and children, have been sent forward to Assouan. A eecond party of CO4 persons had already left Abahamed on the way through the desert to Korosko, when the Egyptian soldiers belonging to it were peremptorily ordered by General Gordon to return to Khan. town. DESPATCH FROM GENERAL GORDON. CAIRO, WRDNESDAY.—Sir Evelyn Baring haa received a despatch from General Gordon, dated the 18th ult., an. nouncing the receipt at Khartoum of a letter from the chief of the Catholic missionaries at El Obeid. The members of the mission were all well. Eleven Syrian and twelve Greek merchants were at El Obeid, as well as a German named Gustav Klotz. A message from El Obeid reported the place to be poverty stricken and almost destitute of trade. There was no considerable number of the Mandi's followers in the town, and an advance upon Khartoum did not appear to be contemplated. The\Kabbabish tribe was stated to be in open revolt against thellfandi. The above news, although anterior in date to the latest intelligence, only reached Sir Evelyn Baring this morning. DEPARTURE OF GENERAL GRAHAM FROM

SUAKIM, CAIRO, THURSDAY.—Major-General Graham left Suakim this morning. Nothing has yet been decided in regard to the garrison that will remain at Suakim. It is under con- sideration to leave either :a force of marines or a battalion of General Wood's army. THE SITUATION AT SUAKIN:I. Spann, SITURDAL—Soree Sheikhs have arrived here from Tokar, requesting the appointment of a British Governor for that place. They promise obedience and sup- port to the British. Sheikhs are continually coming in. The idea of garrisoning tSeakim with Egyptian troops is condemned in military circles here, and the scheme of in- trusting the duty to an Indian regiment is strongly recom- mended. SVAIIM, WEDNISDAT.—Osman Digna is now attempting to cut off the water supply from the friendly tribes at Han- doilb and Tamanieb. The sheik Mahmoud All is raising a force to oppose him, and a battle is regarded as imminent. TERRIBLE RIOTS AT CINCINNATI. DESTRUC- TIONOF PROPERTY AND FRIGHTFUL LOSS OF LIFE. ' NEw YORI, SATCTR.DAy.—A serious riot occurred at Cin- cinnati yesterday in consequence of the popular dissatisfac- tion with the leniency of the verdict returned by the jury in a murder trial. The prisoner had been tried for murder, but the jury, rejecting what was considered .lay the publio to be conclusive evidence of his guilt, convicted him of man- slaughter only. The lenient verdict, coupled with the fact that there were twenty other prisoners in the gaol awaiting their trial for murder, inflamed the people and caused the mob to assemble. They surrounded the gaol,!where some ether murderers were confined. The military were called out, and were compelled finally to fire upon the rioters. The mob, however, increased in numbers, and broke into a gun store, where all the arms and ammunition on the premises were seized. The gaol is still threatened by the populace, and a bitter feeling prevails against the military. The pri- soner succeeded in escaping from the train while being con- veyed to a neighbouring town, but was recaptured. Twenty- one of the rioters were wounded by the fire of the military. Four sustained mortal injuries, and one has since died. Nam YORK, SONDAY.—Last night there was a 'renewal, of a most alarming and serious character, of the rioting at ICincinnati. According to one account the crowd threw dynamite bombs into the gaol, which burst with terrific force, killing three of the soldiers. The rioters also sacked a gun store, and set fire to it, but the fire was soon got ander, and the proprietor killed several of the pillagers. It Wa,l not until after the riot bad gained considerable head 'that the troops intervened., They then opened fire on the mob, and also brought to bear a Gatling gun which is re- ported to have made great havoc among the crowd. The gun was at one time captured by the populace, bat no ammuni- tion was obtainable, and it was subsequently retaken by the 'Police. The number of killed and wounded is variously 'estimated, some reports making.the figure as high as 200. HOUSE OF LORDS.--.MONDAY.
Their lordships met at 4-15. The West Lancishire Railway (Capital) Bill was read a ascend time and passed. VOTES OF CONDOLENCE TO THE QUEEN
AND -ritcHEss OF ALBANY,

Earl GRANVILLE, rising amidst profound silence, moved a humble address of condolence with her Majesty at the loss which her Majesty has sustained by the death of his Royal Highness the Duke of Albany. He said: My Lords,—lt was my painful duty on Friday last to announce to your lordships the death of Prince Leopold, Duke of Albany—a death rendered the more lamentable by its suddenness and the youth of him who has just paroled away. I have now to ask your lordships to join in the address of which I have give. notice. Two years age the question of a Parliamentary grant gave occasion to the leaders of 'both political parties in the two Houses of Parliament to speak of Prince Leopold in words of praise such as are not often applicable to so young a man. Public opinion since that time has pro- nounced its verdict that there was no flattery and no mere exaggeration in the words at that time used. 111-health, which so often destroys the energy of its victims, in Prince Leopold's case anly turned his thoughts into intellectual channels. He studied letters,nzience, and art in different lints, and, in imitation of his illustrious father, and very innh in the same spirit, he applied the results of those stndies with persistent efforts-to raise all classes, especially the poorer classes, of this country to a higher level of en- joyment and of knowledge. 'lt is only three years ago that hie Royal Highness became a member of your lordships' House; and if he did not take a leading part in your lord- ships' discussions, it was exclusively owing to the judicious determination of the members of the present Royal Family that it is better that they should not be mixed up in any political or party strife. For all other reasons he was quali- fied to take a foremost part among your lordships. He had the voice, the manner, the culture, and the thought neces- sary for a first-rate 'speaker. He took great interest in political questions, in home politics, in foreign politics, and especially in colonial politics. He gave frequent assistance to the Queen 'in Her Majesty's daily political work, and his own strong wish, I may say - his concentrated ambition, was to be emPloyed in the service of the-State. I do not think it is now necessary for me to dwell upon the merits of his private life. There are many of your lordships who knew full well-his capacity for friendship, his affectionate feeling, and his simplicity and modesty of bearing, although associated with the con- sciousness of mental power. I ask your lordships to join in these addressee. They express not only our own feelings as one of the great bodies of the State, but they are typical of the universal sympathy felt in this country and the great dependencies of this country with a widowed,mother—the most prosperous Sovereign that ever ruled over this coun- try, who yet has received such heavy blows in her domestic relations,—and they express feelings of es moathy with that young widow, about soon to become for the second time a mother, who has seen in one short moment shattered the unalloyed happiness of a marriage which was based on at- tachment and on love. My lords, I beg to move "That a humble address be presented to her Majesty, to express the deep concern of this House at the great loss which her Majesty has sustained by the death of his Royal Highness Prince Leopold George Duncan Albert, the Milted Albany, fourth son of her Majesty the Queen, and to condole with her Majesty upon this melancholy occasion; to assure her Majesty that this House will ever feel the warmest interest 1 in whatever concerns her Majesty's domestic relations, and to declare the ardent wishes of this House for the happiness of her Majesty and her family." The Marquis of SALISBURY seconded the motion. He said in carrying the vote of condolence to the foot of the Throne and to the wife he had left behind him, your lord- ships will be expressing your sorrow for a grief which has smitten not only the Throne but all classes in the country.— The address was agreed to in silence. Earl GRANVILLE then moved without comment, "That this House do condole with Her Royal Highness the Duchess .of Albany on the loss which she has sustained by the death 'of His Royal Highness the Duke of Albany, and that the 'Duke of Richmond and Gordon do attend Her Royal High- ness with the said address." This motion:also being passed, it was agreed, on the motion of Earl Grimonws, "That the address to Her Majesty be presented by the lowest lords with white staves." - The House met at 4-0. • The chair was taken by Sir A. Otway, the Deputy Speaker, in the absence of Mr. Speaker from illness. A letter was read from Mr. Bradlaugh requesting access to the Library to consult certain papers for the purpose of his legal proceedings, and, en the motion of Sir S. NORTH- cum, the necessary permission was given. QuEsnons.—The Marquis of Hairrnewrow, replying to Sir Stafford Northcote, promised that the Government would give the House such information as was possible with regard to affairs in the Soudan, but he expressed the hope that the right hon. gentleman would defer his ques- tion to some other day previous to the Easter recess. His Lordship said the Government had received from General Gordon a message of a reassuring character as to his own safety and the security of Khartoum. The Government proposed that the House should adjourn from Tuesday, April 8, till Monday, April 14.—Sir S. NOWT:MOTE said he should press for an answer to his question on Thursday.— Mr. GLADSTONE, who had entered the House amid loud I sheers, said he did not think that members who desired to discuss the Congo Treaty would have any difficulty in ob- taining an opportunity of doing so before it became neces- sary to ratify it.—Lord E. FITZILLITRICE, replying to a question, said the amount of the Alexandria indemnity awards was 4i millions. ME VOTES OF CONDOLINCE.—Mr. GLADSTONE, in mov- ing the votes of condolence with the Queen and the Duchess of Albany in reference to the death of the Duke of Albany, said the Duke possessed every capacity and every desire to do good service to his country. He had faculties of no common order, and they had been carefully cultivated from his youth upwards by his own assiduous endeavour. He passed a high eulogiurn upon the late Duke for the public services ho had performed, and said that if a long career bad been permitted him it would have been marked at every point by acts as well as words that would have given him an honourable place in the history of his country. It was little we could do for Her Majesty er the Duchess of Albany, on whom a severe blow had fallen, for the purpose of miti- gating such distress, but whatever could be done by earnest- ness and warmth of feeling springing out of a deep and an affectionate loyalty to the Throne would, he was sure, be done on this occasion, and might be of little if not of great avail in the hour of this sad and crushing calamity.—Sir S. NOETDCOTE seconded the motion, and said he was sure the late Prince bad made a great and notable mark In the his- tory of his country. The one great feeling which domi- nated all others in the House and country was a feeling of sympathy with those who were the two chief mourners in this calamity. The bright prospects of the late Prince's life had been rudely shattered, but she who bad come amongst us as the bride of one of England's sons would feel that the sympathies of England were not wanting towards England's adopted daughter.—The motion was agreed to. THE ADJOURNED DEBATE ON THE FRANCHISE BILL. . On the order for resuming the debate on the amendment of Lord John Manners to the second reading of the Fran- chise Bill, • •
TURDAY, APRIL 5. 1884.

Mr. FORSTER si be question before the Housa was not really the principle of • bill. The real .bject of the amendment was to make a dissolution more probtble. Toe amendment said the House ought to have the scheme of re- distribution on the table, which meant an :Ippeal to every possible interest that would be likely to dday toe passing of the Bill. Perhaps the Opposition thought that the divi- sion on the second reading might make it easier for the House of Lords to take such a course with regard to the bill as might force a dissolution. He hoped that should such a resqlt happen, the Government would very seriously consider whether it would not be their duty to give the House of Lords another opportunity of considering their position. (Ministerial cheers.) Sir ROBERT PEEL supported the amendment. The Bill was clearly introduced for the purpose of giving a party Manipulation to the electoral power, and he hoped the Hbuse would not give the Government a party triumph at the expense of pridciple. Mr. CRAIG SELLAR supported the Bill, and Mr. S. Ilna- BEET argued against the injustice and rashness of disfran- chising law-abiding and loyal constituencies in England in order to add to the representation of disloyal classes in Ire- land. Mr. C. Itussico.. insisted that the mode of procedure adepted by the Government was in accordance with pre- cedent and convenience, and that it would be inexpedient and unstatesmanlike to break the pledge so often given to Ireland that the franchise should be placed on the same footing in both countries. Sir R. CROSS pointed out that the House had to deal not only with the Bill but with the speech in which it was in- troduced, and the House ought to know, before the debate went further, whether the Cabinet agreed with that speech or not, and what was the effect of it. For instance, how , many members was Ireland to have? The Bill was put for- ward as a Bill for identity of franchise, but in many cases it would introduce a much lower class than the householders lin comities, and a demand would shortly be made for a still further redaction in towns. As to Ireland, the Government I were in this dilemma, that if they iesisted on establishing household suffrage they must immediately abandcn their coercive legislation. By passing a Franchise Bill alone, the Government put oat of the power of this Parliament to deal with redistribution; and if the Country was appealed to the Conservative patty would take ears to make it well understood that they did not object to reform, but only to a one-sided and incomplete measure. Mr. SHAW-LEFETRE maintained that the experience of 1866 and 1867 conclusively proved the wisdom of the ceuree which the Government had pursued in dealing with the Franchise first, and it was for their own interest that Redistribution should be dealt with before a dissolution. He controverted also the assertion that the inclusion of Ireland in the Bill would swamp the loyal minority or place all power in the hands of Mr. Parnell's party. Sir M. Iftcxs-linecu moved the adjournment of the de- bate; and Lord R. Cittnacamt. took the opportunity of protesting against the large share in it which had been monopolised by the two front benches, in which he was joined by Mr. Arnold, Mr. Sexton, and Mr. Chaplin. Lord HARTING:TON then moved the adjournment of the House, and, on behalf of the House, thanked the Density- Speaker for the sacrifice he had male of his personal comfort in leaving his sick room to carry on the business in Mr. Speaker's enforced absence. Sir S. NORTHOOTZ added a few words to the same effect, and the House adjourned at 12-15.

BILLS ADVANczn.-The Intestates Estates Bill was reported as:amended, and ordered for third reading. The Fresh Water Fisheries Act Amendment Bill, the Isle of Man Harbour Bill, and the Dublin Museum of Science and Art Bill were read a second time —Lord WATENEY having urged the de- sirability of facilitating public business by introducing more bills in the first instance in tke House eif Lords, Earl GRAN- NILLE said he fully sympathised wiih the object in view, but there was an idea that important measures were not so well received when they came down from the House of Lords as when they were introduced in the House of Commons. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tunsnmr. Sir A. Otway took the chair shortly before 4-0. Tun SOUDAN.—At the request of Mr. A. Bartlett, another Ministerial etatement on affairs in the Soudan was made by the Marquis of Ilmarmarrot4,*who confirmed the report that General Gordon considers himself quite safe at Khartoum. —The PREMIER upon being questioned on the subject of 1 local taxation, said the Government were of opinion that It I was quite possible to deal with the Franchise Bill, with the London Government Bill, and with the Local Government Bill during the present session. LOCAL GOVERNMENT, Ac—Mr. PELL asked what action the Government intended to take in respect of the resolu- tion ef Friday last. —Mr. GLADSTONE replied that the resolution ought to be read in connection with the one passed last year, which was that the relief in counties and boroughs should be by the transfer to local authorities of the revenue received from taxes or part of taxes. The settlement of the financial part of the local government question was a very large subject, involving the removal of a great number of items of local grants from the immediate jurisdiction of the House, and might involve the finding of substitutes for those taxes. The Government did not intend to assume the position that the Franchise Bill must be postponed till they dealt with the financial portion of the local government question. The only action the Government could take would be to press forward to the best of their power the business of the House.—Lord R. CHURCHILL sug- gested that the leaders of the Opposition ahoald place on the table a resolution censuring the Government for not taking immediate steps with regard to the resolution' on which Sir S. NORTHCOTS remarked that this was the first time he had seen his noble friend endeavouring to perform the part of what had been called "a bonnet" for the Government.—ln the course of a reply to Mr. Chaplin, a hope was expressed by the PREMIER that if the House re- assembled after the holidays on Monday, the 21st instant, it would be possible to proceed with the Cattle Diseases 'Bill at a morning sitting on the following day. THE FRANCHISE DEBATE.—The adjourned debate on the Franchise Bill was resumed by Sir M. Ilicars-Bleca' who contended that the real reason why the Government had not proposed redistribution was that they were not agreed about ALDERT GREY argued in favour of retaining variety ef franchise in order to secure variety of representation.— Mr. B. Hops, as one who had voted against the Reform Bills of 1868 and 1887, pointed out that under the system thus established the oscillations in public opinion, accom- panied as the enlargement of the franchise was by secret voting, had been characterised by greater, more sudden, and more violent oscillations in public opinion than had ever been known before. Mr. STANSVILD described the opposition offered to the bill as half-hearted. It did not traverse the proposal to extend the franchise; it only traversed the confidence to be reposed in the Government in carrying such a measure to its legitimate conclusion. —The debate was continued by Mr. G. Denney, Mr. Woodall, and Mr. Marriott.—On the motion of Mr. Bisoammunsr, the debate was adjourned. THE EDUCATION CODE.—Mr. STANLEY LEIGHTON 10150 to move that an humble address be presented to Her Majesty in respect to the new Education Code of various regulations. After some discussion, the House divided, when there voted :—For the resolution, 135; against, 184; majority against, 49. The Honse rose at 1-30. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair soon after 12 o'clock, and in so doing expressed his regret at having put the House to any inconvenience. He also tendered his thanks for the indulgence shown to him, and his cordial acknowledgment to Sir A. Otway, the chairman of committees, in having taken the chair in his absence at great personal incon- venience. THE SUNDAY Ceostaro BILL.—At the opening of business in the House of Commons Mr. J. C. Stevenson presented a huge petition, signed by one hundred and four thousand women and twenty-one thousand men, in favour of the Sun- day Closing Bill.—Mr. STEVENSON moved the second read- ing of the Sale of lotoxicating Liquors on Sunday Bill. He asked the House to agree to the second reading of the Bill, so that its details would be dealt with in committee. What was wanted was not partial closing. It must be total clseing or not at all, and he wanted total closing over as large an area as possible.—Mr. BURT, whe seconded the motion, said the only point upon which he had hesitated had been with regard to public opinion. He would go as far in the direc- tion of limiting facilities for obtaining intoxicating drinks as public opinion would sustain.—Mr. J. G. TALBOT moved " That this House, whilst unable to concur in a pro- posal to close houses of refreshment during the whole of Sunday, is of opinion that the hours during which such houses are open on that day might be materially curtailed." —Lord A. PERCY seconded the amendment. It was, he said, impossible to stop the traffic in spirituous liquors, and it was a question whether it should be carried on openly and under police supervision, or should he done in secret.—Mr. S. SMITH supported the Bill. As a result of a poll in Liver- pool, it was found that six-sevenths of the people were in favour of Sunday closing, and the promoters of the Bill be- lieved they would save twenty or perhaps thirty millions sterling of the drink bill of the country by Sunday closing. —Mr. HOLDSWORTH also supported it, believing the working classes were most anxious to have it passed into law. Ile contended that the experience of Scotland, Ireland, and the colonies was in favour of Sunday closing. Ile thought, bower, that there should be a provision fcr selling beer at meal times on Sunday, as that was considered a requisite among the working classes.—Sir Wm. Ilamoonar thought there was a general feeling on the part of the House that a decision should be taken on the Bill, so that the country might knew the feeling of Parliament on the question. On the general question of Sunday closing he had no hesi- tation in saving he was entirely in favour of It. It was no longer a theoretical but a practical question. The Lord Steward of the Household brought up a mes- bage from the Queen in acknowledgment of the vote of condolence.—The second reading of tha Criminal Law Amendment Bill, the chief object of which is the protection of young girls, was moved by the Earl of DALHOUSIE, and agreed to.—A motion by the Earl of Matrows to refer the bill to a Select Co.nmittee was, after some discussion, with- draw*r=Thelledical Act Amendment Bill was read a third time and passed.—The House adjourned at five minutes past six o'clock. -

The Speaker took the chair at four o'clock. 1 1 THE WELLINGTON STATUE.—Mr. SHAW LEFEVRE an- nounced that the Government had consented to the request 1 of the Prince of Wales and his committee to remove the Wellington statue to Woolwich, and to erect a new statue on the old site, towards the cost of which £6,000 had been promised. Notice of opposition to the vote was given. THE SOUDAN.—Sir S. NORTHCOTE asked if the Govern- ment had decided upon the line of policy they proposed to , pursue in Egypt, whether any informati ,n could be given as to General Gordon's present position and views, and whether it was the intention of the Government to afford him any material support.—Mr. GLADSTONE replied that General Gordon was sent from this country by her Majesty's Go- vernment to report as to the best means of evacuating the Soudan, and he likewise received from the Egyptian Go- vernment executive powers. The Government gathered from reports that General Gordon saw no reason to believe he was otherwise than safe in Khartoum. It would be a ditty incumbent upon the Government to order general Gordon to withdraw if his work were at an end, or if he seemed to be in probable danger.— The Marquis of RAMTINGTON rose and stated that General Gordon had never suggested the employment of a British force for the relief of Khartoum. According to the latest despatches General Gordon was in no danger. If the General four, I it impossible to establish any permanent governmenL at Khartoum he had perfect freedom to with- draw. Upon the departure of General Graham it was in- tended to garrison Suakim with Egyptian troops, and a force of marines would be statiened there.—Sir S. Nownt- COTE then moved the adjournment of the House for the purpose of discussing the present policy of the Government in relation to the affairs of Egypt and the Soudan and the position of General Gordon at Khartoum. —Lord J. MANNERS thought one thing was clear, that the mission of General Gordon as a pacific mission was an utter failure.—The motion, after further debate, was then by leave withdrawn. THE FnANcntsE BILL.—The adjourned debate on the Franchise Bill was resumed by Mr. BROADEURST.—The de- bate was criticised by Mr. W. H. REDMOND and Mr. Jomi MORLEY.—It was continued to a late hour, and several Irish members took part in it.

GOLBORNE. ST. JoßN's AmBuLENCE LECTCRES.—On Tuesday evening the ladies class in connection with the Golborre branch of the St. John's Ambulance Association met in St. Thomas's school-room. There was a good attendance, about 40 ladies being present. Dr. Mapei again gave a very interesting and instructive address. _

NON-ATTENDANCE OF CHILDREN AT SCHOOL.-At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, John Naylor, col- lier, and George Unsworth, collier, were each fined ss. for neglecting to send their children to school, as required by the Elementary Education Act.—A summons which had been issued against George Pennington a labourer, for a similar offence, was withdrawn, as a certificate was pro- Auced showing that the child was 13 years of age.—James Davies, collier, was also summoned for a like offence. The wife handed in a certificate as to the child's illness, but as the certificate did net bear.the signature of Dr. Mapei, by Whom it was stated that the certificate had been written, the Bench imposed the usual fine of ss.

_ CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE Soctrev.—The rum, fortnightly meeting took place on Monday evening, in the infant school. The Rev. Canon Penrhyn presided. An in- teresting programme was gone through, and a tensperance address was given by Mr. T. T. Campbell (of Liverpool). HUTTON Cnonca.—The Rev. John Walton Tyrer, 8.A., at present curate of St. Peter's Church, Birkdale, has ac- cepted the senior curacy of St. Michael's Church, Huyton, under the vicar the Rev. Canon Penrhyn. The rev. gentle- man graduated at St. Catherine's College, Cambridge, and succeeds the Rev. W. T. Southward, M.A., who was recently preferred to the chaplaincy of the above college. He is ex- pected to undertake the duties in May. TEE Duarri OF PRINCE LEOPOLD.—PaIpit references were made on Sunday to the death of the Duke of Albany ; in the morning by the Rev. Canon Penrhyn, and in the evening by the Rev. W. T. Southward, M.A. (of St. Catherine's College), Cambridge. A funeral march was played as a voluntary, and the "Dead March" in "Saul " after the sermon. The flag was hoisted at half-mast, and the bells were muffled. At the Congregational Church a touching reference to the above was also made by the Rev. J. W. Walker, B.A. (pastor). THE LOCAL BOARD ELactiox.—A greater amount of interest is manifested this year with regard to local govern- ment than has transpired since the formation of the Local Board. Four members retire, one of whom does not seek re-election; and to fill the vacancies eight gentlemen have been nominated, namely—George Banner, * Richard Brown, I Tom Dalzell, John Duncan, Charles H. Fairclough, *Edward J. Grimshaw, George Hatchman, and *John Jowett. Those marked with an asterisk seek re-election. A brish canvass is going forward. The voting papers were collected on Thursday. LOCAL BOARD MEETING. An ordinary monthly meeting of this Board was held on Tuesday evening, Mr. T. Dobell presiding. There were also present Messrs. Cooper, Grimshaw, Leventon, Siddeley, Harrison, Jowett, Watkin, Parker, Brown, Buriayeat ; Mr. Swift (clerk), and Mr. Worrell (surveyor). THE HUTTON QUARRY IRONWORKS. Mr. COOPER asked what had been done with regard to the alleged nuisance caused by the noise at the above ironworks. —Mr. JOWETT thought the best plan under present circum- stances would be to resolve into committee to discuss that matter after the meeting. The clerk had been getting up during the month all the information required, and he might give them that information.—lt was agreed that this course should be adopted.

THE WIDNES VAPOURS. The Caratnataw said that at last meeting Mr. Brown complained about the noxious vapours from Widnes.—The CLERK said he had received a communication on the subject in answer to his letter.—The CHAIRMAN asked if the Board thought it desiraJle that the assistant alkali inspector should live a little nearer to Widnes. He lived at Edge Hill, but it seemed to him (the chairman) that that was a long way from where he was actually required. It was for the Board to determine whether it would be well to express an opinion that he should live more in the vicinity of Widnes.—Mr. COOPER thought that very desirable. When it was first moved I that the inspector should be appointed it was stated posi- tively that he should reside i the neighbourhood.—Mr. LEvErrox: That was one of the inducements held out tons to contribute towards his salary.—Tne CLERK then read the letter he had received. This letter, he said, was from Messrs. Thornley and Cameron, solicitors, Liverpool, and stated that Dr. John Affieck, additional inspector for Widnes, had lately , commenced his duties. He lived at Mill House, Muck Woolton, and they might mention that they had seen him recently, and he said that there was a great deal to be done in connection with the waste heaps, which were very improperly laid, and calculated to cause a nuisance at any time. He (the inspector) had been very particularly engaged in making a careful exam- ination of the works at Widnes, and had not yet completed the round. They suggested that in the event of any more serious complaints of noxious vapours being made they should write direct to Dr. Affieek,—M. BROWN considered that seven miles was too far away from Widnes for the as- sistant inspector to SIDDELEY thought the in- spector ought to live somewhere near Huyton, as the smells they suffered from came from the top of the chimneys, and not from the waste heaps.—TheCusumeN said there would be a meeting of the comnaittee before long and the matter would then be considered, and he suggested that they leave it over till the next Board meeting.—This was agreed to. MEDICAL OFFICER'S ANNUAL _REPORT.

Dr. liam:,.-ES-medical officer, read his annual report for 1883, which was in the main a recapitulation of the monthly reports, which have been already reported. The annual death rate had been 14.2 pr 1,000, and there had been a " very fair birth rats "of 32 0 per 1,000 inhabitants.

REW RATE. On the motion of Mr. Bnowrr, seconded by Mr. COOPER, it was agreed to levy a a rate of 28 in the £ to meet the estimated expenditure. This rate is the same as that of last year.--rhe Board then went into committee.

TFLE OVERWOR.E OF TUE PRESENT DAY.—"To have as much work do as one can do, and a little more," has been given as theto recipe for cheerfulness and contentment; i but while readily concurring in the first part of the senti- ment, we cannot but suggest that it may be, perchance, that very "little more" which is at the root of half the ill. health, pale faces, and fractious nerves of the present day. It is that last drop in the already full cup, that last straw on the already well-laden back, which is too much, last one degree too much for the sorely pressed men and women who are fighting in the fight of life, and it is that overplus from which they ought if they can to abstain. They will not see it; they will not do it. Each allows that in the case of another, that other's duty in the matter is plain enough; but for him or herself—and then follow excuses, arguments, and obstinacy not to be shaken. Everybody, it would seem, must attempt something over and above what he or she can possibly accomplish; everybody must drain a little more out of their worrying feverish brains than can be yielded consistently with only wholesome effort or energy; every- body mast fly at game beyond their reach, if only it be within their eight—Good Worde for April. , .

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The ...peak, who has been ill, is recovering, but rag unable to take the chair yesterday. The Hon. Major Chetwynd was knocked down by a trait' while crossing the railway at Worthing on Monday morn. ing, and expired shortly afterwards from his injuries. Vickers and Innes, the poachers who murdered two game- keepers on Lord Roseberry's estate, near Gorehridge, on the 14th December last, were executed on Monday morning ici , the Calton Jail, Edinburgh. It is reported that the Turkomans of Sarakhs, a district lying to the south of Merv, refuse to submit to the Russians, and will shortly send a mission to Cabal to demand their definite incorporation into Afghanistan. There is prevalent in Leeds an epidemic of scarlet fever. In one district 70 persons have been attacked, and three deaths have occurred. The fever, it is stated, was com- municated from house to holm by milk supplied from a snbutbaa dairy.

IYERPOOL CATHEDRAL.—The site of the proposed ca- thedral for Liverpool was definitely selected at a meeting of the General Committee, on Taesday. The ethice will be erected on ground attached to St. John's Church, near the St. George's Hall. A sherif's officer named Michael Downie committed suit cide early on Tuesday morning by leaping down a coal pl- - Airdrie, a depth of 54 fathoms. He fell upon the cage, which was in the shaft, and was instantly killed. The de- ceased, who was a widower, leaves a family. At Burnley, on Monday, Matthew Riley, nCome,n was charged, at the instigation of toe Padiham Local Board, with having exposed for sale 52 pieces of aneound meat, on the 29th of February last, at Paditiana. He was fined £3O; in default, three months' imprisoament. A SCHOOLMASTER FINED.—On Thursday, at Dublin, Mr. Matthew Deylir, a schoolmaster in the local Bluecoat school, was fined £lO and costs for severely beating a pupil for not haying learned his Bible lesson. The lad, who was aged 14, was beaten with a cane on the hands, back, and legs. LONDONDERRY Itiors.—The report of the Commission appointed to inquire into the riots at Londonderry on the occasion of the Lord Mayor of Dublin's visit was issued on Monday. The Commissioners find that the riots originated in a project, afterwards carried into execution, of holding a public Nationalist procession on the day fixed for the Lord Mayor's lecture, but that th,e proximate cause of disturbatee was the forcible occupation by the Apprentice Boys and their party of the Corporation Hall. CHILD MURDER AND SUICIDE.—The wife of a coffee- house keeper, named Blinkho, Springhill, Birmingham. on Tuesday, threw her child, aged nine months, into the Dad - ley Canal, and then committed suicide by drowning herself. It is supposed that domestic trouble was the cause of the crime, a dispute having recently taken place between hus- band and wife about business matters. This is the second murder and suicide in the same locality within a few weeks. The deceased was a steady, sober, and industrious woman. Mimosa mc LONDON.—On Saturday a char-woman was about to clean up offices at 2, Arthur-street, West, London- bridge, occupied by Mr. Bartlett, solicitor, when she saw bloodstains on the stairs, and in alarm called in a Mr. White, who traced the mark of blood to a cellar, where was found the body of a man named Perkins, about 30 years of age, with shocking injuries about the head. The deceased was Mr. Bartlett's clerk, but nothing is known as to the murderers. Two detectives have since left London for Skir- laugh, Yorkshire, where Perkins formerly resided, to pros- ecute inquiries regarding some dispute concerning property in which he is alleged to have been involved. POLITICS IN IRELAND—The Roman Catholic Bishop of Ardagh (De, Barthelomew Weodlock) has addressed a sin- gular circigar to the priests of county Longford. He says: —"As it is likely a dissolution of Parliament will take place very soon, I bog you to announce to your 'flock oa Sunday next that, to prevent dissentions and to secure the iaterests of religion and of our people, I purpose shortly after Easter to invite the priests and people of this ceunty to meet and take counsel together in order Up the selectioa of suitable candidates to be put forward at the approaching general election." This action of the Blehop is regarded as a pro- test against the dictation of the " League.' Thz BANKRUPTCY or Mn. WHALLEY.—At the London Bankruptcy Court, on Tuesday, a sitting eras held befere Mr. Registrar Pepys for the public examination of Mr. G. Hampden Whalley, late M.P. for Peterborough, who was described as of Leinster-square, and who was adjudicated , bankrupt in December last by the order of the Court of Ap- peal. At the first sitting of the creditors proofs to the ex- tent of £2,500 were admitted, and a trustee and a commit- tee of inspection were appointed. When the case was called the hankrupt did net answer, and the matter stood over a short time to enable him to attend. Mr. Beyfus asked that the usual memorandum of non-attendance be placed moon the file. His Honour granted the application. THE CArrtn Bree.—A large deputation, representative of the farming interest, and accompanied by members of both Houses of Parliament, waited on Tuesday upon Lord Carlingford and Mr. Dodson, at Whitehall, in order to urge the retention of the amendments introduced by tbe House of Lords in the Cattle Diseases Bill. Mr. Chaplin, M.F., acted as spokesman, and other gentlemen having addressed the Ministers, Lord Carlingford, in reply, contradicted the statement of one speaker that last week's deputation, repre- senting consumers in large towns, was in the interests of the butchers. Elie Lordship repeated what he told the other deputation—that even from the agricultural point of view the bill as originally brought in was amply sufficient for . purposes of protection.

tANCASHIRE AND CHESHIRE ENTOMOLOGICAL SOCIETY. —The usual monthly meeting of this society was held on Monday evening, in the Liverpool Free Library, the pre- sident (Mr. S. T. Capper) occupying the chair. Mr. F. W. Swinden, of Bootle, was elected a member. Mr. H. H. Cor- bett (Stockport) read a paper entitled, "The causes pro- ducing localisation in insects, with special reference to ' British lepidoptera," in which he described what he believed to be the chief causes which affected the distribu- tion of British butterflies and moths, explaining how these causes would take effect. Alter the paper the compilation of the local lepidopterous farina was discussed'; and on the suggestion of the president it was decided that instead a , mere local list a work be compiled which should treat of the I butterflies and moths of the two counties from which the 1 society takes its title. Tbe secretary (Dr. Ellis) offered to undertake this task, and information with referencs CO lOCIL butterflies was proceeded with. . _

FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE —On Monday, the report made up at the office of the Clerk of the Peace, for the week ended Saturday last, shows that there were no fresh outbreaks or additional cattle affected in the hundreds of LonsAale, Amounderness, or Leyland. There are now, therefore, neither farms nor cattle affected in Lensdale or Leyland hundreds; and as five cattle recovered in the hundred of Arnounderness, it is also clear of the disease. In the Blackburn hundred there was one fresh outbreak, making seven farms infected, and two fresh cattle affected ; 14 animals recovered, leaving only two remaining affected. Though there was no further outbreak in the Salford hun- dred, two additidnal cattle were affected, one died, and 22 animals recovered, leaving eleven diseased. In the West Derby hundred one additional farm was infected, making nine, and two additional cattle; three animals recovered during the week, leaving twelve diseased. According to this return, therefore, the outbreaks during the week were two, and the additianal cattle affected six; the whole num- ber et farms infected in the country being 25, and the whole number of diseased cattle only 25. div.head: SATURDAY, APRIL 5, 1684.
div.p: SATURDAY, APRIL 5, 1684.

The touch of nature which makes the whole world kin has made the nation one in sorrow with the Royal Family at the death of the Duke of Albany, the youngest and well be- loved son of the Queen. The startling sud- denness of the news—coming as it did like a bolt out of the blue—might well cause people to be for a time incredulous of the intelligence. But the swift wires, bringing details of the sad event, soon left no room for doubt, and the past week has consequently been a week of mourning, evoking expressions of sympathy; with the chief sufferers from every part of the civilised world. It was said of old that "whom the gods love die young," and it would seem that the Prince has led a fated if in some respects a charmed life. Within a few hours of his death, when to all outward appearances there was nothing to alarm those about him, he spoke as one almost constantly face to face with the King of Terrors. It is hard for the distressed mother and the stricken wife to find consola- tion at such a time; but when the first pangs of grief are over it will be something of comfort to realise that, amongst those who knew him best, the actions; of the Prince, as of the just, "smell sweet and blossom in the dust." On Monday both Houses of Parliament were fittingly engaged in passing addresses of condolence to the Queen and to the Duchess of Albany. The speaking was brief, but the leaders of both parties in the House of Lords and in the House of Commons were apt and graceful in the expression of what" everybody felt. So many titled great ones live solely to the gratification of themselves, apart from a cultivation of the better nature within them, that the Duke of Albany may be said to have been conspicuous amongst his class. It is no small thing that Earl Granville should have been able with truth to say of him : " He studied letters,

I science, ant. 4 art in different lines and in imitation of hr: illustrious father; and very much in the sal. nte spirit he applied the results of those a tuu-lies to persistent efforts to raise all classeg, :specially the poorer classes of this country, to a higher level of - enjoyment and of knowletVe." The in tellectual similarity of charac.ter and dis- position to the Prince Consort which the Duke of Albany displayed endeateed him the more to his Royal mother, and, yrhila this remembrance will for a time make the trial the heavier, it will, we cannot but hope, be in the end a means of lightening the burden. It is a reflection no less singular than sorrowful as to the two children which Her Majesty has leat the Princess Alice and Prince Leopold that both were distinguishes by their likeness in many respects to their long-lamented father—Albert the Good. The singularity ii in the three having passed from the sphere of their earthly labours, while the sortow lies in the remembrance that they leave a great gap in the Royal household. The Duchess of Albany has not been long amongst us, but as the beloved wife of the Prince, and mother of his darling child, we may well believe that she is nigh heart- broken with grief. But she will bear words of comfort and sympathy on every hand, arm!, it will be in some measure an allevistion 01 the woe which has fallen upon her to perceive that he was universally regarded as worthy or his exalted station. It is interesting to to learn that he as on one °erasion the subject of inspiration of the pen* of the late Dean Stanley, who, in ;875, , referred to him as having then. " Thrice ' trod the pathway to the realms or death "—adding in words which, have n' " tender grace " at the present mOriertt Yet in this plfgrimago of 111 Sweet traebrand isles of pease were Calle; Dear watchful friends, strong gentle tkitl., Consoling wards of love Divine, A Royal mother's seaseless star%• A nation's sympathising prayer, The Everluting Arms beneath That lighten'd even the load of linath.

T%re is war in Warrington, between the twcoP-rs—the Police and Perambtalators ; • the "three R's" are nowhere in the running for public attention, and "the Wks of the Roses," are for a time entirel7 forgotten; VALIANT ROBERTUS has tried to stop people' from proceeding to bowl along the public footpath, and we believe he can lay claim te having ..4 frightened two nurse girls and one timid old woman into moving on -Alen, and where, and how he pleased; .but the cry is "Still they come," and. the " intelligent officer "'is beginning to End that tha Peram- bulators-are altogether too many for him; be has tackled the Perambulator, and fiat's that he has caught a Tartar. It seemed. asimple thing to carry out the instructions of the Chief Constable to "take the names of people with Perambulators, and warn, them off, the footpath ;" but what if they wouldn't' go!, Were they to "wallop them.,?: No, no, no. They could 'not be taken to the stable, or given corn, and the question was—what Was to be done? The obvious course was to , summon those who were guilty. of an infrac:, tion of the law. But was there an infraction r There was the rub. Mr. Hunt isa courageous, but it the same time he is a •discreet officer,' and displayed some faculty for diplomacy in not, in the &I'm instance, going beyond ,it re-- porting" those who were regarded as, the offenders. And there was a goodly, numb of them; no fewer than 44 'cases being before the- Watch Committee. If these gentlemen had said—" Let them go with al warning, but summon all offenders for the future," there would have been apretty-to-de The women, of Warrington would,.Wr,?. believe, have "risen as. one malt.,, and fought for women's, nurse-girls', ana' children's rights. But they are sensible men, these members-of the Watch,Committee, not. unmindful ofr fair play and curtain lectures, and the result was that, so. far as they are concerned, the order was. given that so lonir as people "moved along the footpath!' withi perambulators they were not to be interfere& with. They, may take the footpath,;. but they must "move on." This is, we: venture to say, as it should be; it would be, an act el folly to insist on perambulators.keeping to the' narrow street under all circumstance:---a step' which would be instantly regretted, w'nen, would most likely have happened, "An. in- fant had. its little life crushed, out." Still,. there is the question of Obstruction, and that, fortunately, can be minimised in Warringtort rather more easily than appears to. be. possible' at Westminster. The Chief-Constable has' set his mind upon it, and he is more poW,er" fill in his way than the Prime IVLinistet. believe in the progress of Pedestrians, as- VielL as Politicians; and welcome all reasonable efforts to clear the way. There can be 11° question that Perambulators are in some cases. an obstruction in our narrow busy thorough: 'fares, and, when this is apparent, the Chief"' Constable, who evidently knows the law, has only to insist in his men doing their duty. Fie was quite right' in issuing a summons in the case heard before the Mayor on Monday. le this instance the perambulator was allowed t°, "stand on the footpath for five minutes, and there was not the all-extenuating excuse of "the blessed baby." It contained provi; vions ; and if a perambulator may be wheeleu about and left on the footpath as a conver7 ance for provisions, why not a wheelbarroW • The line must be drawn somewhere, and vre see no hardship in a small pbnalty being itn" posed in a case of this kind. There must be_ temperance in all things, and suffering shill and tortured toes would say, if they cotilu speak—" Especially in the use of Perambe" lators."

Conservative speakers had a good deal to s i ay about their principles at the ward meet i' ng n Warrington on Wednesday evening,: but the puzzle is, in the cloud of words,Lt: find the principles. Captain Litton, '011; led off as chairman, made some ha% allusions to Protection, and a subsequen' !palter "bettered the instruction" by Olt; ing to show how much better off peoP'; were in "the good old times "—before tll,- days of Free Trade—than was commoincli supposed This seemed definite enough, a° f the unbiassed elector, in the pursuit ° knowledge under difficulties, would natural conclude that Protection was a Conservattle principle. But the next speaker, Mr. Georg, Woods, rode a horse of another c010n,,.. and challenged all comers in the narae Free Trade. Others who succeeded expressed themselves as Free Traders ; 01,4 the audience, " mightly impartial," if °rot very clear as to principles, cheered del Free Trade as loudly as they had aPPlauk•so the references to Protection. The Franco?„, Bill vtas commented upon in an equally To definite fashion; it was right enough t° way, but they wanted Redistribution so well. These hungry Conservatives ar°4o eager in the matter that they will not 11"
I
J
vfn man,' , and men.
I

the admittedly excellent dinner which is set before them until tea is also provided! That is their excuse for not lending a hand in the great work of Reform which is now before the country, and Councillor Francomb inad- vertently let the cat out of the bag when he Spoke of the "humbugging Franchise Bill, which nobody wanted ta know anything about." This is how Conservatives venture to refer to the outcome of the loud and long demand of non-electors for the rights of citizenship; the measure which would taise them from the position of serfs to that of free men is a "humbugging Franchise Bill." Is this, we wauld ask, one of those "principles of the Conservative party" of which workingmen are expected to become enamoured? Humbugging! The humbugs are those who pretend to be in favour of an extended suffrage, and then, when the time arrives for doing something, block the way With "words, words, words"—striving with blight and main to prevent the Franchise Bill becoming law. Sir Gilbert Greenall, in whose interest this meeting was held, Was more guarded in his utterance; he ' probably more successful in concealing than in expressing his thoughts. He certainly said that he "venerated Mr. Gladstone," a Sentiment which was deservedly cheered; but all the grace was gone out of the com- pliment in face of the fact that he had already spoken of the " chicanery " of the Reform Bill. Now, as this measure was introduced by Mr. Gladstone, Sir Gilbert will perhaps be good enough to explain how Iht manages to reconcile it with his idea of decency to venerate a man who is guilty of "chicanery." It would be un- fortunate, would it not, if the electors of North-West Ward were left to infer that the veneration of chicanery is another of the "Conservative principles" they are being called upon to support? Sir Gilbert's speech —if we may dignify his small talk with such a title—was a riddle in its way which con- tained a riddle. "Why," he asked, "was Mr. Gladstone like jam ?" And when they " gave it up," he answered, "Because he had so many jars in his Cabinet." Sir • Gilbert has evidently missed his vocation. • What a capital corner man he would make for the Christy Minstrels! He must keep "keep it up." And to this end we respect- fully offer kim a riddle or two Why are • Conservative principles themselves like a ?—Answer:riddle Because they will not hold water. z. Why is Sir Gilbert like a • holly bush? Answer: Because he is de- cidedly "Green all ',' the year round. This has nothing to do with politics, of course, but then the ex-member for Warrington is ' not a politician.
