BEIINSWICI MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CIASS.—At the weekly meeting of the members of this class at Runcorn, on Wednesday, Mr. Duncombe Pink, F.R.H.S ,of Leigh, lec- tured upon "The origin of some of our governing families." There was a good attendance, and a vote of thanks was Passed to the lecturer on the motion of Mr. Shores, seconded by Mr. Craig. Smairr ACCIDINT.—On Saturday afternoon, near the Royal Hotel, a girl, named Finegan, was knocked down and run over by a cart belonging to Mr. George Gorat, grocer. One of the wheels passed over her right arm, which was Seriously injured, and her face also was hurt. She was taken into the shop of Messrs. Smith and Co., druggists, where her wounds were dressed. HUTCHINSON-STRBE PRIMITIVR METHODIST CHAPEL.— The juvenile members of the Band of Hope in connection With this chapel at Widnes gave an entertainment to a good audience on Thursday evening. A programme, consisting of songs, recitations, &c, was gone through in good style. Mr. Elijah Seddon occupied the chair, and delivered an ad- dress in favour of temperance principles. INRUEST.—At the Market Gate Hotel, Widnes, on Mon- day, Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an in- quest touching the death of the illegitimate child of a Young woman named Mary Ellen Divine. Since its birth on the sth of March the child had been in a delicate stairs, and on Saturday morning it died suddenly at the house if Mrs. Burns, at 21, Railway-street, where the mother had been staying. A verdict to the effect that death remitted from convulaioas was returned. A !Unarm Escars.—Whilst walking along the pier at Runcorn on Saturday a boy named Albert Rowe, living at Halton, fell into the river. The tide was on the ebb and flowing swiftly at the time, but the boy had the presence of mind to throw himself On his back, aad he floated down by the side of the wall. A rope was thrown to him, but he was unable to grasp it, and a sailor belonging to one of the schooners in the dock then descended the wall and pulled him out. Some boatmen provided him with a dry suit of Clothes, and he returned home little worse for the immer- sion. Toxic 50r.4.1. Cuss.—The pupils attending this class gave a concert in Ellesmere-street Schoolroom, Runcorn, on Monday evening. There.was a good audience. Mr. John Holford, who has efficiently filled the position of instructor, waa unable to take his place owing to illness, and Mr. Mar- low undertook the onerous duties of conductor. The class gave several part songs in a manner which testified to the thoroughness of their training, and the following ladies and gentlemen contributed songs :—Mies Curzon, Miss E. D. Wright, Miss Marlow, and Miss Jones, Messrs. H. Johnson, R. Moore, and A. Fox. Miss M. Wright, Miss Leadbetter, and Messrs. Ince and T. Fox took part in trios and quartets. SERIOI7B ACCIDENT TO Ma. J. W. LIGHTBI7RN, OW RUN- R 2 --An accident attended with serious results betel Mr. J. W. Lightburn, accountant, Higher Runcorn, on Setae day last. Mr. Lightburn left home about eight o'clock with the intention of visiting his brother at Weston; to discuss eorne business matters. In order to reach his destination he Was compelled to pass along Chesharre's-lane, upon one side of which is a high parapet, avoided by pedestrians, and on the other a declivity of about 12 feet. In avoiding the parapet Mr. Lightburn, who is very near sighted, approached !;e3 near the edge of the declivity, and was precipitated .to !.le bottom. For an hour he lay there in an unconscious. tate.. and on regaining his senses he crawled on his knees to his brother's house, about 200 yards distant. lie was afterwards conveyed home and attended by Dr. Robinson. It is feared that his spine is seriously injured, and the ser- vices of Dr. Owen Thomas of Liverpool, have been obtained, and everything done for the alleviation of his sufferings. Although a fatal result is not apprehended, a considerable time will necessarily elapse before he is restored to health, and he is being attended with sedulous care. Much sym- pathy is expressed for the injured gentleman. A fence, it is alleged, at one time protected the "cliff," but the rails have been broken down, and there is now absolutely no protection for either pedestrians or vehicles. We under- stand that accidents have on several occasions occurred at the snot. A RUNCORN PUBLICAN F 1 lions on Monday, John West,Nßl).--At Runcorn Petty See- landlord of the Duke of Wel- lington Inn, Percivals charged with having at five minutes to midnight on was 25th March, opened his premises for the sale of intoxicattrianvgolllei;moorra, to wit, beer, orison lod- ging a person not being a bona fide therein. lie was also charged will: selllnp a bona fide traveller ting liquor to a person not being lOD lodging in the house. The defendant pleaded not rgauiltyr- -mr. W. H. Linaker, who appeared for the defendant, asked the Bench to amend the summons. He would plead guilty to allowing liquors to be consumed in the house during pro- hibited hours. A captain who was about to leave the town left a pint of beer at the bouse for a man who had been working for him and who was accustomed to call at the Wellington Inn. The man went to the house after eleven o'clock, and was supplied with beer. The defendant was equally liable to be convicted for opening and far for selling, but he (Mr. Linaker) would prefer that the con- viction should take place on the actual facts instead of the summonees served, and if the Bench would so amend the summons the defendant would plead guilty.—lnspector Hollingsworth had no objection to this course, and the Bench therefore amended the summons. The defendant pleaded guilty. Inspector Hollings- worth said the defendant was now charged with allowing his premises to be used for the consumption of liquor. On the night in question, Constables Noden and Kelly were concealed in the backyard of the public house, and about ten minutes to twelve, fifty minutes after the time ef closing, they saw a man named Snapes go to the back door. After looking round to see if there was any Person near, he called out "Jack, let's have a pint!' The door was opened, the man went in, and Constable Noden through the window saw the man &apes supplied with a pint of beer which he drank. Before, however, he could emerge from the house Constable Kelly knocked knocked at the doer and entered the house. In the meantime the man went lute another room, and the jag from which be had drank the beer was removed.—Mr. Linaker having addressed the Bench, Inspector Hollingsworth remarked:that this kind of illicit business was becoming rather frequent.—Mr. U. Reynolds said the Bench had decided to fine the defendant 20i and costs 14s, and warned him that his license would be endorsed if he was again convicted.—James Snape, a boat- man was then charged with being on the premises during Prohibited hours, and P.C. Noden having stated the facts he was fined 51 and costs 98 6d.

Haw POORS' RATE FOR WIDNES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the magistrate laid a poors' rate of 2s. in the J 3 for Widnes, on the application of Mr. Goff, the assistant overseer. The rate for last year was 2s. 6d. in the S. The present rate is estimated to realise £12,600. EVADING THE EXCISE AT RUNCORN.—At Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Thomas Cliffs, contractor, Green- way-road, John Sheldon (who did not appear), and Walter Timmins, engineer, were each fined 5s and coste 106 63, for keeping dogs without a licence. The Ca 81321 were proved by P.C.'. Morris and Steen. MISSIONARY MINTING AT FARNWORTIL—Tbe annual meeting of the Farnworth branch of the Church Missionary Society was held on Saturday evening, when there was a good audience, presided over by the Rev. Geo. Bond. The Rev. S. Coles, deputation from the society, delivered an ad- dress, and the Rev. S. A. Spooner and the Rev. J. Holden also spoke. The collectione amounted to £23 9s. 54. BAND OF HOPE MERTING.—The last meeting of the season in connection with the St. John's Band of Hope was held on Tuesday evening, when a varied and interesting pro- gramme was gone through in a creditable manner by the members, the chief feature of the evening being a humorous dialogue, entitled "Apartments to Let," which reflected great credit on the performers. The tea meeting for the members was also held the same evening, when over 100 sat down, and did full justice to the provision made for their enjoyment. SCALDED TO DEATIL—Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner, held an inquest, on Saturday, at the Widnes Acci- dent Hospital, on the body of Michael Slowev. 26 years of age, who was scalded at the British Alkali Works, on the Wednesday at noon, and died at the hospital on the Thurs- day evening. Mr. C. H. Lewin was present on behalf of the works. Evidence was given by Julia Kennion, of 36, Eleanor-street; Joseph Weldon, 31, Albert-road, Appleton, fitter at the Alkali Works ; and Mies Downie, matron at the hospital, bearing out the facts as already published. Tie jury returned a verdict of accidental death, and did not at- tribute blame to any one. A COLLISION ON TDB MERSEY AT WESTON POINT.— Early on Thursday morning navigation on the Mersey was mach impeded by a dense fog that covered the river and the adjacent country. about five o'clock the data Florence and Cairo, belonging re- p. ctively to the Cheshire Amalgamated Salt Company and Mr. H. E. Falk, left the river Weaver at Weston Point, laden • ith salt, for Liverpool. Whea op. posite Hale Head the b rges collided, the Cairo being dam. aged to such an extent that she sank in a few minutes. Fortunately the captain, ais wife and family, and mate had been taken on board the Florence, or it is probable they would have been drowned. Owing to the dense atmosphere a considerable number of flats were unable to keep to the deep, and went aground on the sandbanks, where they were compelled to wait for the returning tide. EXCITING SCENE IN RUNCORN.—A scene of much ex- citement was witnessed in Bridge-street, on Monday morn- ing. A larry, laden with flour from Sutton Mills, was being drawn down Bridge-street with three powerful horses, and the driver after passing Wilson's Hotel commenced to put on the brake. Through the breaking of a bolt the brake would not act, and the heavy wagon moved down the steep decline, pushing the shaft horse against the leaders, and they rushed down the street at a fearful speed. The driver courageeuely seized hold of the shaft horses's head, and one of the chains fastening the leaders to the shafts becoming unfastened, he, with great presence of mind, unhooked the other, and the animals thus liberated rusheck, down Mersey- street, where they were stopped by Mr. F. Yarwood. The driver guided the Larry, which was travelling at a great rate past various obstacles, and sacceeded in bringing it to a standstill at the incline near Mr. Crowley'e shop without any accident having occurred. HARTLAND WESLEYAN CHAPEL, WIDNES:4D Sid of the building fund of this chapel a concert, under influential patronage, was given in the Volunteer Hall on Monday. The spacious building was filled from end to end with a sympathetic and appreciative audience, and the VariOUS items of an excellent programme were heartily enjoyed. The vocalists were Mies Jennie Owen, of Holywell ; Mies Kate Meredith, of the Liverpool and Birkenhead concerts; Mr. Eos. Mortals, tenor; and Mr. Eaton Batty, bass; who have all achieved considerable popularity amongst the musical quidnunc' of Widnes. Miss Owen sang with her usual felicity of expression and power the songs" Hopes and fears," "When the heart is young," and Ganz's Sing sweet bird," and she was thrice recalled. For her render- ing Of the songs "Waiting," " Home" and "Daddy," Miss Merideth received the hearty plaudits of the audience; whilst Mr. Batty was highly successful in his interpretation of the songs placed to his name, viz,, "The raft," "The desert," and the Toreador's song from Bizet's opera of "Carmen." Mr. Eos. Mortals was heard at his best, and his rendering of Handel's: "How vain is man," and Cowen's "Children's home," and " Ainabella Lee," left nothing to be desired. Miss M. E. Evans, who acted ably as accom- panist, also favoured the audience with two exhibitions of her skill as a musician in the solos "Balmoral" and "Pasquinade." During the ev ii the Star of Temper- ance Brass Band gave several selections of music in unim- peachable style. Mr. E. Carey was the chairman. It is gratifying to be able to state that the funds will be largely augumented. ATTEMPT TO DEFRAUD THE RAILWAY COMPANY AT WIDIES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, before Mr. John Brock and Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, junr., James Logan, a young man, was summoned to answer a charge of having, on the 19th March, attempted to avoid the payment of his railway fare by travelling on the London and North-Western Railway from St. la dens to Ditton. He was also further charged with committing a nuisance in the railway carriage.—Mr. Preston, jour., of the solicitors' department, Lime-street Station, prosecuted, and Informed the Bench that ,they had power to inflict a penalty of 40s and costs on each charge. On the 19th March,j when the 2-25 p.m. train from St. Helens to Ditton arrived ' at Farnwortb, the attention of the guard was called to a third-class compartment in which were the defendant and two women. The women complained that the defendant, , who was in a beastly state of drunkenness, had committed a ' nuisance in the carriage, and the guard placed them in another compartment. On the arrival of the train at Ditton, it was found that the defendant had neither ticket nor money, and when asked to leave the carriage he was very abusive to the officials. The guard noticed that the defendants dress was disarranged.—William Higham, guard, was called, and confirmed the statement.—Mr. Brock said the Bench were bound to protest the public from people committing nuisances of this description, and the defendant was fined 20s. and costs 12s. for committing the nuisance, and 103. aid costs 12s. on the charge of travelling without a ticket, in all £2 143. In default of payment the defendant was sentenced to 21 days' imprisonment. ALLEGED OUTRAGE ON A DOMESTIC SERVANT. —At Runcorn Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. James Handley, George Brimelow, fish dealer, Bridge-street, was charged under a warrant with indecently assaulting Riles.- beth Langford, his domestic servant, who is 21 years of age. Evidence was given by the prosecutrix, Joseph Brimelow, the prisoner's son, Isaac Bradbury, a lodger, and Sergeant McMichael. It appeared that the pri- soner has been addicted to drinking to excess for a number of years, and the business had to a great extent been car- ried on by his wife. Langford had lived at the shop as domestic servant for seven years, and on Wednesday after- noon, the 19th March, Mrs. Brimelow went out, leaving her in charge. There were also in the house Bradbury and the son Joseph. Langford went upstairs to clean a bedroom, and she had been so occupied for about an hour, when the prisoner made his appearance at the door. He said "Will you give me my trousers." Langford understood that he wished for a better pair of trousers than those he was wear- ing, but Mrs. Brimelow always kept his clothes under lock and key to prevent him from pawning them in order to ob- tain money to bay beer. Langford replied that she could not give him the trousers without her mistress's consent, and he left the room. In a few minutes be returned,walked up to Langford, and committed the assault with which he was charged. She threatened that she would tell "the missus," but Bradbury persuaded her not to do so. A few days afterwards, in consequence of his conduct, she informed her mistress of what had taken place, and a warrant was issued for his apprehension. He was apprehended by P.S. McMichael.—The priaoner, who made no defence, was com- mitted to the Knutsford Quarter Sessions for trial. Roarcosor SCHOOL BOARD. The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the offices, Bridgewater- street, on Wednesday. The Rev. Canon Barclay presided, and there were present the Rev. Father Fennelly, Messrs. Briscoe, Lea, G. Hazlehurst, and F. Rigby (clerk). The Accommodation Question—A New School Projected: The Chairman observed that the first business of the meet- ing was to consider whether it was best to adopt Mr. Bris- coe's suggestion to convert Mill Brow Board School into • standard school.—The Clerk said the inspector seemed to a an view, ienw used d as a is t think that it would be a good thing for Mill Brow School to ee clerk) retained a held the th it e w same s he infantul d savacehthoeole.xpenHsee attending the alterations and would be convenient for the neighbourhood. In one • litle room where the gallery was there were now 60 infanta crowded—Father Fennelly: The inspector has condemned that. —The it officially in his report.—The Visit or Clerk: (M : He condemned they were constantly turning infants away fr.r Bowyer) said ill Brow School, upon which Father Fennelly remseodnithaMt t v an argument why it should be kept as an infant school.—vas Mr. Briscoe said that in 1878 there were 808 boats registered In 'Runcorn, and of these about 200 were manned by "Duke's flatmen." Many of these had houses in Run- corn.—The Clerk inquired how many of the boats actually I belonged to Runcorn 7—Mr. Briscoe could not answer that' question. Many of the registrations had lapsed, so that there were fewer than 806 now.—The Clerk said as far as providing school accommodation for boat children went, if the Board could show that many of the boats had no direct connection with Runcorn, they would not have to provide accommodation for them. The Canal Boats Act distinctly said where the boat was registered there should accommo- dation be provided, but no one had dared to put that Act in force. He thought they would have no difficulty in proving that it would be a hardship to provide accommodation for more than the children on 200 boats, because there was nothing to prevent any London boat being registered at Run- corn.—After some further conversation it was resolved that it was expedient to provide accommodation for 200 girls, 200 first standard mixed, and 200 boys , • that it was advis- able to secure a central site capable of taking one building to provide accommodation for 600 children, distributed as in the preceding resolution' and, further, that it would be necessary when the new schools were opened to convert the Board School at Mill Brow into a school for infants. Several sites for the new school were suggested, and the Board de- cided to inspect them at some future day, and instructed the clerk to invite the architect to meet the members at the next
meeting.

OPENING OF A QUARET AT RUNCORN.—Ia the course of a few days Messrs. Brundrit and Hayes intend to re-open a quarry at Higher Runcorn that has been closed for some time. A manager has been engaged, and there will be cur pleyment for about 70 men. WIDNES BRANCH OF THE C.E.T.S At the weekly meeting of this society, held in the National Schools, on Thursday evening, Mr. Frank Cave, the secretary, delivered the remaining portion of his lecture on "Reminiscences of the Indian Mutiny." He narrated in a graphic manner various incidents in the campaign, in several of which he had taken part, and he was frequently applauded. At the close the Rev. Hamilton Wilson delivered an address, urging the members not to rest until they had succeeded in closing the public houses in Widnes. He moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Cave for his lecture, Mr. Foley, Scripture reader,

pro .. the.llll ST. JOHN'S RAND OF Mom—The members entertainment of the season on Tuesday night, in Scheol•room, Runcorn. Mr. Wm. Leach occupied the chairs I 23i the programme of songs and recitations was creditabfl gone through by the children of the society. LECTURE ON Inatawra—Under the auspices of the Iristi Society a lecture was delivered in Holy Trinity Schoof,. Runcorn, on Monday, by the Rev. Dr. Porter. The Rev. W. Preston presided. The lecture, which was on the subject of" Irish scenery and legends," was illustrated by views , thrown upon a screen by a powerful magic lantern. SONS MIT TEMPERANCE.—With the object of raising funds for the annual treat, the lifeboat crew division of the Sons of Temperance gave an entertainment in Regeat-street School, Runcorn, on Thursday evening. There was a large audience present, and the various items in a long pro- gramme were heartily appreciated. Mr. S. Coventry pre- sided. WIDENS FOOTBALL Cum.—ln a severe thunderstorm on Thursday evening the first team of the Widnes Football Club played a team brought together by Mr. T. R. Sutton, of Manchester, at Peelhouse-lane. As was to be expected, there were few spectators, but the game was splendidly con- tested, and ended in a draw, each team scoring one try and five minor points. WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL UNION—The annual meet- ing was held on Monday evening:in the large class room, Brunswick-street, Runcorn. The Hey. E. J. Robinson was in the chair, supported by the Rev. S. Mess. The report was read by one of the secretaries (Mr. S, Pope), showing that there are on the books of these schools 2,259 scholars. The meeting was a very interesting and successful one. APPOINTMENT OF OVERSEERS AT RUNCORN.—At Run- corn Petty Sessions, on Monday, the magistrates, Messrs. H. Reynolds and James Handley, appointed the overseers as follows :—Rancorn : William Handley, William Whittaker; Aston-by-Sutton: George Percival, William Wilkinson; Aston Grange: George Percival, William Wilkinson; Clif- ton: William Baker, Joseph Stokes; Stockham: Joseph W. Baguley and Daniel T. Baguley; Nertan ; Thomas Per- cival, Clement Baguley; Sutton : William Lowe, Thomas Rigby; Weston: Edward Aaron, Themes Ford; Halton: Thomas Wright and Hugh Rowe. ELECTION OF GUARDIANS AT RUNCORN.—OIIt of the many townships in the Runcorn Union contests only take place at Runcorn and Weston. For the five vacant seats that Runcorn is required to fill, 14 candidates were nomina- ted, but this number has been greatly reduced by with- drawals, and the election now lies between the following gentlemen :—Messrs. W. Whittaker, W. Handley, T. Nor- man, P. Speakman, S. Taylor, if. White, W. Fisher, and J. Williams. The first four are at present members of the Board, and until twelve months ago Mr. Fisher occupied a seat, and it is the general opinion that those five gentle- men will be the chosen of the ratepayers. It is understood that the members of the Ratepayers' Association, whilst not taking any official part in the election, will use their in- fluence in favour of Mr. W. Handly, who was last year second on the list as their nominee. The voting papers will be distributed on Monday, callected on Tuesday, and the votes will be counted at Dutton Workhouse on Wednes- diy. Mr. H. Linaker, clerk to the union, is the returning officer. The gentlemen who have withdrawn their nomina- tions are Messrs. F. Fairhurst, W. J. Wigg, Dr. Steele, E I Imison, J. N. Lello, and G. Bellamy.

BRUTAL CRUELTY TO • HORSOI AT RUNCOB/L—John Mulhall, a carter, from Warrington, was brought before the Runcorn magistrates on Monday charged with cruelly ill- treating a horee.—From the evidence of P.C. Ronson*, it appeared that on the evening of the 24th March, the defen- dant was in charge of a horse and cart in Percival's-lane. After a load of ropes had been removed, and a start wai about to be made, the horse fell down and broke the shaft. The defendant kicked the horse savagely en the head with his foot, exclaiming that he would not be able to go to Warrington that night. The constable said the horse, wkich was in a poor and weak condition, was owned by the de. fendant's brother—Defendant: I am very sorry for it. I atm out of work now.—Mr. Reynolds: Serve you right, ton are not fit to be in charge of a horse.—The defendant was fined £1 and costs 15s, or in default a month's hard

labour. A YOUNG RUNCORN THIEF INGENIOUSLY EXPLAINS.- At Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday, before Captain C. W. Hautehorst and Mr. G. L. Davies, William Smith, 14 years of age, who lives on one of Mr. S. Taylor's flats, was charged with having on the previous day stolen 41bs. pt rope, the property of the River Weaver Navigation Com- pany. About seven o'clock on Wednesday evening William Hough, watchman for the River Weaver Navigation Com- pany, was standing en the river wall at Weston Point, when he saw the prisoner go to an engine that was working there and pick something up. The prisoner placed it in a bag, and the watchman upon making an examination found the rope produced.-The prisoner said he was taking it to a flat. P.C. Finney took charge of the prisoner, who now stated that a man en board a flat under the crane shouted to him to fetch the rope, and he was doing so when Hough stopped him. H. told Hough to go to the fiat, but he would not do so.-Hugh denied that there was anybody on the flat.- The prisoner stated he should know the man again, and the Bench remanded him for inquiries to be made. In the after- noon he was again brought before the Bench, and Superin- tendent Williamson said it had been discovered that there were no persons on board the flat at the time stated by the boy.-The prisoner was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod. WIDNES LOCAL BOARD ELECTION. Yesterday, when the voting papers were collected, this election practically closed. The rival Ratepayers' Assacia- tions have conducted the contest with vigour. Accusations and counter accusations have been poured from the local printing presses, and the walls and hoardings of the town are almost covered with electioneering literature. During the past week canvassers have been very busily occupied on behalf o! all the candidates, and the footsteps of Vie distributors of voting pipers were followed by quite a small army of these gentlemen. Perhaps least has been heard of the candidature of Mr. Quinn, but the Catholic population is to a great extent plumping for him, and the prevailing feeling is tkat his name will occupy a kighly-respectable position when the result of the contest is made known. We understand, how- ever, that should he be so fortunate as to be elected his qualification for the position will be testel—The votes will be counted at the Local Board offices ti-day (Saturday), and it is expected that the result will be publtsked in the evening.

1. ke MA:mama FROM Surrow.—Before Captain C W Bazlehurst and Mr G L Davies, John Lockett was brought up at Runcorn Police Court, on Thursday afternoon, charged with having on the let inst. stolen six sheets, six blankets, twelve knives and forks, and sundry other articles, the property of William Povey. The prosecutor said he was a labourer and lived at Sutton, near Frodsham Bridge. The prisoner had lodged with him for seine time. On the let April he (the prosecutor) went to his work about four o'clock in the morning, leaving his wife and seven children at home, and everything appeared as usual. The prisoner was a watchman at Weston Charcoal Works, was on night duty, and therefore not in the house. He (the prose:odor) did not return home until eight o'clock in the evening, when he found the house had been ransacked of its contents, and his wife and children were not to be found. Upon inquiry he learnt that the prisoner had been seen re- moving goods from the house, and that his wife and family had then departed with him to Manchester. He (prosecutor) informed the police of what had taken place, and took out a warrant for the prisoner's apprehension. On Thursday morning he went with P.C. Egerton to Manchester, and there found his wife and family living with the prisoner, who was taken into custody by the constable and brought ito Runcorn. The prisoner was remanded until Monday to enable the police to tiring witnesses from Manchester. We understand that the faithless wife was in court during the hearing of the case, and had piomieed to return home with her husband.

FRBB LIBRARY Coancrrrna.—The monthly meeting was held on Thursday afternoon in the Commissioners' Board Room, the Rev. Canon Barclay presiding. There were also present Messrs. Briscoe, Lake, Handley, Simpson, Riley, and Jones (librarian and secretary).—Lararian's Report: The Librarian reported that during March there had been 1,460 books borrowed from the lending department, being a de- crease of 118 on the corresponding period last year. From tbe reference department there had been borrowed 74 volumes. The books were classified as follows: Theology 21, philosophy, political economy, &c., 10, history, rayels, and biography 149, science and art 50, poetry and the drama 17, prose fiction 1,203, miscellaneous 84. The receipts for the month amounted to £3 10s. Mr. James Handley, J.P., had presented a revolving book case. Mr. Simpson four volumes and several pamphlete, Mr. J. H. Harrison several numbers of Belgravta, Dr. Bagnall "Phantom Fortune," and Mr. T. Rigby, Sutton," Frodsham; a historical lecture."--The Accounts: The financial state- ment for the past year was submitted by the Librarian and showed that there was a balance in hand of £25 10s. The recetpts included £4 17s 3d for the sale of borrowers' tickets, and £lO 14s 83 for fines. In the expenditure were the following amounts .—New books £67 3s, magazines £5 3s 10d, advertising 8s 63, salaries £3O, binding books £2O 17s Ild. stationery £lB 4s 6d, sundries £B4a 7d, total £l5O 12s 43.—0 n the motion of Mr. Handley, seconded by Mr. Riley, it was decided that application should be made to the commissioners for the balance of the rate for the past year.—There was no other business. There were pre- sent the Rev J Lockwood, Messrs .1 Knowles, W Pickering. After a great deal of trouble they suc- ceeded in getting the clauses submitted to the Board at the last meeting. There was only ene alteration, which was that the matter of way leave, if any, should be left to the Local Government Board. The Clerk: It was left to the Local Government Board if, after taking into consideration i all the circumstances of the case, they considered that the I Ship Canal were entitled to it. The chairman observed that the clerk had been put to some expense in connection with the work, and he moved that a cheque for £5O on account be signed. The cheque was signed. In reply to .the charge he said, "Yes, I know I did, but he kicked at me be- ttors I kicked him."—Mr. Swift addressed the magistrate on behalf of the prisoner, and submitted that this was an im- proper case to be sent to the Sessions. He suggested that the best and proper course would be to remand the prisoner to Wednesday next, so that the magistrates if they thought proper could deal with the case as a common assault. The officer appeared to have made a mistake in charging the prisoner with unlawfully wounding. It was clear that the prisoner could not be convicted on that charge, because there was no wound in existence, and it was not even proved that he had inflicted grievous bodily harm.—The magistrate , thought there was a case for trial, and the prisoner was for- mally committed to Liverpool Quarter Sessions.

The hint appears to have been acted on in Newton, and already we believe that steps have been taken towards forming a branch, to be held at the Congre- gational School, Crow-lane._

EABLISTOWN AND NEWTON lINITZD TIDIPERAIII MOVEMENT.—A meeting of the committee of the Earle-- town and Newton United Bands of Hope and Temperance Societies was recently held in the Good Templars lodge. room, Bridge-street. The secretary (Mr. J. H. Graham) presented a report referring to the recent week's special temperance mission in Earlestown. The question of holding the annual united demonstration was mooted, but after some discussion it was decided to re-consider it at the next monthly meeting. ()Berm:Tarim* TI!! HIGHWAT.—At the Newton Petty Sessions, on Saturday last, James Lawrenson was summoned for obstructing the highway at Newton, on the 25th ult. The defendant pleaded guilty.—P.S. Commins stated that in consequence of the coursing meeting at Ilaydock Park on the date named there were between 30 and 40 convey- ances standing in Mill-lane. A little after eleven o'clock in the forenoon a crowd of persons came from the railway Mation, and the defendant in his eagerness to get passengers drew into the middle of the road, which was completely blocked thereby.—The defendant was fined 5s and costs. THR CHURCH DISPUTE AT EASILBSTORX.—No agreement has yet been come to between the parties who have been connected with the dispute which has existed at St. John's Church, Earlestown, for a considerable time past. The ser- vices on Sunday last were again of an unusual character. Though the choir was in attendance, there was not the least attempt at singing; no hymns were given out, and there were but few responses to the prayers, ac., on the part of the congregation. In the forenoon, when the Vicar (the Rev. T. R. Matthews) entered the pulpit to preach, a num- ber of persons, including the sidesmen, left the church. In the evening the preacher was the Rev. H. E. Smith (curate), but the service was of the same character as that of the forenoon. On both oocasions the organist (Mr. R. a Durman) occupied a seat among the choir.

This year Mr. Waterhouse, whose works are certainly not un- known, seems to be absorbing the attention and respect of his brother artiste, who predict for him a brilliant career. He has gone back to the early Israelite days for his subject, which is called "Tb. Oracle." A Hebrew prophetess is exercising the rites of sorcery with a ghastly head that has booziest off for the purpose of divination, according to notes from the works of Talmudic commentators respecting the makers of Toraphim, or Juinan household gods, of which for accounts are extant. The moment chosen is when the grim face is supposed to be interpreting its utterances, and Israelite maidens surround it with looks of terror and ex- pectation. The subject will scarcely be a congenial one to live with; bat every purchaser of pictures has his own idea of what the province of art should be, just as in the theatrical world there are votaries of tragedy and comedy. _ The annual meeting of members for the election of I officers for the next twelve months was held at Wilson's Hotel, Bridge-street, last evening. There was a good at- tendance, and Mr. J. R. Frith, the president, occupied the chair.—ln a short address. the Chairman said it afforded birn great pleasure to meet them on that occasion, knowing that the first team had not been beaten during the season, and he believed that the second /earn had only been con- quered on one occasion.—Mr. W. Pownall moved that Mr. J. R. Frith be re-elected president.—Mr. Brody seconded the motion, which was carried with acclamatien.-The Chair- man thanked the audience.—The following gentlemen were elected vice-presidents :—Messrs. J. Brundrit, J.P., C. Hazle- hurst, J.P., G. L. Wigg, E. A. Charlton, W. D. Jolliffe, F. A. Lake, J. Handley, J. Meadowcroft, F. Fairhurst, W. Towns, S. Pope, W. Timmins, and A. Timmins. Messrs. C. Pownall, J. E. Longshaw, and H. Wright, were nom- inated for the office of secretary. On the ballot being taken Mr. Lonphaw was elected amid applause. -.- On the proposition of Mr. Longshaw, Mr. J. C. Pownall was unanimously appointed assistant secretary. For the office of treasurer Mr. Johnson was appointed. Mr. Hughes was re-elected captain of the first team, and Mr. W. Wright sub-captain. Mr. J. B. Clarke was appointed captain of the second team, and Mr. J. Gittens was elected sub-captain Mr. R. Hughes was unanimously elected umpire for the first team, and Mr. A. Riley for the second team. Messrs. W. B. Brimelow and W. Riley were appointed auditors. The committee was constituted as follows :-Messrs. H. Andrews, W. Hughes, J. Stubbs, J. Gatley, A. Lightburn, James Clarke, R. Roberts, T. Johnson, W. Dunb tvand, W. Brody, T. E. Booth, and H. Wright.-1 vote of thanks was ac- corded to the officers and to the chairman for their services during the past year.

BRUTAL ASSLULT AT DITTON.—TRE PRISONER COMMITTED. Before Mr. Holbrook Gaskell, jun., at Widnes Police Court, on Thursday, John Mallett, a labourer, was brought up, oa remand, charged with having, on the 15th March, unlawfully wounded Patrick Brophy, a labourer, living in Johnson-street, Ditton.—Mr. J. 0. Swift appeared for the prisoner.—On the day in question Mallett and Brophy were drinking together in the Blackburne Arms, when the former began " humbugging " the latter about a man, named Collins. Brophy made no retort; but left the pre- mises, and visited the house of a man, named Jones. In a short time he returned to the Blackburne Arms. Mallett paid for him a pint of beer, which he drank, and then they left together. Brophy had no sooner got to the door than, according to his story, he became insensible. At this time, half-past four, Emma Wood, wife of Albert Wood, who lives in Duke-street, Ditton, heard a noise in the street, and she went to the door. The two men were quarrelling about the man Collins, and she retired inside. A few minutes after- wards she heard a scream, and she again went into the street, where she saw Mallett run to kick Brophy, but he failed to do so, and struck Brophy's mother, who was stand- ing near. With great violence Mallett then kicked Brophy on the lower part of the stomach ; the force of the blew causing him to fall to the ground. Mallett repeated the blow whilst Brophy lay upon the ground, and Brophy rising was again felled by a kick in the stomach. Mallett kicked him again, and then Mrs. Wood and her daughter and Mrs. Jones dragged Brophy into Mrs. Wood's house, where he remained for upwards of an hour in an insensible condition. Brophy informed the magis- trates that he did not remember anything that took place after he left the public-house. He had no injuries at that time, but when he regained consciousness at his own house, he had pains in his stomach and other parts of his body, and next day he had a pain in his left knee and the back of his head. For twelve days he was confined to his room, and he was taken to the workhouse hospital where he had re- mained until that morning. He still had pains in his stomach, and was very weak and unable to follow his em- ployment. He had had four pints of beer on the day of the assault, but was sober until he drank the pint paid for by the prisoner.—ln cross-examination by Mr. Swift, Brophy said he was not drunk when he left the public-house but he became insensible immediately after leaving. He had been drunk many times, and had been locked up for it.—Mr. Swift: Then it was a kind of fainting fit ? Brophy: Yes. All the time we were in the house we were good friends.— Emma Wood was examined, and gave evidence confirmatory of the above account. In answer to Inspector Wood she said the prisoner was quite sober, but Brophy seemed stupid. —Sarah Alice Wood, daughter of last witness gave corrobo- rative evidence, and a etatement of a similar character was made by Ann Jones, wife of William Janes, of Lugsdale- road, Widnes. On the day in question she was visiting Mrs.

But his just indignation has overshot the mark in his description of the World, and is calculated to create a revulsion of feeling in favour of the journal and its proprietor. The particular End of _paragraphe which form a portion of the weekly fare of the World, and which no one need read unlees they like, are contributed by the very class of society on whose behalf the Lord Chief Jus- tice puts lance in rest. If Mr. Yates liked to speak he could doubtless tell some moving stories of the intrigue, which members of the higher rank of society eater upon to get inserted in the World little paragraphs about themselves and their doings, "our lives and our movements, our drama recorded, OUI company catalogued, and our most private re - lotions dragged into the light of day "ad Lord Coleridge says. Liberals above all should not forget the great ser- vice the World did daring the Jingo days when, alone among high-class fashionable papers, it dared to question the semi-divinity of Mr. Disraeli, and bearded soziety in its drawing-room.

The people listened with deep interest to the address, whisi was pe7- tinent and forceful in Scripture illustrations. CROFT.

CONCERT AT THE CROFT BOARD SCHCOL.-In excellent and very successful concert was given in the above school- room on Friday evening. The artistes were again from Warrington, and Mr. George Riley was the accompanist and conductor. There was a good audience. The chairman, Mr. James Hatton, of Southworth Hall, made an appropriate address. A gavotte (piano and violin) by Messrs. Riley and Walsh, was followed by "Angels ever bright and fair," by Mrs. Walsh. Mr. Sherlock was heartily applauded for the well-known song "Sailing." "Come back to Eric" was excellently sung by Mrs. Dagnall. The comic song "Two spoons," by Mr. Mercer, called forth a hearty encore, in response to which "You get more like your dad every day," was given. Mr. Macauley's reading on "Gentlemen's names" greatly interested the audience. The "Maid of Athens," by Mr. Dell, was admirably rendered. Mies Cavanagh's " Saper Torestte" was heartily applauded, and Miss Horton and Mr. Mercer effectively sang the duet "Very suspicious." After a short interval Messrs Riley and Walsh opened the second part by giving a. selection of Scotch airs on the piano and violin in excellent style. MT. Sherlock was encored for his rendering of "Simon the cellarer," and responded by giving "The Friar of orders grey." Miss Cavanagh and Mr. Dell followed with the duet "Home to our mountains," which was well received. Mr. Mercer again came forward and ceased much merriment by naming several of the gentlemen in the district in his song "When the world's turned upside down ;" and was suc- ceeded by Mrs. DagnalL, who was enthusiastically applauded for the song "0 rosy morn." No less warmly received was the song "1 dreamt I dwelt in marble halls," which was ad- mirably sung by Mrs. Walsh. "Just as well" was excel- lently rendered by Miss Cavanagh, and the duet "Flower gatherers," was sung by the Misses L. and H. Horton in good style. "When ether lips and other hearts" was taste- fully sung by Mr. Dell, who was heartily applauded. The next, and last, " Tidings of comfort and joy," sang by Mr. Mercer in character, was encored. Votes of thanks to the vocalists, etc., brought the proceedings to a close. DA.RESBURY. HAYDOCK. Harnocx Locax BOARD.-A monthly meeting of the 'members of the Haydock Local Board, was held on Mon- day afternoon, when there were present :-Messrs. Thomas Jackson (in the chair), John Jackson, W. Balharry, Cun- life, and Thomas Turnbull (clerk). The minutes of the last meeting of the Board, aid also those of a special meet- ing, held on the 19th ult., were read, and on the motion of Mr. Balbarry, seconded by Mr. Cunliffe, were confirmed, with the exception of a minute relating to the Medical Officer's annual report, which it was decided to discuss at the next meeting.-Apnainfment of Medical Officer: Mr. John Jackson moved, and Mr. Balharry seconded, that Dr. J. W. Watkins be re-appointed medical officer of health for the ensuing year. The motion was adopted. - Water * Hayclock Lodge: The Clerk read a letter from Dr. Beaman, proprietor of the Ilaydeck Lodge Lunatic Asylum, asking the Board to lay down a service pipe to the asylum, on con- dition that he paid a small interest on the outlay. There was a supply of good water for domestic purposes, bat be required an additional supply to fall back upon in case of necessity. It was decided, on the motion of Mr. Balharry, seconded by Mr. Cualiffe, that a copy of the usual water charges should be forwarded to Dr. Beaman.-The Proposed Loan: The Clerk reported that he had received from the Local Government Board sanction to borrow £4OO, to cover expenses incurred in connection with the service reservoir. -This was the only business of interest. LYMM. Lyam LOCAL BOARD.-The ordinary meeting of this Board was held on Thursday evening, under the presidency of Mr. Cameron, the other members present being Messrs. Dewhurst, Rogers, Woolley, Gibson, Appleton, Thomason, Ridgway (clerk), and Mallard (assistant clerk).-It was decided that a general district rate of two , shillings in the pound be laid.-Mr. Griffiths, estate agent, Manchester, wrote on behalf of the trustem of the estate of the late C. F. Bennett, asking if the Local Board had any intention of widening both sides of Pepper-street, as his clients thought if the widening was only to extend to the strip of land belonging to them it would be no improve- meat at all. They would be willing to fall in with a plan that would embrace both sides of the road, although they thought that as trustees they would scarcely have power to part with the land in the way proposed, except on payment of something like its value. A fair proposal would meet with their consideration.-The report of the sewage farm stated that during the past month the whole of the different areas of land had been treated with sewage with good effect. The osiers in the ploughed portion of the field were, looking healthy, and daring the month two rows had been planted at the lower end of the field.-This was all the business of interest. WHISTON. AINIAIILT ON • SCHOOL TF.ACHER BY • SCUOLA.I.-At the Prescot Police Court, on Tuesday, a school girl named Sarah Ellen Almond was charged with haying assaulted Miss Owen, a teacher at the National Schools, Whiston.- From the evidence given by Miss Owen it appeared that on the 25th March the head master was away from the school, 'and complainant and a fellow teacher were in charge. The defendant, taking advantage of the master's absence, became unruly, and upon the other teacher attempting to chastise her she refused to hold out her hand, and, getting upon the form, began to kick and bite. Miss Owen came to the rescue of her fellow teacher,but defendant turned upon her, kicked her on the legs, and bit her hand very severely. Defendant's brother also came out of his class, and threatened to assist his sister, but was ordered out cf the school.- Defendant's mother said one of the teachers had held the defendant whilst the other beat her brutally. When she mote home her head and body were market: by the strokes she had received from a cane.-It was, however, denied that a cane had been need at all.-The Chairman (Mr. Earle) said parents were very ready to take advantsze of the laws against the unfortunate school teachers for ilLtresting their 1 children, but they did not remember that their children Light be very naughty.-A fine of 55. and casts was jot- posed. A CASH OF DOI7BIFITL PATERNITY --Peter Viney, an elderly n on Tuesday man, belonging to Woolto , • ,appeared, before the Prescot bench of magistrates to show curse why he should not be committed to gaol for not having paid £3 18s arrears, including costs, towards the maintenar.v of hi son in an industrial! school. The defendant put i the plea that he was not the child's father, nor was he titaz i lea tu I the child's mother, although he had lived with 'Se for some time. The bench said the defendant had, ~hot taken the proper steps to prove what he had alleged, and he would be committed to gaol for six weeks.-Chriatoplam Walsh, who was £3 19s in arrears, was committed ler a similar period and John Leech, who owed 30s arzearst was c. inoltttzd far a month for similar offences.

div.head: Xetttrs to tlte editor.
div.p: Xetttrs to tlte editor.

- - DISESTABLISHMENT. Sir,—l have come to look forward with feelings of plea- surable anticipation to the weekly treat the reading of your correspondence column affords. It is a most interesting psychological study, and th 3 last two weeks have been especially fruitful- in this respect. Here again we have the hysterical "CE" (the sexless diothong affords me no clue as to the gender of your correspondent, but from the excitability of temper displayed, I should say female—spinster—elderly and disappointed) to the front again with a profusely ver- bose reproduction of some antiquarian lumber having as much bearing upon the essential questions at issue as would the history of the man in the moon. And all this arose from my saying that the Established Church of England —that is the State connected and State controlled Protestant Church as we have it now, with the Crown as its head—was set up, instituted or established, in the reign of Henry VIII. when that monarch was installed as its head, before whose reign it was non-existent. That is quite sisfficient for my argument. The truth of this statement must have been evident all along to every impartial and evenly balanced mind. But there are some antique-minded people who, from-the constant habit of retrospection have their faces so much over their shoulders as to be incapable if looking mat- ters of modern moment straight in the face. As an instance let us analyse the sayings of the irrepressible CE." In his (or her) letter to you of March 20th I find this statement, "tithes are not taxes. They are neither levied, collected, nor appropriated, as are taxes." To this I reply that to the tithe-payer there is little or no difference, except this, that from the payment of taxes he expects to get some little benefit in the shape of national protection and government; whilst from the payment of tithes he expects' nor gets the slightest benefit. I say that unless they be levied they caneot be collected, and if not collected they oannot be appropriated—" a consummation devoutly to be wished." Then it seems "when a man rays tithes it is not to the Church. It is a gift, pure and simple, from the land." This is news. But is it true ? If not the Church, then the par- son gets it, which comes to much the same so far as we are concerned. limn as to the gift ; how does that come about? Well, Ills extracted from the occupier of the land by threats of imprisonment and distress in case of refusal ! Cer- tainly an equivocal mode of asking a donation ! Then we are told it is from the land. Which it distinctly and decidedly is not. If this were true Salisbury Plain would a be paying tithes along with our own mosses and commons. k The land is there. But nothing short of a miracle would be . required to get tithes from it without the intervention of the cultivator and his capital. So that we see it is not the land which is taxed with tithe, but the capital and labour of the farmer. As well might you expect to get interest from a bank or dividends from a trading company without previous investment as tithes from the land before the tiller has in- vested his capital and labour into it. Then, and then alone, can the Church step in and demand the tenth part of the product of this investment. Now, sir, what are we to think of such an argument as this ? It is either insincere or it is insane. Either the writer did or 'did not believe it to be true when advancing it. In the first case it calls for our commiseration, as being weak-minded; in the latter our contempt as being untruthful and intended to mislead. The alternative I leave "CE" to chose. It is his to say whether u, we shall consider him foolish merely and pity bins, z t or knavish and despise him. Such wild and d.• unfounded statements as these are calculated to discredit the advocates of any cause, however just and _IL • reasonable. Nor need we wonder that such advocates seek to hide behind a convenient pseudonym. Whether it be • that they are ashamed of the cause, or are afraid the cause might be ashamed of its advocates, I know net. When we have him dogmatising upon a subject about z• which, as a defender of Church abuses, he can know noth- ing, viz., conscience. It seems Dissenters do not con- scienciously object to the paymenb of tithes to the Church of England. But let" (E "ask this question of a Dissenting farmer—taking good care the while to keep a good arm's length between the catechised and catechiser, for an accident might happen. I knew such a question, from such a ques- tioner, would be likely to send a thrill down to the seat of the man's most anew.o feelings--the breeches pocket—and •ti, might result in awkward consequences to one of them. -it Then we have the dictum that if a man pays tithes "he etc pays so much less rent." To this 1 give an emphatic er denial! Tithes are a surcharge upon the rent. Just think of it for one moment. If tithes were paid in lieu of a like amount of rent, it would be the landlord who would really have to pay it, and not the occupiers—that is, the latter would first pay it out of his own pocket, and have it a- refunded to him by his landlord in the shape of reduced ens:. rent. Now,when we consider that the landlords have had, ail for ages, the making of the laws; when we consider their ea, well-known ability in shifting their own burdens off their le own and on the shoulders of other people, we may well doubt their quiet acquiesence in this arrangement. But ea• such is not the fact. Tithes from their very origin were i.e imposed directly upon the tiller of the soil without refer- ence to the owner. Indeed, this must be so when the par- -au son used to enter the wheat-field and take therefrom every In tenth sheaf, or from the hay-field every tenth cock, and carry, Int it off as the "gift from the laud to the Church.' This being so—if it is the cultivator of the soil who pays— it is easy to see the injustice of the impost. Say a man holds ten acres of land, the minket value of which, irrespec- tive of tithes, is £5 per acre yearly. That amount added to the value of the labour and capital employed in the work- ing of that land may be called his remunerative investment, the outlay from which he expects to get a fair profit. But over and above this come a surcharge for tithe for which he gets no return. I know of no better definition of the word robbery than this. And it is none the less a robbery be- cause it still disgraces the statute book. Again, tithes were anciently divided into four positions, one of which went to the relief of the poor. And I believe that to this day they (the poor) ought to be in receipt of at least one quarter of the whole amount of tithe raised in England. But do they get it? No! I believe that the poor are this II robbed annually ef over one million sterling. Now this de- ficiency has to be made up by poor's rate, of which the • farmer ha to pay his share according to assessment. In ▪‘. this way he is compelled to pay two poor rates—one to the r•c- overseers and the other to the Church. Can any but the most rabid defender of Church abuses uphold such as ye- tern of reduplicate robbery ? Churchmen! please apply the 2nd and.3rd chapter of the Gospel according to St. Luke, and also I. Corinthians, iv., 2. I am gratified to find that "A Churchman" can be at one with me even en one question. lam puzzled to know what is meant by "compulsory commutation of tithes." I thought this commutation took place in 1836 by the Com- mutation Act. Does he mean rendering the payment op- tional? If so, we are again at one. Then he asks how the members of the Church of England can enjoy their own if she is disendowed ? Thus: In my view she is "endowed" with other folks' goods, and it is that alone we wish to de- prive her of, leaving to her all that in equity belongs to her. I hope in this again "A Churchman" will be at one with me.—Ever years, JOHN PEERS. Penketh, March 31st. LOCAL POLITICS. Sir,—lt is interesting to notice the efforts of our War- rington Tories, who are at present certainly working with a seal unprecedented, at any rate since 1868. It behoves those who have at heart the interests of Liberalism in the borough to look to their laurels if they would retain their present position. There is little doubt that if the Liberals or Warrington are disposed to do it they can easily win the next election by double the majority obtained in 1880, and for many reasons. For one thing the workingmen of War- rington ate decidedly Liberal, and on the other hand the Tory candidate is not popular even with his own party. The opinion of many Tories even is that Sir Gilbert is a bad candidate, and is sure to be beate' n but his supporters are in this position, that having no one else who will "shell out so cien y they are compelled to keep him to the " ffitl fore. It is a shame to deceive the old gentleman in the way his friends are doing, taking him round to ward m g t which perhaps a dozen or twenty "bona Ode" reet' siediennt: CiLt the ward are present, and the remainder of the " moderate attendance" is made up of people from all parts of the borough. It is interesting to note the speeches made adt these meetinge. At the Public Hall the other night w a reverend gentleman excusing himself for being a " politi- cal "parson. He needn't apologise; if his own fiock are content it matters little to anyone else, but still be might have explained how it was that instead of fulfilling a clerical appointment at the Parish Church the same evening, for which he was duly announced, he so unfortunately mistook his avocation. Rumour has it that in consideration of a large subscription Is his recently erected day schools this rev, gentleman is working oil the sum by so many political speeches, and consequently being anxious to square up the abcount early, is performing as the "general utility man " at each Tory meeting. Then we have a celebrated gentle- man with a military title, sympathising with the wire- drawers in their proposed reduction of wages; to be con- sistent be might help to raise the low pay which the labourers at certain tanneries in Warrington are at present receiving, where it is said that if a man is late he is not only" quartered," but fined into the bargain. Sir Gilbert tells us trade is bad; then why doesn't he help to make it

better by spending a little more money amongst us, instead of being so fond of civil service stores and the like? He has had during the last few years several opportunities of find- ing employment for Warrington workpeople—why has be not done it? Sir William Harcourt described the Tory dodge in the House of Commons a few days ago as a "dirty trick." Let the Liberals of Warrington be on their guard. The Tories know they are fighting a forlorn hope, and some of the more indiscreet members of their party are certain to overdo their work; in fact they have already done so. There are men in my district who are bound to spoil their own game —they, as I already know, "on the job." Liberals, keep you eyes and ears open !!—Yours, A NORTH-EAST WARD ELECTOR.

THE FAIR TRADE QUESIION. Sir —I think tha workingmen of Warrington have a most serious charge to make against at least two gentlemen of this town—the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton and Mr. Lawrenson —each of whom has missed no opportunity for ventilating his ideas on this question during the last year or two. Now, when acknowledged Free Traders bring into the town a well qualified man, ready to discuss the question of Fair Trade versus Free Trade, throw out a challenge to this effect, and cordially invite anyone to come forward to thresh the question, really for the welfare of the whole community, where are theea Fair Traders? Why, coward like, they stay away. It is no use saying they do not want to disturb the Liberal meeting. They know very well that at this particular time an atten- tive audience would have listened with an earnestness that I may almost say is born of desperation, could they have been shown a way out of their troubles, and yet these Fair Traders stayed away from the meeting. I say it was verg- ing on the criminal on their part to withhold what know- ledge they may have on this subject. lam not wedded to Free Trade. Let any man prove to me that by adopting Fair Trade I can prevent this heavy reduction in my wages from coming about, and I will soon "Jack up the Free Trade bogey." As it is, lam bound think that our Con- servative friends merely use the question because they know that

Bombast and riddle best do puppies please, For fools admire and love such things as these. And a dull quibble, wrapt in dubious phrase, That to the height does their wise wonder raise. The parson may well be left out of this clue stion; be knows nothing about it, and cares less. If by insinuating, as ne did at the last Conservative meeting, that the Free Traders are driving trade out of the country, he can catch a few votes, and so preserve his dear church, both Egypt, trade, and the workingmen might perish for what be cared. With Mr. Lawrenson it is somewhat different; he has some argu- ments, or I should say fallacies, and they deserve to be dealt with. About a fortnight ago he and myself attended a moat important meeting in Manchester called to discuss a wage question. At that meeting Mr. Lawrenson told me that the wage question would be constantly cropping up until we stopped the Germans from sending wire into England. We had no time for argument on this question. But why in the name of all that is honourable was Mr. Lawrenson absent from Mr. Howes's lecture? If he can prove that it would be for the nation's welfare to go in for Protection then accept Mr. Howes'n challenge for debate, or else never mention the subject again.—Yours, kc., H. WHITHAM. March 26th,1884.

div.head: TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: TEMPERANCE MISSION AT WAR- RINGTON.

A series of gospel temperance meetings has been conducted in Warrington during the. week by Mr. T. B. Anderson, of Liverpool, under the auspices of the Warrington Temperance Union. The mission has been attended with considerable success, and there were large audiences at each meeting, at the close of which a good number of pledges were taken. A choir, under the conductorship of Mr. Williams, rendered excellent service. The first meeting was held on Monday evening, in Wy- cliffe Hall, Bewsey-road, when Mr. Richard Roberts pre- sided. In hie opening remarks he referred to the time when they first began the temperance movement in Warrington, and when there was only one minister in the town who was a total abstainer. In those days it was impossible to get a gathering like the one he saw before him, and the ser- vices of such a choir. They had something to do during the last thirty years to maintain their principles under all circumstances, but they knew—and were now more con- vinced than ever—that they were right. There was a time when the great bulk of the people had an idea that they could not work without drink, but the greatest difficulty with a vast majority of the people had always been to play without drink. There were many who cauld not spend a holiday without drink, whereas if they used those holidays aright they would be better prepared for the work that fol- lowed. •,:eThey would not need the number of police that they had in Warrington if it were not for the drink, for whoever heard of a 'teetotaller being taken before the magistrates. A teetotaler might possibly go there if he had a perambulator and wheeled it on the footpath—(laughter)—but be did not think there was any risk of his going for anything more serious.—Mr. Anderson then sang the " Little bit of blue," and several people in the audience' at his request, spoke of the benefit that they had derived from total abstinence.—Mr. Am:ma- son, during a brief address, denied that alcohol was condu- cive to health and strength, instancing Weston's tour of 5,000 miles as evidence in support of his argument.—The Rev. T. RIPPON referred to the custom of paying wages in public-house, and expressed the hope that the master forge- men of the town would help the temperance cause by pay- ing their men, if they must pay them in a public room, in the cocoa rooms instead of the public-kouses. He also hoped that refreshment stalls at railway stations and other places would supply teetotal drinks at a more reasonable price, and upon a mrich quicker and better system than at present prevailed.—Mr. W. Roberts also addressed the meeting. A second and equally successful meeting was held on Tuesday evening in the Workmen's Club, Market Place, when there was a good attendance. Several hymns were sung by the choir, and an address containing some interest- ing statistics was given by the chairman, the Rey. E. Moore. He said that he sometimes liked to estimate the progress of the movement and the effect it had upon society by the testimony of those who were opposed to it. A conference, he read in the papers, had just been held in St. James's I Hall, London of representatives of the liquor traffic. Earl Wemvss presided, and said that the trade was in dagger from the opposition of a well meaning but meddling philan- thropy. It was satisfactory to know that his lordship gave them credit for being well meaning. He designated their efforts as philanthropy, and surely anything that was phil- anthropic was entitled to the noble lord's support. But he said that their policy was meddling. He (the speaker) should not find fault with that, for he did net know that they had ever obtained any great reforms in this country without a policy of meddling, and he might say that the liquor traffic was meddling with then* seriously, with their pockets, their health, and their morals, day and night, always and everywhere. He thought, therefore, thet they were entitled to meddle with it, and he advised them to continue meddling until they did away with it. They would be looking forward with in- terest to the proceedings in the House of Commons when the bill for closing public-houses on Sundays came on for second reading. It had passed the first reading, and if it passed the second, would stand a good chance of becoming law. Everyone there, he was sure, Liberal or Conservative, would wish success to the efforts of Mr. Stephenson tie get the bill passed. These interested in the liquor traffic were fond of telling them that the Sunday Closing Bill was a failure, and that where it was observed, not only did drunken- ness net diminish, but that in some caries it actually In- creased. When the subject was investigated it was found that those statements were not true. The head constable of Edinburgh gave figures in respect of the crime of drunkenness. Since the operation of the bill there the yearly average of cases brought before the magistrates had decreased from 6,047 to 2,327. Before the passing of the Act the average of cases between eight o'clock on Sunday morning to eight o'clock On Monday morning was 367, and since the passing of the Act, between 1871 and 1882, the average was 51. (Applause.) The average for Saturday drunkenness had already ceased. As regarded Ireland, it was shown that in 1876 the spirits for home consumption were over 6,000,000 gallons, which, at the end of 1383 had decreased by 737,880 gallons. The cases of punishable drunkenness in the year ending 1877 were 110,903, and in the year ending 1883 they were 37,526. He had no doubt that if the bill were passed a considerable diminution in drunkenness would follow. He impressed upon his audience that all persons, of whatever politics or religion, should unite together to preserve sobriety and temperance.— Addressee were also given by Mr. Anderson and Mr. Eddy, of the Gospel Temperance League. On Wednesday, Mr. Anderson was again, as he terms it, "catching fishes with the Gospel Temperance net," the meeting being held in the Workmen's Club, and proving the most enthusiastic of the series. There was a large audience, and the choir was listened to with great attention. A notice- able feature of the meeting was the presence of a number of soldiers in uniform, which attracted Mr. Anderson's attention, and drew forth a short allusion to General Gordon and his mission.—A soldier amongst the audience was invited to "testify," which he did in a very earnest manner, exhorting his hearers to stand firm together and help one another in the cause. Where there was unity, he said, there was strength in all cases and all causes, and they must all help to battle for the right. They must stand firm to their posts, and not be temperance men one day and drunk- ards the next. Some who professed to be temperate men, as soon as one's back was turned went straight into the public-house, which was nothing bat a mockery.—Mr. Anderson put in the remark that ridicule must be met boldly, for it was often easier to stand against bullets and bayonets than the shafts of ridicule.—An abstainer of 22 exhorted railway years experience next spoke, and was followed by the Rev. J. McTurk.—A railway servant then spoke on behalf of a rawilaws class who, he said, were subject to a great many tempta- tions. servants,e a' agosince several osifgwned homthehep esdagwe , tand thehe room, to do the same.—An abstainer of 25 years experience denied that alcshol was necessary to a man who worked hard, and the Rev T. It'lPP on in a short th address, said that the longer he lived e more was he con- vinced that the temperance position was that of truth and wisdom —Mr. ANDERSON in a concluding address said that if there was anything more than another that he 'liked the temperance movement for it was its unsectarian and can- political character. Politics could be talked at the clubs, and each party could respect each other and shake bands on the temperance platform. They wanted to win people and not blackguard them. They should not be bigoted and dogmatic, but should remember the circumstances of others and be charitable to those who opposed them, at the same
