div.head: ROYAL COUNTY AGRICULTURAL
div.p: THE ROYAL COUNTY AGRICULTURAL
SOCIETY.

SHOW FOR 1885 ABANDONED, On Wednesday morning, a special meeting of the mem- bers of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, aed North Lanca- entre Agricultural Society was held at the Lion Hotel, War- rington, to complete the revision of the prize list for the show at Stockport, and consider and decide upon an appli- cation from the Preston Local Committee to the Royal Agricultural Society of England "for a subscription to their funds, and for the society to withhold its show ia 1885, and co-operate with them in promoting the success of the show of the Rayal at Preston in that year," or to fix upon the district of the society in which its show of 1885 shall be held if resolved upon. On the motion of Mr. T. Fair J.P , it was resolved that G. C. lisle, Esq , the agent to Lord Derby, should preside. Amongt the other gentle- men present were—C. R. Janson, Esq., J.P., DL.; T. W. Tatton, Esq., J.P. P • T. W. Fair, Esq. (Haigh Hall) ; R. R. Thompson, Esq. (Preston); Messrs. W. Scotson (Aig- burth), J. Dickinson (Wigan), A. J. Howard (Blackburn), J. Hallsall (11alebank), P. Blundell (Kirkham), T. Wilkinson (Garstang), John Warburton (Dallam), W. Langton (Pres- cot), R. 11olland (Frodsham), James Tunstali r,r_tigang), , W,_Forrestar (Leyland), R. Lonsdale (Boothstown), R Cat- I terall Limber (Preston).

, The SECIIETARY said he had received a letter from the Mayor and Council of Preston asking that in view of the Royal Saciety coming to Preston next year, the society would subscribe to their funds, and would be good enough to withhold its show, and co-operate with them in promot- ing the success of the Royal Show. There would be a meeting on Saturday next of the Local Committee at Pres- ton, and they seemed to wish to have a decision placed be- fore that meeting, in order that they might proceed to invite other local societies to join with them in the same work.— The CHAIRMAN asked where the show of their society was to be held in 1885.—The SECRETARY replied that it was to be held in the Chester divisidn.—ln reply to a further ques- tion, the SE RETARY SAid that in Manchester, some years ago, the sum of £5OO was subscribed and the show was withheld. When the Royal was at Liverpool a few years ago, that society subscribed £3OO and gave up its show, but the subscription at Liverpool was awarded chiefly in prizes for farms. When there was no show held the subscriptions had mere than covered what they had given to the Royal and paid the expenses, so that they had really had a profit after the two Royal Shows at Manchester and Liverpool.—Mr. SMITH asked it any falling off in subscriptions was apparent.—Th. SECRETARY said it did seem to affect them the next year.— Mr. WMITII said that by subscribing a guinea to the Royal a person might ceas3 to become a subscriber to the County Society, and might not again renew his name on the sub- scription list of the County.—The SECRETARY said that was why he wanted the Royal Society to take them as members. —Mr. Scovsene thought they should consider that question pretty fully if they were not to hold the County Show and were to give a subscription. It seemed tq. hint that the Royal should give all their memhers the privilege of exhibiting as well As seeing something for the subscriptions which might be given. They might (eel honoured with the Royal Show coming to Preston, but they mast not forget that they were there for the benefit of their own society as much as for the benefit of the Royal. It behoved them to act justly towards their own members. If they gave a subscription of £2OO or £3OO he thought that the Royal should make some sort of provi- sion that the members of their society could compete for prizes in the Royal on pretty much the same grounds as their own members. Mr. Jourr HODGSON said be had mixed with outside mem- bers as much as most members of the Council, and he found that on the occasion when they gave £5OO to the Royal at Manchester their members only received one day's admis- sion to the show, and that did not give the satisfaction that might have been expected from the Royal. They went out of their way to hold the great show at Preiton during the Guild week, and then Preston was out et a turn. Mr. Bracu asked whether not only the members of that society would be allowed to compete on reasonable terms, bat whether they were likely to have classes they could com- pete in. Their county society had always promoted dairy stock, whereas the Royal had to do strictly with herd book cattle. As to horses, he believed they had restricted them to animals entered italh,e Cart Horse Sted Book. He thought that proper prizes should be offered for which Lancashire farmers could compete. The SECRETARY said the Local Committee were offering prizes this year for dairy cattle, and all questions of that kind could be arranged by the Local Committee. Whatever sum was subscribed to the Royal, the Local Committee would have the privilege and right of recommending aseries of prizes, and practically the prizes would be adapted to the district. The Local Committee of Preston would keep that very muck before them. As to the subscriptions from their society, he thought that they might reasonably say which way they would have it spent in prizes.—Mr. LONOTON said there had been a competition between Preston and Chester for a long time with regard to securing the Royal Show, and it was thought by many member, whichever town the Royal selected, the society should hold its sheer at the other.

Tho Sanaa-rens .aid if they held a show in 1885, with the Royal Show at Preston, their show would be a very limited one. If the meeting consented to deferring the show until 1886, he believed they could make a grand show, but if they were determiced to hold it next year, he was afraid it would not be a success.

Mr. J. W. Fern thought the meeting should be unani- mous on the paint, and he hoped gentlemen would reconsider any position they might have thought of taking. In all cases where the Royal had visited a county, the county ex- hibition had not been held, and he hoped the Royal county of Lancaster would not be the first to break this recognised rule.

Mr. T. W. TATHAM felt very strongly that they ought to withhold their show this year, and assist in promoting the success of the Royal Show at Preston. They would not be doing their duty as the parent society of the district if they did otherwise. He would not suggest a large subscription, but one of £2OO or .£3OO. Ha proposed that they withheld their show meeting for 111455. Mr. T. FAIR seconded the motion, reminding the meeting that the county society would have a large representation on the Local Committee, so that the interests of Lancashire and Cheshire and North Wales would be very carefully looked after.

Mr. IieLsALL said they would lose a large number of Subscribers if they had no show. He thought that a two days' show might be held in a part of the society's district which would not interfere with the Royal Show at Preston. He proposed, as an amendment, that they hold a small show in 1885.

Mr. LANGTON seconded the amendment, which was lost the voting being 11 for and 15 against. The original motion vise then carried unanimously. The CHAIRALAN said the next question was what should be the amount of subscription. Whatever they did subscribe would be apportioned as they might direct, through the Local Committee, to prizes more particularly relating to this district. Therefore he submitted that they should contri- bute a handsome sum to the funds of the Bova' Society, through the Local Committee, for the distribution of prises for that district.

Mr. C. R. Jecsos said they had now arrived at a point at which they could start at the practical working out of a scheme. Tie local Execative Committee had not yet had an opportunity of turning their attention to the prize list. They had arrived at this stage, that they had been able to undertake that at least £1,500 should be distributed in prizes. He did not know that the Royal Society would accept a stipulation that the money should be applied in any way excepting so far as the local executive determined it : but there could be HO doubt if that society thought proper to attach any co .dition to any sum of money it was dis- posed to give the local committee would pay proper heed to their request. The subscription list at present, he might tell them, exceeded £5,000, and the Mayor aud Corporation of Preston were, he assured them, doing mach more than was usual to do under the circumstances. Mr. R. LANSDALE proposed that the sum of £3OO be paid to the local committee for the Royal Show.—Mr. SMITH seconded the motion. _ . _

—,...........- .................,... The resolution was unanimously adopted, and on the •uggestion of the secretary seven members of the Council— Messrs. Lonsdale, Smith, Scotson, Halsall, Tanstall, Lang- ton, and Cotterill—were appointed to act on the Preston Local Committee.

The meeting then proceeded to revise the prize list for the show at Stockport, to be held in the coining summer, and at which the society will offer £1,700 in prizes, in addition to special prizes given by the local committee. At the close of this business a vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Hale for presiding, and the meeting terminated.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETING
div.p: CONSERVATIVE WARD MEETING

AT WA RRINGFON. On Wednesday evening the annual meeting of the Conser- vatives of the North-W,st Ward was held in St. Paul's School, Heathside. There was a good attendance. Captain Litton presided, and there were also present Sir Gilbert Greenall, Captain Reynolds, Rev. S. Wilkinson, Mr. R. Pierpoint, Councillors John Pierpoint, T. Sutton, and J. E. Wright, Messrs. Thos. Jolley, Edwd. Bolton, H. Greenall,. D. W. Finney, George Cr)pper, Joseph Grine C. Riggin- botharn, W. Porter, J. Hampson (secretary to the Conserva- tive Association), die. On the motion of the Criainualr, seconded by Sir GILBERT GREENALL, the following resolution was agreed to:—" That this meeting respectfully offers its sincere condolence with her Majesty the Queen, the Duzhess of Albany, and the other members of the Royal Family on their sad bereave- ment in the death of the Duke of Albany."

The CHAIRMAN, proceeding the business of the evening, Said they had every occasion now to hope that the Conservative cause would predominate again in Warrington as it had done up to within the last three or four years. Unfortunately before the return of Mr. McMinnies they had had a long period of bad trade in the town, adverse weather, and all sorts of impor- tant things that caused people to hesitate very much about returning another Conservative candidate. Warrington un- fortunately shared with the rest of the boroughs and counties he being robbed of its proper representative—that was a Conservative representative. (Hear, hear.) The great promises that were made by Mr. Gladstone in his Midlothian expedition, as they were all aiiire, had not been fulfilled—in fact, he could scarcely enumellte any that had been fulfilled. They promised "peace, retrenchment, and reform;" but they had had nothing but war, great expendi- ture—and as for reform he did not know what it was going to be. The Government were bringing before Parliament a sort of Franchise Bill that was to help the Government, but he maintained that they had no right to introduce a Franchise Bill without a redistribution of seats. (Hear, hear.) He, however, hoped the Conservatives of the House of Commons would do everything to oppose the passing of the Franchise Bill until we knew what we were going to get in the form of redistribution. From what they had beard, Mr. Gladstone was disposed to allow Ireland her pre- sent number ef representatives, although the population of that country was much less than it was some years ago. He was going to give Scotland more representatives at the expense of England, and he did not think that was at all fair, as the population of England had increased. He con- cluded by attributing what he described as the disgraceful wars and the present state of trade to the Government hav- ing no definite policy, and advocated the development of trade with India instead of encouraging teade with other countries which imposed protective duties. (Applause.) Mr. EDWARD BOLTON moved the appointment of the Ward Committee and delegates to the Council of the Con- servative Association, the chairman being Captain Litton, J.P., and the vice-chairman Councillor J. Pierpoint. Mr. R. Isnmewoon seconded the motion, which was carried. Mr. D. W. FINNEY moved that the remainder of the Ward Committee be the same as last year, with the addition of all Conservatives in the ward who offer to work voluntarily without payment at all tlection. He thought that Conser- vatives might very well congratulate themselves upon the progress of their principles, he believed, in all ranks of society. He even believed Conservativdprinciples were per- meating the Liberal ranks. He thought they might con- gratulate themselves upon the progress of Conservatism in Warrington. He did not think there was a time when the Conservatives of Warrington were more united or were even in a better position for an election than at present; and he believed if an election were to take place to-morrow they would return Sir Gilbert Greenall by a very large majority. The majority at the last election was a mere accident, and assured those present that it would be reversed on the next occasion—at least he could only say he really and truly hoped it might be so. (Applause.) Mr. G. CROPP a seconded, and remarked, in view of the Corrupt Practices Act, that they should be very cautious at the next election. Mr. Teomes Jotter moved a resolution condemning the policy of the present Government for carrying in unneces- sary, costly, and aimless wars, for neglecting the trade in- terests of the country; while their whole energy was now being used to push through Parliament an incomplete and unjust Franchise Bill. He maintained that the whole policy of the Government had got into a mess that nobody ' could unravel, and the only thing they could do was to turn the Government out and put a Conservative Government into power. Mr. E. GRERN seconded the motion, and criticised the speech of Mr. Howes at the late Liberal meeting, maintain- ing that things were not so bad amongst the agricultural population years ago as that gentleman represented. Mr. Georiom WOODS supported the resolution, and spoke strongly in favour of Free Trade and a vigorous foreign policy. Councillor ERANCOMB also spoke in support of the resolu- tion, and although believing it would be a dangerous thing to go back to Protection, he still thought the Government might slaw their respect and good feeling for the working- men in giving a commission of inquiry. As to Egypt, while they were pining for news as to the position of the in- habitants of Sinkat, Mr. Gladstone went into the House of Commons with "this humbugging Franchise Bill, which nobody wanted to know anything about." Councillor J. PIIIRPOINT moved a resolution pledging the meeting to do its utmost to return Sir Gilbert Greenall to Parliament as member for the borough at the next general election. The way in which Sir Gilbert GreenalPe name was from time to time received led him to believe, he said, that at the next general election they would all join in forwarding the Objects of that Association—the great deter- mination to return their well-tried friend, Sir Gilb3rt Greenall, to Parliament. (Applause.) Mr. T. Surroe seconded the resolution, and urged them not to despair. Mr. R. PIERPOINT, in supporting, after congratulating the ward most sincerely upon the large attendance that evening, remarked that Mr. McMinnies was away getting into his mind the substance of that speech which was promised them four years ago. As to the Franchise Bill there was no cry for It, but merely a whine manufactured by the Caucus. _ _ .

The resolution was carried, and in replying Sir GILBERT GREENALL observed that he was no coward. He never in his life, before the thousands in Warrington, had, and he hoped he never should have, a moment's hesi- tancy in declaring openly, clearly, and manfully, what he thought and what were his opinions. Conser- vatism in Warrington had always had the right ring about it. They lost an engagement but they were not defeated. No man ever saw a cloud of disappointment on his face. He never felt it personally. He felt the disappointment with the hundreds of his friends. To himself the defeat was of trifling personal importance, but it was of importance that his discomiture was their discomfiture. (Hear, hear.) He said lately that he spoke plainly, and he was speaking plainly about what he was calling their discomfiture. They saw the Conservative party defeated in 1880. He said fear- lessly that they were defeated because the Conservative party were asleep. (Hear, bear.) Now they were up and doing. (Hear, hear.) They were not now asleep, and they did not intend to nod even. (Laughter.) He asked them to keep their wits about them, and to keep their eyes open; and then where would Conservatism be in Warrington ? He knew where it would be. It would be in its right place. They must not think he was speaking of himself as the Only person who could put it is the right place. He would be guilty of no such folly as proclaiming himself a hero. He was with them if they were with him; and they would remain bound together for the same objects and the same purposes. He thought it would not be fair if he did not allude to the question of Free Trade. He was a Free Trader. He had been a Free Trader—a consistent Free Trader, but he agreed with his friends in the opinion that such was the state of trade in this country, that to satisfy the desires and enquiries of a great many men, the Government would do well if they agreed to a commission on the subject or a committee of enquiry; so that the matter could be fairly discussed, and every man could have an opportunity of fully investigating, and, if he would give himself the trouble, of fully understanding the whole question. (Hear, hear.) Personally he would never consent to any tax being put upon corn; he would never consent to any tax being imposed upon the necessaries of life which the working classes of this country consumed. With respect to the franchise, he had no objection whatever to its extension. Ho thought as a matter of justice that in the agricultural districts the franchise should be extended. end made analogous with th• franchise in the towns. But he did not accept the chicanery and the indistinctness of the present measure of reform. Let them know from the beginning the end of the whole matter, and no one would vote more willingly than he for the extension of the franchise if there was an equitable redistribution of seats. (Applause.) He disliked the present Government excessively, but he respected and venerated Mr. Gladstone. (lieu, hear.) He had had the honour and pleasure of some slight acquaintance with Mr. Gladstone. Be was a "grand old man"—(laughter and applause)—and he meant right, but he was not always right. He talked upon a great many subjects; he knew as much about gardening as their friend Mr. Green did. (Applause.) He talked of raspberry beds, end he talked of Englishmen making jam. (Laughter.) He (Sir Gilbert) would offer them a riddle, "Why was Mr. Gladstone like jam ?" Did they give it up? (Yes.) Because he had so many jars in his Cabinet. (Laughter and applause.) It was pleasant to him (Sir Gilbert) to come into the ward. Conservatism in Warrington dead! Why it was more lively than ever it was. It was disposed to show more vitality than he ever remem- bered it. In conclusion, he expressed his gratification at the kind reception they had given him. (Applause.) The usual votes of thanks terminated the proceedings.

A henpecked gentleman determined to sup with a party of friends against the will of his wife. He was resolved that he would, and she that he should not go. He did not go. His friends missed him, and, just for a lark, invaded his residence, where they found him and his wife sitting in their chairs fast asleep. He had given her an opiate that he might slip away, and she had given him one so that he might not.

_ Webster. MOTHER AND Sow.—Luke Tulley, a young man, was charged on a warrant with assaulting his mother on the 25th December, 1882, but the prosecurrix did not appear.— Prisoner's sister, who was in court, said that her mother did not wish to press the case, as she was now of opinion that she herself was to blame.—Re was consequently dis- charged.
FilDAT.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and Alderman Webster.

BREACH OF THE PEACE.—Joseph Tavlin, fish dealer, Orford-street, was ordered to be bound over in his own recognizance of £5 to keep the peace for six months for committing a breach of the peace by fighting with a man named Brian, in the Market-place, on the previous day. PROVOKING LANGUAGE.—JSMOS Moffatt, labourer, Web- ster's-yard, Dial-street, was summoned for having made use of language towards Martha Taylor, calculated to provoke a breach of the peace.—The defendant was ordered to be bound over in his own recogaizances of £5 to keep the peace for six months. "Sommario ELSE TO DO. WITH HIS MONEY.—Patrick McDernaot, a man of simple appearance and of no settled residence, was charged with being on the premises of Bow- soy Forge, the previous night, with intent to commit a felony. P C. Taylor deposed to finding the prisoner sleep- ing close to a heating furnace. He had money, but when asked why he did not go to a lodging house, he re- plied that he had "something else to do with his money." The prisoner had been in an asylum, and as be was a mad- man when in drink no one would employ him.—The Bench committed him for 14 days' imprisonment. His 81ST APPEARANCB.—John Bohan, labourer, Dol- man's-lane, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street, on Thurday night—P.C. Hennessey proved the case.—The prisoner, as usual, promised to be "teetotal regular" if let off, but the Mayor remarking that that was the prisoner's 81st appearance, fined him 20s and costs, or one month's imprisonment in default. NIGLIGIINT WORKMEN.—James Coiley, residing in Back Crossley-street, was summoned by Messrs. Platt and Son, who claimed £1 43 compensation by reason of defendant having neglected to fulfil his contract with them.—The de- fendant, who had left work without giving notice, and also done damage, was order to pay the amount claimed forthwith. --Jas. Ooulden, of Back William-street, was similarly sum- moned by Messrs. Platt, who claimed 123 compensation.— Defendant offered and was ordered to pay the amount at the rats of 2s. per week.----Annie Barrow, Cambria-place, King-street, was also summoned for having, she being ap- prenticed to Messrs. Platt, neglected her work, whereby they had been put to a loss of .Ll, which amount they claimed.—Orelered to pay the amount claimed at is per week.

Dxssner.—Before Messrs. John-Ry-lands aid Peter Stubbs.
DRIYMINNASS. - William Regers, Caerdlen Jelin Welsby, Rizton ; and Joseph Wood, Orford, were each fined for drunkenness.

A CHAPEL KEEPER CHARGED WITH ASSAULT.—Joseph Andrews, Padgate, was summoned for having, on the 23rd March, assaulted and beaten Joseph Weston, a boy.—lt appeared that a stained glass memorial window has been erected in the Padget° Wesleyan Chapel, and com- plainant, who is a scholar, went into the school half an hour before the time for the purpose of showing another boy the window. The boys were found in the school by the chapel keeper who, complainant alleged, got hold of him and struck him on the head and side.—Mr. W. H. J. Jen- kins, who appeared on behalf of defendant, admitted that Is took held of the boy and put him out of the school.— The Bench, however, dismissed the case, remarking that there was no positive evidence that undue severity was used in the chastisement of the boy. SCHOOL AITENDANCE.—George Travis, Hollins Green, was fined Is for neglecting to send his daughter to school as required by the Elementary Education Act.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDLY.—Before Mr. LI. Reynolds and Mr. James Handley. AUTHORITY.—AIbert Musgrove was granted temporary authority to sell at the Grapes Inn, Halton-road. MISCELLINEOII3.—Margaret Morris, for allowing the chimney of her dwelling to be on fire on the 26th inst., was fined 6d and costs, 11s McConn and Elizabeth Doyle were each fined 103, and costs Os 61—James Richard Owen, who stated he was &O years of ago, and Matthew Loftus, a cripple, were convicted of begging on the 29th March, on the evidence of P.S. Walley, and were each sen- tenced to seven days' imprisonment.

Gaskell, Junior. DIIIINVINNESS.—George Miller, James Dennett, Anthony Mulligan, Joseph Stanley, and Peter McLoughlin, were each fiawl for being drunk.—James Tilley, butcher, was, on the evidence of P.S. Strickland, fined 7s. eland costs for being drunk in charge of a horse and trap, in Warrington-road, on the 21st ult.—A sinailar penalty was imposed upon Charles Bill, for a like offence, committed at the same time and place.

WILFut, DAXAGE.—EIIen Goodall, a married woman, living in Arthur-street, was summoned on a charge of wil- fully damaging the premises of Daniel Thomas, in the same street, to the extent of Bs. 6d.—lt was proved by the com- plainant and his wife that Mrs. Goodall smashed three win- dows, a window blind, and other articles.—Mrs. Goodall said she had been compelled to remove into another street to live.—The Bench ordered the defendant to pay the costs, 83. ad., and the damages. OPPANCES AGAINST THIA HIGHWAY ACT.-012 the evi- dence of P.C. Hunter, Thomas Lightfot was fined 2s. 81. and costs, 4s. 6d., for being asleep whilst In charge of a horse and cart.—Richard Owen, a carter, was charged with obstructing the highway by allowing his lurry to stand there an unreasonable time.—P.C. McGinnis stated that on the 18th March there was a lurry and three horses standing in Ann-street West for 20 minutes. At the end of that time the defendant emerged from a public-house and took charge of the horses.—lle was fined 2s. ad. and costs.

The Queen's Bench Division on Wednesday passed sen- tence of imprisonment for four months on Mr. Edmund Yates, proprietor of the World, for a gross libel on the Countess of- Lonsdale. The defendant was admitted to bail pending the result of an appeal on a technical point. GREAT FIRE IN LONDON.—A great fire occurred on Wednesday evening in Paternoster Row, London, and caused the destruction of some buildings occupied by various firms of publishers and booksellers. The flames spread to adjoin- ing property, and the lose will be enormous. PRESCOT PETTY SESSIONS. TtlESDAY.—Before Mr. F. Earle, Mr. T. Pilkington, and Mr. W. L. Evans. ASSAULT.—AIice Donoghue, a married woman, for having assaulted Bernard Philips with a fish-tin, at Prescot, on the 20th ult., was fined lOs and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment.

div.head: PRESCOT.
div.p: PRESCOT.

-- - - • Punscor LOCAL BOARD Eurcrlow.—Great interest is tie- ing manifested in the election ef two members in the place of Messrs. T. 3. Preston and C. Spencely, who retire by order this year. Mr. H. Fogg is the returning officer, and when the time expired on Saturday last for the nomination of members to serve on the Board, he received the names of nine qualified persons. The following gentlemen have de- cided to contest the two vacant seats :—Messrs. J. Beesley, J. Berry, T. Dennett, J. T. Hall, T. P. Hewitt, T. S. Preston, T. Prescot, C Spencely, and J. Saggerson. The voting papers were delivered on Wednesday last, the 2nd of April, and will be collected on Monday next, the 7th of April, when the votes will be immediately counted and the result known. It is expected that there will be a strong poll. APPOINTMENT OF OVERSEERS LT PRESCOT. At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday, before Messrs. F. Earle, T. Pilkington, and W. L. Evans, the assistant Overseers of the undermentioned townships presented the list of persona nominated as fit and proper persons to serve as overseers, and the gentlemen named were appointed, viz. :—Cronton : W. B. Longton and T. Worrell; Ditton : John Edwardson and Joseph Longton ; Huyton : T. Dobell and W. i. I..vans; Knowsley; I. Syder and R. Gore; rreseot : J. B. Pratt, t'. (I. Twist, and C. Wycherley Ranhjll: W. Lowe and John Elubbersty; Tarbock : John Kenveright and James Cartwright; Widnes: John Matthews, James White, and I A. Cowley; Whiston : William Gerrard and 0. Ward. SYSTEMATIC NEGLECT OF A FAMYLY AT WIDIMIS —At the Prescot Petty Sessions, on Tuesday last, before Messrs. F. Earle, T. Pilkington, and W. L. Evans, Thomas Grine, of Widnes, was charged under a warrant with deserting his wife and two children, whereby they became chargeable t.A. the common fund of the Prescot Union.—The prisonff pleaded guilty.—Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk to the Guardians) appeared to prosecute. He stated that it appeared that the prisoner up to the beginning of February was in fall work at Messrs. Goulding, Davies, and Company, chemical manu- facturers, Widnes, and could earn on an average 28s per week, but, unfortunately, he was of a very roving disposi- tion. About four times every year he left his wife and family, and en the particular occasion in question he left the entire district and journeyed to Jarrow, Newcastle. They sent after him there, and the man subsequently , came back to St. Helens. The re,lieving officer found that 1 the woman and her children were left in the house without I any food or clothing whatever.—Mr Scannell, relieving officer, gave evidence in support of Mr. Hartley's statement, after which the Bench committed the prisoner to prison for two months with hard labsur.

LOCAL BOARD MEETING. The annual meeting of this Board was held in the Board Room, Prescot, on Wednesday evening, Mr. C. Spencely presiding. There were also present Messrs. Preston, Hatton, Fogg, Whitfield, and Beesley; Mr. Cross (clerk), and Mr. Goldsworth (surveyor).

FINANCIAL MATTERS. The CHAIRMAN said the amount of rate collected during the past month was £232 73 10,1, leaving uncollectad £lO5 3s 3d ; that was without allowing for the irrecove:ables.— Mr. PRESTON: What is the amount of the irrecoverable rate P—The CLERK: About £75 —lt was also mentioned that some more of the rates had now been got in by the col- lector, so that there was only a comparatively small amount now outstanding, exclusive of those which were ir- recoverable.
RE-APPOINTMENT OF MEDICAL OFFICER. On the motion of Mr. Foaa, it was resolved to re-appoini Dr. Hall to be the medical officer of the Board.

THE FINANCIAL POSITION OF THE BOARD. The CHAIRMAN, referring to the financial position of the Board, said that at the 25th March the Board was entirely out of debt. On the other hand, they had various debts owing, amounting to £7l 4s Id, which might reasonably be regarded as assets that might be got in in the ordinary course. There were also uncollected rates amounting to £5l 14s 2d; and these sums, together with £127 14s 9d, cash in hand, made a total of £250 14a. He thought the Board would agree with him that that was a very satisfac- tory state of things for that Board as a result of the year's , working. The affairs of the Board had now been put into such a state that they could do with only one rate instead of having two rates running at the same time as heretofore. The town, he added, was also in a very good state from a sanitary point of view.—Mr. WHITFIELD : It is not in such a good state as I would like.—The CHAIRMAN said the sanitary state of the town was now much better than it had been daring the past few years. The Chairman, continuing, said that the surveyor's estimate of the expenditure during the coming year amounted to a total of £1.744 4s lid. He (the chairman) had estimated that this could be met by a 2s rate, so that they would see they were in a position to reduce the rate which had been last year 3s 4d in the £ and the year previous 3s 10d.— Mr. WHITFIELD thought it was the duty of the members of the Board to get the rate as low as possible, even so low as 2s or Is, which would be better still.—The Glummest : No doubt; but there is one thing better still : it would be better if they could do with no rate at all, but they could not. (Laughter.) THE BOARD AND ITS OFFICERS. The Crientmax referred in complimentary terms to the way in which the offcers of the Board, and particularly mentioned the Surveyor, had performed their duties during the past year, and concluded by moving a vote of thanks to them, which was unanimously agre,s.d to. THE NEW RATE. On the motion of Mr. FOG, seconded by Mr. BEESLEY, it was agreed that a rare of Is 6d should be levied at once, and another rate of the same amount at the end of six months.—A vote of thanks to the Chairman for his services during the past year, which was unanimously carried, con- cluded the business.

BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The usual fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday. Mr. William Tyrer presiding. There were also present the Rev. T. Chambers, T. Finegan, and John Barnacle; Messrs. John Fidler, W, Newsome, J. T. Hall, Joseph Griffith, John Ken- wright, T. Dobell, S. Marsh, T. Sadler, E. Syder, John Mat- thews, R. Tuson, T. F. Hill, James Buckley, John Leather. barrow, James Fisher, W. Gilbody, W. A. Meadows, and William Swift; and Mr. S. H. Hartley (clerk). MASTER'S REPORT.—The Master reported that there were 470 inmates in the Workhouse last week, 477 in the preced- ing week, and 541 in the corresponding week of last year. Fifty-four vagrants had been relieved during the week, as compared with 66 in the corresponding week of last year. There were 169 boys and girls in the Kirkdale schools. There had been 2SI inmates sleeping in the hospital on the previous night. THE Ismaalse or BILARIffs.—It was stated in the minutes of the Finance Committee that applications for increase of salaries had been made by Mr. Scannell, relieving officer for Widnes, and Mr. Williams, porter at the Workhouse. The committee ree .mmended that the matter be postponed until the applicants had held their respective offices for two years, and also that no application for increase of salary be enter- tained until the applicants have occupied their respective offices• two years, except in exceptional cases.—Mr. Fidler asked if it would be desirable to draw a hard and fast line about the in- crease of salaries ?-111r. Chambers mentioned that the Local Government Board had informed them that they could not entertain applications for increase of salary unless the appli- cants had been some time in the service of the Board.—The Clerk said the present applicant had almost been two years in the service of the Board. In the case of Mr. Stuart and Mr. Bullock, relieving officers, the increases had not been given before they had been two years in the service of the B.rard, and they wished to treat all their officers ann.—Mr. Matthews said the case of Mr: Scannell was an exceptional one, as he had a large district, and was a 'moat deserving officer.—The Chairman understood that the whole of the committee were In favour of the increase but for what the Local Government Board had laid down.—The minutes were then confirmed. A Raworons Qtmarrox.—A letter was read from the Local Government Board calling attention to a communication which bad been sent to them by the Bev. Father Henry, of Portic ), relative to the religion of two children named Lewis. These children, Father Henry stated, had been put down as Protestants although they bad been brought up in the Catholic faith.—Mr. Eider and Mr. Chambers expressed surprise that Father Henry had not communicated with the Guardians in the matter before writing to the Local Government Board.— This subject was referred to a committee. PROPOSED DIvISION OF lINION.—A report by Dr. Mouatt and Mr. P. G. Smith, Local CI overnment Board inspectors, as to the state oi the Workhouse, was read. It was the °Pinto., of these gentlemen that a Lew infirmary should be erected on the high ground to the east of the present workhouse.—Mr. Hall proposed that the whole matter be left to a committee, and that the local Government Board architect be asked to consult with the Board's architect.—Mr. Chambers seconded.— The Rev. Father Finegan raid there was some talk of having a division of the Union, and thought this would be a suitable op- portunity of carrying out that intention before the additions were made to the workhouse.—The Chairman aid not know that the Board was prepared to divide the Union.—Mr. Bather said it was as well to give a hint for he had heard that Widnes would be making a move before long. Tug CLERIC'S FEES—The Clerk stated that the Assessment Committee had voted him Rl5O as remuneration for services rendered in connection with the committee, and he asked them to confirm that vote. The Assessment Committee had also voted him the som of £5O for extraordinary services, but he did not want that confirmed as he intended to ask the com- mittee to re-consider that matter.—Ths vota of £l5O was con- firmed without discussion. AN INQUISITIVE Es OFFICIO MEMBER.—Mr. Newsome said there bad been a report very current and had not been non- , tradicted. that resolutions passed by that Board had been deliberately set at naught by an ex-officio Guardian. His in- formation was that an ex-offi 10 Guardian had visited the workhouse to obtain information, although there was a resolution on their books that no information was to be given to any Guardian unless at the meeting of the Board. In order that this reliort might be dented or substantiated, he moved that the matter be referred to the Visiting Committee. —Mr. Hall seconded Mr. Newsome's proposal, which was carried.

VOTE OF THANKS.—On the motion of lidr. Fidler, seconded by Mr. Meadows, a vote of thanks was accorded the chairman for his services daring the past year.—The Chairman having responded, the meeting ended.

--- NORTHERN COUNTIES OF ENGLAND FIRE INSURANCE COMPANY, LIMITED—The case of this company, which has been before the civil and criminal courts in various shapes for several years, came on again on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Chitty, on a summons taken out by the liquidator of the company to make certain directors and the manager liable to repay nioney improperly paid out of capital. The company had branches in all the towns of any size in the North of England, besides Dublin and Bel. fast : and the directors, some of whom are dead, and some have been tried and convicted, while others were acquitted, declared dividends of 10s, 355, and £2 108 per share, and r 10 per cent. Mr. Hall iwell was one of th persons convicted. i and after he had served his time he was one of the directors the liquidator now pursued for repayment Of the money improperly paid. Mr. Justice Chitty declared the liability, and directed an account to be taken of the loues and profits,! the company.

• WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the above body was held At the Board-room, the Workhouse, on Wednesday moruingr under the presidency of Mr. Greening, the other men3bere present being Major Cartwright, the Mayor (Alderman Jur' rison), Messrs. Cooper, Kilsball, Bladkhurst, Jolley, Bon' nell, Brown, Owen Appleton, Derbyshire, 110114 Humphreys, Forster, Grange, J. Elc,ughten, W. Houghton, Jeans, the Rev. IL F. Roberts, and Mr. J. C. SitttOrt (clerk). SCHOOL COMMITTEE. This committee reported that the doctor stated the chil' drea to be all well and in good health, and also recour mended that the schoolmaster and mistress be allowed It holiday; that the acaount of Messrs. Artingstall and Hindi/ for shrubs, hollies, and evergreens, amounting to £lO 3s. 7dl be paid ; that Mr. Shearer, the enquiry officer, be authorisee to visit children three times in the year who are hired ont or apprenticed by the Board, and also to visit the homes of those applying for children previous to the Board making final arrangements as to hiring and apprenticing children. Mr. Henry Stephens, of the Industrial schools, reported ItS follows :—I have inspected these schools, and find the chil- dren looking remarkably healthy and strong. Two or three of the boys have an affection of the skin which scarcel/ seems to have received the requisite attention, supposing it to be contagious. The wards and the bedding and the clothing of the children appear to be in good order! Mr. DARBYSIIIRE moved, and Mr. BLACKHURST seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Major CARTWRIGHT asked if there was not a report about the hospital that did not apPeer on the minutes—a medical officer's report.—The Catamaran There is nothing here.—Major CARTWRIGHT I Should like to know what that report is.—The CHAIRMAN : Perhaps let are alluding to the Inspector's report. —Mr. &town: s think that in the Medical Officer's book there is a minute that the docter made perhaps a fortnight ago, recommending that in cases of sickness of the children they should be re' moved to the house for proper nursing. I think it is Borne thing to that effect.—The CHAIRMAN : We have nothing te that_effect on the minutes.—Mr. DARRYSHIRE did not con' , elder that It was incumbent upon a committee to enter * matter on the minutes if a majority of the members did nct wish it.—Major Caarwaionx thought that an important matter of this description should appear on the minutes, and that it was a negligence on the part of the committee not to enter the report.—The minutes were approved. SCHOOL FEES CASES. The CLERK reported that there had been 51 old cases and 9 new ones, total 60.—Approved on the motion of Idr. BLACKHURST, seconded by Mr.Bnowtr. THE VACCINATION RETURNS. Mr. George Holford, vaccination officer, wrote saying that if 22 cases unvaccinated in the supplemental return of 1852 and of the 143 unvaccinated in the period January to June, 1883, a great majority of the cases were unfit for vaccination. and the reason they were unaccounted for was the fault ef the medical profession. He was doing his best to bring them up and get postponement certificates, and hoped in hie next returns to show a more satisfactory state of things. A RIIFRACTORY BOY. A letter was read from the School for the Blind, Liver. pool, stating that tie lad Joseph Finch, from the Warring; ton Union, bad been a constant source of trouble to them au the time he had been there. He had confessed to an at' tempt to break open the money box in the concert-roontr and was now discharged by the committee. THE CLOTHING OP PAUPER APPRENTICES. Tie Local Government Board wrote informing the Guar' diens with regard to the granting of outfits of clothing to children upon their going to servicelthat where a child wee in tie Workhouse, and the clothing was given as in-door relief, and entered in the master's books as such, no sane" tion on the part of the Board was required. If, however, the child had been out on trial, and the outfit was suplolied by the Relieving Officer and entered in his accounts, it Wei necessary that such allowance of clothing should be report*, for the sanction of the Board —Mr. DARBYSHIRE said Oast when the clothes were taken from the stores they did nol require the sanction of the Local Government Board. there was any way that they could adopt without having t.e keep asking the sanction of the Local Government Board it should be tried. It was not likely that the children should go out in Union dress. They bad never been in the habit of sending them out in Union dress, and even when oe trial they were sent in ordinary dress.—The CLERK said that one of the difficulties of giving the clothes was that the child might not like the place, or the persons might net like the child, se that the clothes would have to be re• accounted for in some way and pat back again. They else required different kinds of clothing, according to tke bug- ness to which the chiklren were apprenticed —Mr. BOSSILY, thought that if they turned the children out in Unior7 drape it would be very detrimental to their interes.s.—The sub- ject then dropped. • TOTES OF THANKS. Major CARTWRIGHT proposed a vote of thanks to the chairman for his services during the year, remarking that it gave him great pleasure and gratification to perform tkat duty. He knew that he would be expressing the feeling 01 the whole Board whea he said that their chairman had con' dueted the business of the Board with great credit to bier, self, the members, and the public (Hear, hear.) Re hop*, that Mr. Greening would again be asked to undertake th duties, and that the time was far_ distant when the Boar's would be deprived of his services.—Mr, "Lava; sow said that it was no mere matter 0' form that he rose to support the Pre. position, and he wished that the term of office of the chair, man was the same as that of the Guardians—three yeare: Mr. Greening had fulfilled the office with a zealous ane honest desire to do his duty to the public, the Board, the people in the House, and those connected with it; and be had without a doubt been successful, and had earned the respect of the Board by the impartial manner in which be had discharged his duties. He hoped that Mr. Greeniag would again be asked to take the office, and pointed out thst that course would be according to-precedeut.—Mr. JoLanf and Mr. APPLIFLON supported the resolution in suitable terms.—Mr. OwEE, speaking to the resolution, remarked that he was the one to propose Mr. Greening as chairman last year, and the Mayor said something about his being e junior, and that Major Cartwright should hall been entrusted with the duty. The Mayor had ee reason to treat him in that way. The procedure of the Board of Guardians was not the same as that of the Toell Council, and he thought that he had a perfect right t,e, make the proposition. It had been " resting in his skin ever since, 80 they would pardon him for giving it up nole• (Laughter.) He did not see why any member should take exception to another under any circumstances —Mr. Mazur 03N replied that Mr. Owen must have misunderstood him,' some way; he had never had the intention of giving hiet, offence, and if he had done so ht (Mr. Owen) must forehim.—Messra. Jeans, Brown, Derbyshire, and Cooper all? Supported the resolution, which was carried unatteii mously. The CHAIRMAN, after replying, mov a vote of thanks to Mr. Cooper, and the Rev. G. r• Roberts, vice-president and junior vice-preaident.—s_„r* Amarrow seconded, and Messrs. Derbyshire, Forster, 17' Houghton, and Harrison supported the resol °don, which was carried with acclamation and suit ably acknose; lodged.—A vote of thanks to Mr. Harrison for his eagle.' mace concluded the meeting. Arrange- 'manta have been made for the game to come off on the ground of Hartford, St. John's Club at Hartford, on Saturday after- noon next, at three o'clock. WARRINGTON WANDERERS SECOND V. RUNCORN VICTORIA. --The Wanderers Youngsters j ,urneyed to Runcorn to com- plete their last fixture, when they had the satisfaction of re- ,,*prding another victory by one try, two minors, to two minors. xne Warrington Wanderers have now completed a most sue- ` dessf ul season. The first team have played 18 matches. won 12, drawn three, lost three. and scored 11 goals, 18 tries,'67 miners, to their opponents' five goals, five tries, 59 minors. The second team have played 17 matches, won twelve, drawn one, lost four, and scored nine goals, 17, tries, 74 minors, to their op- Aonents four goals, two tries, 42 minors. OUGHTRINGTOV PARK V. MANCIIESTER.—This fixture was Played off at Oughtrington on Saturday, and resulted in favour 21 the home team by three goals to one. The match was very t°tl3' contested throughout. Two of the goals for Oughtring- Km. kicked by C G Emit'', would have puzzled a good many ,sgtsilkeepers. The otter was obtained by a scrimmage near the Teams—Oughtrington Park: Goal. G013101E13 (SECOND) —The second 4;44 of the Havdock Temperance Football Club have credited -our elves with another victory. The Golborne second team tab-4jed to Haydock on Saturday last to compete with the 4.„_°v.e team in the first round of the Earlestown and District _l7l..tiorlie Challenge Cup competition. The Golborne team arrived field about a quarter to four o'clock. and the toss was I„bY the Golborne captain. The leather was set in motion ,t!ts Temperance men, who had to play uphill during the ...rBL half-time. It looked rather doubtful for the first quarter titraeoiizii hour, but gradually the Temperance men got warm, and aghtbeautiful scrimmage succeeded in planting the leather e.at Of g ...he uprights, to the great delight of the large number it _Peor9 witnessing the game. The ball set in motion, and _rovras not very long before it was again seen skimming through rM another scrimmage, making the second goal for the Tern. rance team. Shortly after this half-time was galled, the ,`?nle team now having to play down brow. Play being --mulled. the Golborne territory was the scene of action. The I. ..,atotallers showed good combined play. At tne close of the gauze the result was four goals for the Temperance to Golborne • HaLTolf v. Mu. WAINWRIGHT'S TEAM —A team, under the ca,ytaincy of Mr. Wainwright, journeyed to Halton, on Satur- rY. to meet the village club, who were assisted by Messrs. W. Broady and R Roberts, of the Runcorn Chub, a very plea- sant game being played. Wainwright won the toss, and elscted to play up Mb. Halton kicking off against a slight breeze. Woods returned, wheo Rogers, by a good lying kick. IMOughhabout the first scrimmage in the visitors' twenty-five. a Minor point in favour of Hatton shortly afterwards being Scored. FJllowing the drop out, another scrimmage was termed in the visitors' quarters; and on the ball being kicked out by the home forwards, R ogers planted it over the cross- bar, scoring a goal for the home team. This was a particu- larly smart performance. From now until half-time the play was of a give and take character, each side scoring tries, which, however, were not improved upon. The second half was evenly contested, both sides working hard to avert a defeat, the visitors scoring two tries one of which Woods converted Into a neat goal' the borne team also obtained a try on the ed.., Be of touch, Broady making a splendid attempt at goal. Pile brought about time, th 3 game ending in a draw slightly Ili favour of the home team. The scores were—Halton, one goal, two tries, and five minor points; Wainwright 's team, goal, two tries, and two minor points.. For the visitors nwright and Antrobus put in a lot of good work, and .Were ably supported by the remainder of the teams The home '''''rakewzi Played well together, the pick of them being Broady, Hogeand J Dugdale. Booth and Wishlade played Euitt full -bra fo r their respective sides. Teams :—Halton ll 1k'461, Booth; threequarter-backs, Broady, Hassell, and ton; half-backs, Roberts and Rogers; forwards, J. EVERTON. final tie in the competition for the Liverpool and Dis- lrootball Association Challenge Cup was played on the V 01.11,1 -- of the Bootle F.O Liverpool, on Saturday afternoon hat ' 40, —e nompeting teams being Earlestown and Everton. The pro 484,7" of the Earlestown Club during the present season 'sea a most extraordinary and creditable one, and now it is I.— .„„,_ t, gulled on all hands as one of the best football organise- ..ons .o South-West Lancashire. The exceedingly smart man- ner tont;:n.ich the team fought their way into the final tie of the —4 Will be fresh within the recollection of our readers, and the t xi übborn rivalry which was known to exist between the 3 ats„t "town and Everton Clubs was sufficient to attract nearly wee, spectators, who throughout the game manifested great ezeite Wei 'flea. *specially lv towards the finish. The day was beau- doe, with scarcely a breath of wind stirring; Ishite „ starjeet_ 'act turf was in excellent condition. The ISPpee '`'W* Players were the first to put in an ratio*, and they looked in the pink of condition.

Their opponents followed a few minutes later; they, too, seemed in their very beat form, and they were cordially wel- comed by their supporters. The usual preliminaries having resulted to the advantake of the Everton captain, no time was out to waste, and shortly before 3-30 Daguall in behalf of Earlestown started the game. Marriott returned the ball;bnt a free kick for "hands" In front of the Earle stown uprights passed off harmlessly. For some few minutes Everton pressed their opponents, and shots began to fall heavily on the Earles- to an citadel, the principal aggressors being Pickering and Gib- son. Preston meanwhile being very conspicuous in feeding the forward rank. At length the serge was raised and Earlestown gained a corner kick which Gibson turned to a trifling advan- tage, as that player sent the leather back. The Ja'arlestrown lett and centre, composed of Sim m, Cameron, and Dagnalt next broke away, and on being checked, Higgins and Parry again transferred hostilities to the opposite end, a final shot at goal passing outside, whilst a closely-following shot by M'ollloolll- - Champion to use his hands. Dux sury then contributed a fine bit of play, but Williams securing possession spoiled a good chance by making a wild shot at goal, succeeding a high a capital passing movement was ex muted by M Gill, Berry, and ' Williams, the former eventually being successfully tackled by Bowker in front of goal. Notwithstanding some clever head- ing by Berry and Preston, Whalley eventually cleared danger: and half-time was reached without a goal being scomd. The excellent defence of the Earlestown men and goalkeeper exeted much enthusiasm among the supporters of the country club. After a shoo rest ends were changed, and Weill re-started the leather for Everton. The Earlestonians very early made an attask on their opponents goa', and for a considerable time it was seriously endangered. Cheered on by the encouraging shouts of their supporters, the Earlestown men redoubled their exertions, and severely pressed the Liverpud liens. The latter were evidently becoming "fagged." and after ten minutes fast play they appeared almost unable to make a stand against the attack of the Earlestonians. Several splendid attempts to score were made, and to all appearance Everton was in for a thrashing. The latter commenced to play rough, however, and the Eariestown men were much knocked about. About quarter or an hour after the redommencement Rich, while dribbling the ball, was violently charged by one of the Everton backs, and was 'knocked to the ground. For about ten minutes he remained in bad condition, many persons be- lieving that he had been fatally injured. The play was stopped for over that period, while efforts were made to restore tim. and the gains was afterwards resumed by Earlestown with ten men. From now, for a brief interval, the play assumed a more even and interesting character, the cheers for Earlestown being loud as Duxbury and Dagnall headed an attack which caused Lind- say to use his hands. The play was fast and exciting, Cameron and Whalley for Earlestown and Parry and Higgin for Ever- ton playing up with marked ability. Earlestown secured two corner kicks in quick succession, the last being well met by the Everton backs, who passed over to Berry, and the latter taking the tall along the wing delivered the hall to the centre, when Parry rushed up and shot the ball through the Earles- town uprights amidst tremendous cheering, some twenty-five minutes having elapsed from the time ends were changed. An objection was raised on the plea of off-side play, but as the referee declared he had not seen any informality the point was recorded. No sooner had the game been re-started than Hig- gins and Preston traversed the sphere into Eariestown's quarters, the final shot of Williams beng erratic. Still the onslaught was maintained, WGIII being prominent in the at- tack, whi e the defensive play of Duxbury and Emmett was very fine. By a series of throws-in, the Earlestonlans forced their way to the opposite end, where Simm from the left sent in a hot shot to Marriott Again Earlestown had the ball at the corner, but nothing came of it, and the lines being cleared Preston contributed some exceedixgly clever play, which en- abled the Everton captain to make a futile shot at goal, the ball going high over the bar. Gibson also failed, and on Em- mett, who was ably supported by others, transferring the play to the Everton camp, Duxbury sent in a stinger, which almost steered, the goalkeeper just managi og to tip the ball away with the toe of his boot. The twrst of the leather sent

it spinning just outside the post, and from the corner kick which ensued an existing scrimmage ensued in front of the Everton goal. Danger was temporarily averted, but, on the ball being again brought near to theEverton gual,a discreditab!rs scene was witnesses'. One of the Everton team deliberately struck an Earlestown player, and as the latter retaliated the spectators rushed over the field from all quarters The excited parti ace of both elevens indulged in high words, blows were struck between several parties, and a general fight appeared likely to ensue. A police constable with his staff drawn. assisted by officers of the associatien, succeeded in quelling the disturbance, however, and the game was again resumed, after the field of phy had beedcleared. In the few minutes that remained for play the Earlestonians made a gallant attempt to secure an equalising point. but this they were unable to accomplish, and when the whistle blew Everton were left the proud winners of the district trophy and gold medals by one goal to nil, after a hard-fought game. Champion in goal played superbly for the losing side, and the defenders were in splendid form, while for Everton, what little fell to Lindsay was admirably done, the pick of the others being Marriott, Preston, Parry, Higgins, Gibson. and Berry. On the result becoming known there were great rejoicings in Everton, the winning team being driven triumphantly through the streets. the following were the teams :—Everton O. M. Lindsay, goal ; T. Marriott and R. Morris, backs; J. Pickering, W. Parry, and J. Preston, half-backs; E. Berry and D. H. Williams, right wing; J, M•Gill (captain), centre; M. Higgins and W. Gibson, left wing; umpire, Mr. Gunning. Earlestown :T. Champion, goat; R. Green (captain) and F. Emmett, backs; J. Whalley, T, Duxbury, and R. Bowker, half-backs; W. Rich and J. Elli- son, right wing; A. Dagnall, centre; J. Sims and J. Cameron, left wing; umpire, Mr. P. Haatie. Referee, Rev. 0. A. Carter (of the St. Mary's P.C., Liverpool).

div.head: "A DAY ON THE HILLS."
div.p: "A DAY ON THE HILLS."

Numerous intellectual treats have been afforded the peo- ple of Warrington by means of the Educational Fund of the Warrington Co-operative Society, and one of the most interesting, instructive, and enjoyable lectures given under its auspices was the last, which was given in the society's hall on Monday evening. A large number of persons assembled at the rendezvous, and under the able guidance of the Rev. W. Tuckwell, of Stokewell, near Rugby, spent an imaginative "Day on the Hills." Amongst the com- pany were the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, Rev. M. Stephen- son, Mr. Charles White, Mr. T. Birchall, Mr. G. Woods, Mr. H. Whitham, dre.—Mr. WHITE, in introducing the lecturer, spoke words of commendation of the society under whose auspices they met, and indeed whose guests they were; and, after referring to the attempt made N years ago by Dr. Birkbeck to impart to the working classes something of the elements of a superior education by means of Mechanics' Institutes, said he thought if Dr. Birkbeck were alive now, and could have seen what that society and other kindred societies had done throughout the length and breadth of the country for the education of working men, he would have said that if this was not a child of his own it was a grandchild. Mr. TUCBWELL, at the outset, followed the workers of the East end of London to their various holiday resorts, and- from the manner in which they spent the day, concluded that Sir John Lubbock's boon to the working classes of four holidays in the year was only half a boon, as it needed some one else to show them how to use it. With this view he asked those present to imagine that they had just emerged from a little roadside railway station within a mile or two of a hill on which they were to spend the day. They were not by any means empty handed, for they had much to do with the hill that day. In a humourous manner he then described the equipment of the botanists, geologists, and entomologists of the company as they set out for the journey, proceeding first along the hedge side, and then through fields of waving corn (the flora of which he vividly described) to the foot of the hill, where they sat down to rest by a pretty little labourer's cottage. Here they entered into conversation with the intelligent labourer (who was spending his holiday in his garden) respecting his beehives. The labourer gave them the history of a bee, explained to them the use of bees as fertilisers, and pointed out that they taught a moral lesson by their industry, a practical lesson through their wonderful and inexplicable foresight, a social lesson by tneir community of labour and discipline, and a political lesson by their equality of rank, equality of labour, and equality of pay. Ascending the hill, the lecturer dwelt upon the floral treasures to be found iu the marshy ground, in the belt of woodland and on the hill top, where if they looked they would see a soaring kite go up in enormous circles while all the little birds hide themselves in the valley. They would hear the humming of invisible bees, the ' warbling of invisible larks, and the hissing of invisible grasshoppers, and in many parts of the hills the murmuring waterfalls in the distance; and every now and then that bleating of the lamb which they thought nothing of in the valley, but which was so startling on the hill; sometimes the croak of a great raven which flies away emitting an angry note—just like a cracked church bell. In a cap- tivating style he proceeded to explain the for- mation of the hills, and said there were thousands of their fellow-men —he might almost say hundreds of thousands who never had enjoyed, and never could enjoy, such a sight, who never saw the country, and did not know what meant the waving crops, the luxuriant trees, and the beautiful pastures, who had never strayed far beyond the streets in which they lived. Was it to be always so? or was there "a good Li me com- ing" for these hapless wretches? The answer lay with the working men. An epoch was coming in English history such as never had come before, when working men, by their voting power at the poll, would shape the future history of England. Let them use their power for themselves and for their order, for with the prosperity of the wage-earning classes lay the prosperity of England. Let them use it to turn ugliness into beauty, use it to turn miserable overwork into wholesome leisure, use it to turn starvation into plenty. There were two black spots in this country of ours which would bring it to ruin if they were not eradicated—the ex- cessive poverty of the many and the excessive richness of the few. (Applause.) He next adverted to the superstition Of the inmates of old English homesteads, and again passing out of doors, alluded to life in the ponds, which he illus- trated by sketches hung en the walls. The lecture throughout was listened to with deep interest, and a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. Tuckwell at the close, on the motion of Mr. E. Green, seconded by Mr. Birchall. A like compliment to the chairman concluded the meeting.

The large fly-wheel, and one piece, weighing about four tons, was driven through the engine-house Wall and thrown a distance of 40 yards. ALLEGED FRAUDS BY • MAGISTRATE—At Rye, on Mon- day, Mr. James Collins Hoad, a shipbuilder, alderman, and magistrate, was charged with conspiring with his son, who has absconded, to defraud the London and Counties Bank- ing Company of £6,970 by forged acceptances to bills of exchange: Bills were drawn upon smack ownems at Hull, Grimsby, and Ramsgate, with whom flout did business. There were altogether between 60 and 70 discounted by the son, and credited to the father's account. 'rue prisoner was committed for trial at the assizes. CORONERS' SALARIES IN LANCASHIRB AND CHESHIRE.— A return in reply to an address to the House of Commons of Lord Randolph Churchill giving the number of coroners for counties and boroughs, together with the salaries and emoluments respectively paid to each, has just been issued. Blackburn district: Salary, £520; Salford, £800; Rochdale, £550; Bolton, £450; West Derby, £800; Preston, £330; Lancaster, £llO. None of these had any emoluments. Manor of Furness, £150; Manor of Walton-le-Dale, £10; Manor of Prescot, £10; and Manor of Hale, £l. These four coroners are appointed by the Lord of the Manor with no emoluments. Wigan by emoluments, average for the last three years, £97 lie id. Bolton borough paid by fees, average for three years, £152; Chester division, salary, £510; Knutsford division, £386; Stockport division, £407; and honor or fee of Halton, £B5. None of these received any emoluments. Borough of Birkenheal, salary £2lO, in lieu of fees and travelling expenses; City of Chester average emoluments for the three years, £46 13s 4d.. _Manchester

Orford, Was brought up in custody befovo the Mayor (Alderman Harri- son), .-s4d other magistrates, on a charge of stealing a pina- fore, value 6d., from a stall in the Warrington Market, on Saturday last. Prosecutriz, Margaret Shaw, a second-hand clothes dealer living at Altrincham, attends Warrington Market an Wednesdays and Saturdays. On the Saturday previous, the prisoner irspectel various articles on Mrs. Shaw's stall, and finally she agreed to purchase a window blind and curtain, which she rolled up into a bundle. Mrs. Shaw thought that the bundle was rather bulby, and on sbening it she found the pinafore in question inside.— Prisoner was fined 10e. and costs, or 14 days in default of payment. &rarer ROWDTISII.—At the Warrington Borough Polies Court, on Monday, before the Mayor kAlderenan Harrisou) and ether magistrates, William Connor, fish hawker, fledgecock, and Thomas Hugh Skellen, waterman, Sankey, were ‘charged with committing a breach of the peace in Sankey-street, on the 24th ult. -Skelton also charged Con- nor with assaulting him at the same time and place.—The police having given evidence as to eeeing the two men fight- ing, Mr. Browne, solicitor, Warrington who appeared for Skellen, admitted that his client struck Conner, but sub- mitted that it was in self defence. Skellen, be said, was walking past the site of the new Conservative Club when Connor pushed against him, and on being remonstrated with struck him. Skelton then punished him.—The Bench hound Conner over in one surety of £5, and himself in £lO, to keep the peace for six months, and discharged

A VIOLENT WOMAN SENT TO PRISON.—At the Warring- ton Borough Police Court, on Monday, before the Mayor (Alderman Harrison) and other magistrates, Anne Jordan. a powerful looking woman, was charged with assaulting and wounding James and Julia Rourke' on the 2fith ult.—Mr Hunt (chief constable) said that the complainants, James Rourke. a farm labourer' and Julia Rourke. his mother, lodged in Kiaders-yard, Bridge-street, and the defendant, a single woman, employed as a field hand, had lodgings at the same house. About nine o'clock en Friday night a quarrel arose between the defendant and the male complainant. They had all been drinking beer, and James Rourke was in- clined to go to bed, but the defendant wished him to pay his share towards another glass of beer being fetched in. This he declined to do, and the defendant then got into a rage and threatened to run a knife into him. She then hit him on the mouth with her fist and he hit her back again. Julia Rourke interfered and Jordan struck her with the knife, causing a serious wound on the temple. James Rourke was dragged into the yard, and when on the ground defendant struck him three or four times with a poker that she had got from a neighbour's house. The police were then called in and the complainants were attended to by Dr. Fox.-Prisoner was sentenced to four months' hard labour. EIPRNSITI JCPURNISTS FROM LIVERPOOL TO WARRING- Tole.—/t the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Satur- day, before Aldermen Chandley and Burgess, Geo. Foster, a tanner, of Howley Quay, Warrington. was charged with riding on the Cheshire Railway from Aintree to Warrington, without having previously paid his fare, with intent is defraud the company. On the previous evening a special train from Aintree to Warrington was stopped by a signal near the White Cross Wire Works, and the prisoner was area to leave sine of the carriages and make across the field as though trying to escape. He was followed by a porter named Hudson, who brought him back towards the station, but he again escaped. Hudson ince more gave chase, and ultimately found him hiding in 'some farm build- ings. Prisoner pleaded guilty,And was fined 40s and costs, or one month's imprisonment.—At the same court, on Mon- day. before the .Mayor ',Alderman Harrison) and other magistrates, John William Best (20), of Manchester, was brought up on a similar charge. The prisoner and two other nen were seen to enter a carriage of a train from Liverpool to Manchester on the previous day, and a detective pro- ceeded with the train as far as Warriugton, where he searched the carriage in question, and found the prisoner concealed under the seat, the other men trying to screen him from observation. lie admitted not having paid his fare, and said that he bad no money, but on being searched 2s Bd4 was found in his possession. Re was fined 40e and i costs, n default to go to gaol for a month,-4.1 the! norouch Police Court, on Thursday morning, Matthew Fielding, a respectably-dressed man, was charged with riding in a third- class carriage without a ticket from Lime-street, Liverpool, to Warrington, on the day previous. On the arrival of the train from Liverpool he war found concealed under the seat of the carriage. Re was fined 401 and costs, or a month. TELE WIRB-ROD TRADE IN ENGLAND AND GERMANY The Loado-a Iron Trade Exchange says :—The Warrington iroa drawers should remember the Eastern adage of the last straw and the camel's back. The vertebra of the English wire trade has:already been severely strained by Continental competition, and disinterested observers have not failed to notice that, in at least this one branch of British industry, John Bull has been pushed into a corner by the intelligent foreigner. In this issue we print a letter from Mr. Claude J. Morris, honorary secretary of the Iron and Steel Wire Manufacturers' Association, in which he gives a short ex- planation of the circrunstancea under which the Wartington wiredrawers continue on strike. A short time since we re- ferred to a paper read by Mr. Thomas Morris, of Warring- ton, on the "Westphalian Wire Manufacturing Industry," the result of his observations in that district. Mr. Thomas Morris dealt more particularly with the wire rod or rolled wire industry, showing the great advantage which low-priced labour gave the German over the English manu- facturer. Referring to the wire drawing industry which at Warrington is suspended by the strike, it was stated in the paper referred to that in England it cost £6 13s 7d to draw annmber 4 wire rod down to No. 20 wire gauge; whereas in Westphalia the same work is accomplished at a cost of £3 10s 5d This shows that the wire drawers here earned nearly double the wages of their Continental competitors. We do not suggest that they should work for such low wages as the Germans, knowing that this would in this country mean starvation. We do suggest thhat the men should open their eyeamtoeteh.ettancett tihnatthuisnlecsosutntre wiredraw- ing industry is to become men must adapt themselves to altered circumstances,yill work with a will, and be satisfied with such wageseyasmul:t result of their labour entitles them to. Mr. Claude Morris strikes a note of warning to the men if they will hear it, when he states what we know to be a fact, that although the world's consumption of wire has increased enormously during recent years the production in this country has declined. It appears that in Birmingham and elsewhere the wiredrawers have accepted the reduction, and have been working under it for three weeks, and informa- tion afforded has shown their average earning to be from 40a to 45s per week, but the Warrington men have held out against what to us seems the inevitable result of foreign competition—a reduction in wages. The wire trade has been " very sick" many months, and if the Warrington drawers were only desirous of extinguishing what little vitality is left, they could not have taken a more effective course at a more opportune moment. But if the Warrington men, knowing that we are losing our hold on the wire trade of the world, are anxious to do their part towards regaining Our lost position,or at least retaining what trade we have, then they are adopting a TNT unlikely laethod for further- ing the object.
