There were also present Aldermen Reimers, Kean, Pickmere. Webster, Councillors Platt, Pier. point, Greening, Brown, Dixou, Dakin, Marsh, Belton, Bur- gess, Wright, Caldwell, Hutchinson, Barker, Francomb, Sutton, Litton, Whittle, Messrs. W. li. Brook (town clerk), J. L. Whittle (deputy town clerk), C. Cherley (boroogh treasurer), J. Paterson (gas manager), T. Longdin (borough surveyor). 'aren comettrtwn : 'SUNDAY NIWIT IN GAMEY- sYRRET. The MAYOR moved, and Alderman WEBSTER seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Watch Committee. Couucillor DIXON wished to ask if the regulation of the traffic in Sankey-street on Sunday evenings could not be improved. As an instance of the necessity kr a better regu- lation of the traffic he mentionoil haying seen a girl very rudely treated by a number of boys near the site of the new Conservatbre Club. He should like to know if they could not do something more to put a stop to -tuch practices. It was not that the traffic was too great, .bot it was the way the peoplecondected themselves. Tiro traffic should be. regulated.in 'Sankey-Street, down Parker-street, and along! WilSott,Patten-street. Alderman WEnsrErt thought thct it would have been better if Councillor Musa had assisted the police instead of complaining to the Council. All that the police could do was to keep the crowd in its proper direction, and he thought that when gentlemen saw occurrences of the kind described.bv Councillor Dixon they should do their best.to

prevent them. Councillor FRANCOMB said that at 8-30 on the previous night he went through Sankey-street, and he was astonished to see it so quiet with such a crowd. The Watch Cornmit. tee tad had the subject before them on several occasions and they had given Mr. Hunt, and through him the polite, verions orders to do all in their power to prevent anything like unseemly behaviour in the streets, and he believed that the instructions of the committee had been thoroughly carried oat. Considering that there was only such a small apace for the public to parade in, he did not think Coen- cillor Dixon should be so hard and take a case which might be very exceptional. (Hear, hear.) Alderman PiCEntERE said that at the last meetiag of the frown Hall Committee the idea was suggested of snaking more ample space as a means for the public to walk about in, in front of the Town Hall. He did not see why that should not be done, for it would be a very pleasant walk to the inhabitants. Councillor SrerTox said that he SAW nothing objectionable in Sankey-Street on Sunday evenings. The crowd Was largely composed of young people who mast have some where to walk, and he did not see anything particularly ob- jectionable in their conduct. The MAYOR expressed himself confident that the police I did everything in their power to preserve order in the streets, and said that it must be obvious to anyone that the large population of Warrington together with the narrowness of its streets, must occasionally lead to a block, and particu- larly on -Sunday evenings, when there were a large number of people about. He was sure that the police did all they could to reduce the nuisance, if one existed, to a minimum. Witioregard to the suggestion as to widening out the land near the Town Hall,he certainly believed that it would relieve the traffic of Sankey-street. and many people shared the same opinion. He hoped that when the subject came before the Council they would give it their support. The minutes were then adopted. EATING AND SEWERAGE COMMITTEE. Alderman KEAN moved, and Councillor Baown seconded, the adoption of the minutes of this committee. Councillor PLATT drew attention to an item of £3OO for the wood paying of Sankey-street inserted in the estimate of expenditure by the committee for the ensuing half-year. He had no doubt that wood paying, being noiseless and comfortable, was very nice to the inhabitants of the street, but he had a doubt whether it would be found economical or useful in any other way. He instanced a street in Man- chester that bad bsen wood paved, saying that it now pre- sented a sorry st clack, the weather having affected it to a large extent. lie thought that wood paving was a luxury that they would not be prepared to adopt to any large ex- tent. Alderman WEBSTER hoped that the committee would give wood paying a fair trial. In favour of wood paving he alluded to the condition of Bold-street, Liverpool. In the centre of the town the streets should be almost noiseless for the proper transaction of business in the shops, and he hoped therefore that the committee would give it a trial, and adept the best method that they could. Councillor Bonuses expressed a similar hope. Councillor SUTTON, while supporting the scheme, said theta must be borne in mind that Bold-street, Liverpool, had sot to bear the same traffic as had some of the streets in Warrington. The traffic was considerably heavier in Warrington than the traffic through Bold-street. The MAYOR thought that it was now too late to discuss the question, as it had already passed the Council. The Togra c,x,..ar slid that as a matter of procedoeo *Loy lasJ a right to discuss amount or tau estimate, but not the question as to whether they should adept the principle of wood paving. The MAYOR remarked that Ludgate Hill, London, was paved with wocd sets, and said that he understood it had been a success wherever tried. The minutes were approved. MARKETS COmMrrrES. Councillor DIXiN moved, and Councillor Lorron seconded, the adoption of the minutes of the Markets Com- mittee. Alderman WORM]; alluding to an estimated expendi- ture of £3OO for flagging additional ground in Market street, said that he presumed the land to be flagged was that which would accrue to the committee by the palling down of the buildings now in course of demolition. He should like to urge upon the committee the propriety of adding the ground to the street, and permanently widening it as far as pos- sible. It would be an improvement to the market and a boon to the stall holders. The proceedings of the committee were approved. SANITARY COMMITTEE. The adoption of the minutes of the Sanitary Committee was proposed by Councillor Suwon, and seconded by Coun- cillor Efaancouis. Councillor WHITTLE called attention to an item of £ll4 for new boilers and remodelling the hot water apparatus at the hospital. The building was comparatively a new one, and had already cost a lot of money. It was a white elephant which had cost them a deal, and he wanted to know where all the money went to. He did not think that lit was right to pass the amount asked for. This work had been done about three times in four years—(laughter)--- aad there were only two firms who seemed to do any of the work—John Chorley and Greening and Son. (Increased laughter.) CoEl=lllol' GREENING said that Councillor Whittle was the sort ot man whe spoke without thinking. He did not think at all—(laughter )—but merely opened his month and let it say whatever it liked. (Loud laughter.) Perhaps the £ll4 did look a large sum, but be was not going into the de- tails of it. It was quite true th it Greening and Sin did do the work, and that John Chorley had supplied goods to the hospital, but before they were ordered. some gonsidta- tion took place, and the committee thought that it would be to their interest to employ those firms. He thought that if the Sanitary Committee consulted the well-being of the tows they would elect Mr. Whittle a member if the com- mittee, and thee he would be able to show them how the money ehoald be spent. The recommendation "that the borongh surveyor be in- structed to adapt the existing condenser at Longford depot for suppressing stink through water, and that this be done at once," gave rise to some discussion, bat it was explained that it was only intended to try it as an experiment, which it was hoped would be successful. With regard to the minute "that the T°W.l Clerk submitted a notice from the clerk to the Guardians and the Rural Sanitary Authority of the intention of the Rural Sanitary Authority to terminate the agreement with this Authority for the reception and treatment of patients in the Hospital for Infectious Diseases," he remarked that that was simply a notice from the Authority to the committee, which they were bound to accept.

FINANCE COMMITFEE: THE INCREASED IMPROVEMENT RATE.

Alderman HOLMES moved, and Councillor GREENING seconded, the confirmation of the minutes of the Finance Committee. Councillor BOLTON called attention to the increased im- provement rate which was now 3s. in the £. He found in 1870 a 25. 9d. rate brought in £8,647, and in 1883 £15,779. The borough rate for 1870 realised £2,352, and in 1883 £9,164, giving a total for 1870 of £10,999, and for 1883 of £24,943. That increase was rather more than in proportion to the increased population. The rates were now over 10. per head, whereas they were previously only 6s. Bd. • He attributed this increase in the rates to the tendency of com- mittees to carry on experiments. In reference to Longford, he found in 1881 the estimate for the sale of manure for the half-year was £BlO, but for the present half-year the esti- mate was £6OO. On the proposition of Alderman EIOLICES the following resolutions were passed :—(1) That the Council hereby es- timate that the amount of £4,512 16e 7d will, in addition to the borough fund, be required and sufficient for the pur- poses to which the borough fund is applicable, under the Municipal Corporations Act, 1882, or otherwise by law, for the half-year to end 29th September, 1884; (2) that the Council order a borough rate to be made to raise the said amount; (3) that the Council assess the contributions to be made on the several parishes and parts of parishes in the borough; (4) that the overseers ot Warrington, Latch- ford, and Thelwall be called upon for their contributions out of the poor rate made for the taid townships : (5) That the estimate for an improvement rate as recom- mended by the Finance Committee be confirmed, and that the Finance Committee do make an inaptovement rate ac- cordingly at one shilling and sixpence in the pound, and be authorised to affix the common seal of the borough thereto. (6) that the estimate for a sewers rate, as recom- mended by the Finance Committee, be confirmed, and that the Finance Committee do make a sewers rate accordingly at twopence in the pound, and be authorised to affix the common seal of the borough thereto. THE QUALITY OS THE OAS. Councillor Limos moved "That it be an instruction to the Gas Committee to have the gas analysed daring the month of April, and to submit the result of such analysis to the Council at its next meeting." Councillor Bovrox formally seconded the motion, which, however, met with no encouragement, and was lost.

SALE OF WORK AT WARRINGTON. The large room at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Chapel, War- rington, was on Thursday afternoon resplendent with that motley host of attractive articles which go to make up what is desirable as a sale of work. For some months now the ladies of the congregation have been busily engaged in manufacturing and begging a varied collection of goods, with which they desired to raise funds to complete the fur- niture of the church, to purchase crockery for use at their frequent social gatherings, and also an organette to render more attractive the week night services. The result of their I labours was the eminently satisfactory array of articles dis- played upon the stalls, of which there were three—one being laden with toys, wearing apparel, dec.; another with books and fancy goods; and the third. Cat a choice collection of plants and cut flowers. Ample provision for the visitors in the shape of creature comforts had also been made, the re- freshment stall being replete with delicacies of various kinds. The stalls were under the management of Mrs. Horton, Mrs. Hayward, and Mrs. Rippon, ably assisted by several other ladies. The Mayor (Alderman Harrison) had consented to open the sale, and when his Worship arrived, accompanied by the Mayoress, there were also present the Revs. T. Rip- pon, J. McTuric,J. Bennett Anderson (Liverpool), J. Yonge (Congregationalist), and W. Morton (Primitive Methodist) ; Messrs. W. Barlow, W. Horton, I. Hayward, J. Shaw Greeo, E. Place, F. Wright, J. W. Hall, T. B. Carter, drc. The Rev. T. likprosr, in the absence of their esteemed superintendent, the Rev. J. Eglinton, who he was sorry to say, was from home owing to physical indisposition, asked 4 his worship to open the sale of work. He referred to the readiness of the Mayor to comply with any invitation that had for its object the good of the town generally, as well as the good especially of the churches—(hear, hear)—and alter expressing their sympathy as Wesleyan Methodists with all other churches, and especially the Church of England, of . which their founder John Wesley was a clergyman, and the Mayor was now a member, he proceeded to speak of War- rington Methodism. The circuit ex'ended from 98, Bewsey- road, Warrington, in one direction to Antrobus in another, and from Martinscroft in ens direction to Penketh in another; so that their parish was fairly wide. After his last visit to Warrington John Wesley described the War- ringten Methodists as a very steady people, and he would like to say, speaking from his three years' experience of Warrington Methodists, that they were an enterprising people. He thought that was proved to-day when he told them that at Bold-street they were just now building schools that would cost upwards of £2,000, and at Sankey Bridges they contemplated building a new chapel, that at Penketh they were going to extend the premises at a cost of £l,OOO, and that at Padgate they meant to extend their school premises. He thought all that went to show they were a fairly enter- prising people. He then explained the object of the sale of work, the success of which was probably due to the labours of Mrs Horton, who had been ably assisted by her husband and the members of her family. (Applause.) The Mayon, after alluding to the display of goods, said he though the most practical way in which they could show their appreciation o, the ladies' devotion was to carry home with them as many of the beautiful things as their pockets would permit. (Hear, bear.) Ha believed the fair ladies who presided at the stalls woulcttake care to give them in exchange for their money a substantial equivalent, and not only so, but they would give them plenty of gracious smiles and courteous thanks. (Hear, hear.) He thought he might without hesitation congratulate the three rev, gentlemen, two of whom he saw before him, upon having such zealous industrious, persevering, self-sacrificing church workers, and he hoped the pecuniary result of the sale of work would far exceed their most sanguine expectations. In pursuance of the authority vested in him, as the lawyers said, he pro- eeeded to delare the sale of work duly open, and added words which had special significance at this very time—

_ "God save the Queen." (Rear, hear.) On the proposition of Mr. VV. Basitost, seconded by Mr. W. Hoßrosi, and supported by the Rev. J. TONGIE, a Tote of thanks:eras accorded the Mayor,land business began.

WARRINGTON A-SSESSMENT COM- MITTEE. The monthly meeting of this Committee was held at the Workhouse yesterday, there being present Mr. J. Bylands (in the chair), Major Cartwright, Messrs. G. Blackhurst, W. Darbyshire, E. C. Cooper W. Balharry, John Greening, G. Appleton, J. Sutton ?clerk), S. Sutton (assistant clerk), Wiliam Owen (valuer), and the Assistant Over- seers. THId ASSIISSMEITY OF RAILWAY PSOPIRTY.—After the hearing of the assessment appeals a discussion took place as regards the assessment contributions paid by railway companies, and Mr. Cooper remarked that there was a deal of people who thought that the railway companies did not pay a proper portion.—The Chairman remarked that the question was a difficult one. The railway companies paid a large proportion of the rates, and instead of bringing paupers into the district they really had an opposite ten- dency, and therefore they should not be harsh upon them.— The subject then dropped. Tea Vatuna's Sat.any.-A. letter was read from the valuer, Mr. Owen, stating that he had now for some time occupied the position of valuer for the Warrington and Latchford districts, and that he was willing to undertake the duties for the whole Union—taking properties of all kinds, only excluding railway lines—for the sum of £2oo:a year, or he was willing to take the duties for six months. and then brine forward a proposal for payment, showing the amount of work devolving upon him.—On the motion of Mr. Black. burst, seconded by Mr. Balharry, it was decided that the committee recommend the Board øf Guardians to accept Mr. Owen's offer for 12 month. Tin CLERK'S SALARY.—The Clerk claimed the attention of the committee to a statement in respect to his salary. He pointed out that it had stood at the same figure since his appointment, whereas, as was shown by the minute book, the work in connection with the office had yearly in- creased. He had been told that there was a general pression that his emoluments from the Union were £1,200 a year, but altogether they were not half that, and out of the amount he had three clerks to pay, so that his own salary did net come to more than the salary of a junior clerk. He had certainly never asked for an increase, and simply made these remarks because he thought that a person should be paid according to his abilities.—Mr. Sutton then retired, and the Board discussed the matter.—Mr. Cooper said that he appreciated Mr. Sutton's services very highly, and they could not hare a better clerk, but he thought that perhaps Mr. Sutton would not mind it the question was left over for 12 months, considering how bad was the state of trade.—The Chairman remarked that £4O or £5O was nothing to what they would have had to pay if they had bad a professional man as clerk. He thought Mr. Sutton was very much underpaid.—After some further coaversa- tion, during which the services of the clerk were highly eul.gised, it was decided, en the motion of Mr. Greening, seconded by Mr. Appleton, " that be receive £25 extra in consideration of the extra work." A vote of thanks was passed to the chairman at the close of the meeting, for the year's term of office, en the motion of Mr. Cooper, seconded by Mr. Greening. Mr. Rylands Lae been chairman of the committee for 22 years.

. LORD EUSTON'S DIVORCE CASE. In the London Divorce Court, yesterday, the Earl of Euston presented a petition for the nullity of his marriage with Kate Walsh Smith, on the ground that she had another husband alive. It was proved, however, that Smith him- self was a married man when he married the present Countess of Euston and that, therefore, she was legally free, when she married the Earl of Euston. The petition was I therefore, dismissed. I ACCIDENT TO THE DUKE OF EDINBURGH.

A telegram from the Channel Fleet has reached the Exchange Telegraph Company stating that while the fleet lay in Marmonica Bay the Duke of Edinburgh met with a slight accident while landing from a boat. He fell owing to the gangboard slipping, and sprained his knee. The doctor ordered him to take a few days' rest. FOREIGN SUGAR BOUNTIES.—DEPUTATION TO LORD DERBY. Lord Derby, replying yesterday afternoon to a deputation of West Indian sugar planters and merchants, said he would be very glad to see foreign sugar bounties abolished, but unless the countries concerned could be persuaded that such abolition would be to their interest, representations from Her Majesty's Government would not have much weight. He would, however, consult Lord Granville on the subject. Lord Derby added that he had speken to the United States Minister about placing West Indian Islands on the most favoured nation relations with America, but nothing had been done, and he was awaiting an opportune moment foe reopening the question. SEAMEN'S DEPUTATION TO MR. CHAMBERLAIN. Replying to a Deputation of Seamen who waited on him In support of the Merchant Shipping Bill, Mr. Chamberlain said it was his firm intention to adhere strictly to the two main principles of the Bill, viz., that shipowners should not be able to make a profit out of the loss of vessels, and that shipowners should be liable for neglecting the interests of the officers and seamen. He was not certain but that undermanning was not a more serious evil than overloading, but he objected to any minimum scale of crew as it would probably have the effect rather of lessening the number of men employed by conscientious owners. Moreover the strongest penalties which the Bill proposes to impose for undermaaning would, Mr. Chamberlain believed, have the desired effect. He added that he fully recognised the right of pilots to compensation where direct loss was proved to result from the abolition of compulsory pilotage, and the Bill will, if needed, be amended in this respect. MANCHESTER SHIP CANAL BILL.

The Lords Committee met again yesterday morning, the Duke of Richmond presiding.—Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., was the first witnessed called, examined by Mr. Pember, Q.C. Mr. Bright said the population of Lancashire was growing, he believed, considerably faster than that of the kingdom generally; and they mast of course find employment at home or they must mi- grate. There was a feeling in Lancashire, which had much to do with the support given to the scheme, that they were too much dependant on one industry, end the de- mand for the canal, he believed, was based quite as much upon the belief that it would attract varied industries to the neighbourhood of Manchester as that it would greatly re- duce the cost of carriage. The current of opinion in favour of the scheme was wide and deep, and the meeting of the Chamber of Commerce in February last was the most re- markable he had known. There was now a feeling in favour of the scheme which did not exist when the scheme was first before Parliament. With regard to the moneyed classes and capitalists some, no doubt, were timid, and some few did not sympathise with the scheme ; but the statement that they were opposed to it was entirely untrue. It was very foolish to make such a statement when the list of subscribers was considered.— Rave you any doubt that there is a bena- fide intention to carry out the scheme if sanctioned ? None whatever.—Will the capital be forthcoming ?--• If the bill is passed, the canal will be made.— Mr. John Slagg, M.P., who was next examined, gave statistics to show the inferior position this country occupies as compared with other countries in the matter of inland navigation. It was desirable to enlarge the basis of trade in Manchester, and he thought the canal would tend in that direction. As regards the allegation that this scheme was a speculation the provision relative to the trust arrangement was a complete answer. CtENERAL CtOItDON AT KIIARTOUM.—ANOTHER REVERSE REPORTED. Canto, THIIRSDLY.—A telegram which has been received to-day states that Gordpn has met with another reverse; but as the report does not appear to be officially known it must be received with caution. TERRIBLE FIRE ON A STEAMBOAT: GREAT LOSS OF LIFE.

New YORK, FRIDAY MORNING.—A shocking accident is reported from Georgia. The steamer Everingbam, plying In the Chattalooehec river, in that State, was found at about four o'slock yesterday morning to be on fire. She carried a cargo of cotton, and had besides about thirty pas- sengers on board. Owing to the inflammable nature of the cargo, the flames spread very rapidly, and before she aould be run to shore many persons had either been burned to death or drowned in their frantic endeavours to escape the flames by leaping overboard. Eleven passengers are known for a certainty to have thus perished, and it is feared that the total of deaths when ifecurately ascertained will mach ex- ceed this number, some estimating it as high as 20. The cause of the fire is said to have been a spark from the elec- tric light used an board—a mode of lighting which had been supposed to obviate all danger of the kind. ANOTHER INVINCIBLE CONSPIRACY: EXTRA- ORDINARY REVELATIONS. _ . .

The Dublin Express of yesterday states that the Irish authorities are in possession of important information as to continued plots by the Irish Invincibles, who are working in conjunction with the American dynamitards. Some months ago Scotland-yard detectives brought into Dublin discovered that a clandestine correpondence was being carried on between leading members of the Invincibles un- dergoing penal servitude in Dublin prisons and the con- spirators outside. An investigation was held in Mountjoy prison, and warders were brought from Spike Island convict prison. The investigations were continued, and in James Mullett's cell eventu- ally some important letters were discovered. These disclosed a plot to blow up Mountjoy Prison aid the rescue of the Invincible convicts. The warders were to be bribed from the skirmishing and dynamite funds in Rossa's .hands, and were to convey infernal machines into the prison. In the confusion caused by the explosions the prisoners were to escape. One of the letters contained an I order to murder Delaney, the Invincible convicted of attempting to mufder Judge Lawson. Delaney gave all the assistance in his power to the Government officials, and through his information many arrests and convictions were I brought about. The plot to murder Delaney was that as he left the prison chapel after mass he should be thrown over the balcony. The removal of the Invincible convicts to English prisons as recently reported WAS immediately car- ried out. Delaney, however, still remains in Mountjoy Prison for his own safety. When the lavincibles were taken from their cells for removal to England groans were given by them for the Government and hearty cheers for the Invincibles. Immediately afterwards a number of war- dote were dismissed, receiving a month's pay in lieu of notice.

div.head: LATE DUKE OF ALBANY.
div.p: THE LATE DUKE OF ALBANY.

ARRIVAL OF THE BODY AT PORTSMOUTH. Leaving Ckerbourgh on Thursday morning, the Royal yacht Osborne, having on board the body of the Duke of Albany, rounded the Spit buoy at twenty minutes past Mx on Thursday evening, and moored alongside the south rail- way jetty ten minutes later. The Alberta and Enchantress, which followed, passed into the harbour and dropped anchor. No minute guns were fired on the arrival of the Royal vessels, and only a few privileged spectators were present on the pier when the Osborne glided silently along- side. As soon as the semaphore announced that the yachts had been sighted General Prince Edward of Saxe Weimar and Admiral Sir G. T. Phipps Hornby, with their eta, who had been awaiting the signal, proceeded to the landing stage, and on the arrival of the Osborne, went on board. They were accompanied by Prince Albert Victor of Wales, who had arrived at Portsmouth about an hour previously. THE REMOVAL OF THE REMAINS TO WINDSOR. The ceremony of transferring the Duke if Albany's re- mains from the Osborne to the funeral car for removal to Windsor was performed in the Dockyard, Portsmouth, -resterday morning, in splendid weather. During the night airmen.' had been busy completing the arrangements, and I the time the special train arrived, shortly after nine, all was in readiness. The distinguished occupants alighted immediately on the south railway jetty, and proceeded on board the royal yacht. The Prince of Wales was evidently muck affected, greeting the Crown Prince of Germany, the Prince of Waldeck-Pyrnaont, and the Marquis of Lorne as they stepped from the train. Prince Albert Victor and the Duke of Cambridge also went on board the Osborne The first-minute gun boomed from the garrison battery at half-past nine precisely, and firing continued until 30 guns had been discharged, when the tale was taken up by the flagship Duke of Wellington. A detachment of the Sea- forth Highlanders had, meanwhile,. paraded on the pier, and the funeral car was drawn to the Jetty. Exactly as the fifteen-minute gun was fired the coffin was lifted out of the Osborne' deckhouse, covered only by the Union Jack, and placed on the bier. This was then carried along the gang- way and placed in a mourning car which was attached to the train. Walking after the coffin came the Prince of Wales, the Crown Prince of Germany, the Prince of Wal- deck-Pvrmont, Prince Christian, Prince Albert Victor, the Duke of Cambridge, and other distinguished mourners; and as the procesesion moved the funeral service was read, while
Iwol 'by

bands played solemn marches, and the troops reversed arms. At half-past ten, the funeral co having been closed, the mourners entered the saloon, and the train ds. parted for Windsor. The body of the late Prince ArtiVed Windsoi Station about half-past twelve, and had a reception amounting almosrto the proportions of a State funeral, and was met by Her Majesty, the Princess of Wales, the Princess Christian, the Princess Beatrice, and the Ladies-in-Waiting. Her Majesty affectionately greeted the Prince of Wales as he stepped from the train, and seemed much moved. A party of the Seaforth Highlanders carried the coffin, covered I with the Union AO, to the royal waiting-room, where Her I Majesty viewed it as It tested on a bier. SHORT SERVICE LAST EVENING. The Queen, the Duchess of Albany, and all the members of the Royal family now at Windsor, proceeded, on the arrival of the Duchess, to the Albert Memorial Chapel, where the remains now rest, and a short service was con- ducted by the Dean of Windsor. "Thy will be done" and other hymns were sung, and the Dean read selected passages from Scripture. After engaging in silent prayer, the Royal party left the chapel. THE BEREAVED DUCHESS.

A Central News Esher telegram Bait; that the Duchess of Albany passed a tranquil night on Thursday. Her cendit tion is still considered satisfactory. She left Claremon- yesterday for Windsor, accanpanied by the Queen of Hol- land and the Princess Waldeck. She arrived at Windsor about three o'clock, but took no part in the ceremony ex- cept in the private chapel of the Castle. The Duchess will return to Claremont after the funeral, accompanied by the Princess Christian. Floral wreaths and crosses contiuue to arrive at Claremont House hourly from all parts. PROGRAMME OF TO-DAY'S CEREMONIAL.

The Central News has received from the Lord Chamber- lain's office a copy of the programme of the ceremonial to be observed to-day at the funeral. The Que.±n will be accom- panied by the Princess of Wales, Princesses Christian, Louise, and Beatrice, the Grand Duchess of Mecklenburgh and Strelitse; and Princess Frederica of Hanover, and will be shown to chairs prepared for Her Majesty and their Royal Highnesses on the north side of the choir. At half - past eleven the Prince of Wales, the Crown Prince of Germany, the Grand Duke of Hesse, the Royal personages, the representatives of absent Royal personages and their attendants, with the gentlemen of site Royal household and others appointed to take part in the procession will assemble in the Albert Memorial Chapel. Immediately afterwards the procession will move down the lower castle yard, through the Horse Shoe Cloisters, the west door of the chapel and the nave to the choir of St. George's Chapel, where it will be met by the clergy and choir, by whom it will be preceded up the aisle. The coffin will be borne by men of the Seaforth Highlanders, and the pall bearers will be Lord Brook, Vis- count Castlereagh, Lord Harris, Hon. H. Bourke, Hon. Sidney Herbert, Mr. Walter Campbell, Mr. Raglan Somer- set and Mr. Algernon Mills. The chief mourner will be the Prince of Wales. As soon as the choir reach their places, they will sing the hymn "0 God our help in ages past." Then will follow the first part of the burial service, and Spohr's anthem. "Blest are the departed," after which the coffin will be lowered into the vault, and at the close of the service the choir will sing "Lead kindly light," during which the Queen will retire. A silver name plate has been placed upon the lid of the coffin in readiness for the funeral to-day. The inscription to be borne upon this plate has been specially prepared by Her Majesty, and runs as follows : DEPOSITUM. Diustrissimi Principis. Dunes Albsuix. Cemitus Olariencim et Baron's Arislaw. STOCK AND SHARE MARKET. Messrs. Joseph R. and W. P. Baines, share brokers. 13 Queen's Chambers, Market-street, Manchester, write (April The advance advance In home Investment and speculative securities continues, but ths stimulus is derived this week more from the inluence of cheap money and supply of stock being small than from traffics. the latter not being encouraging, exhibiting a condition of trade which can hardly be expected to help pro- spective values. The reduction of the bank late will probably give a further Impetus to prices unless a stronger counteracting influence presents itself. Foreign funds are nearly all better.

Signor Deprotis, at Rome, on Thursday, presented the new Cabinet to the Chamber of Deputiee. At the meeting of the Board of Directors of the Suez Canal, it was resolved that the special pilotage dues on ships passing through the canal should be abolished. Mr. Fawcett has re-introduced his bill for amending the law with respect to the protection of the Post Office and to offences committed in relation to the Post Office. The Earl of Pembroke, in gratitude for the good nursing he received during his recent severe illness, has sent a cheque of £lOO to the Salisbury Diocese Nurses Association. The authorities of the Kent County Lunatic Asylum at Chatham, near Canterbury, have determined to dis- continue the uss of Australian frozen meat in that establishment. Mr. Hugh Mason, M.P., writing on the subject of delay in legislation, says the Tory obstruction just now j "in- famous," and he can see no other remedy than a vigorous application of the closure. It is understood that the Iltueen will leave Windsor Castle, with Princass Beatrice, for Osborne, according to the latest arrangements, on Thursday next, about a fort- night earlier than usual. COLLIERY EXPLOSION.—The explosion at the Park Slip Colliery, Bridgend, turns out to be less serious than at first supposed. The men were just going to work, and only five had entered No. 4 level when it occurred. Two escaped un• injured, but David Jones, brother of the manager, and a man named Howells, were killed. Griffith Roberts was badly burnt. Jones leaves a wife and family. REPORTED ROBBERY OF £l,OOO, IN LITERPOOL.—It is re- ported that a daring robbery has been committed at the office of a Liverpool merchant, close to the Exchange. The cashier of the firm in question went to dinner, leaving his cash drawer unfastened, and during his absence some one abstracted two Bank of England notes of £5OO each. The police refuse to give any information, but it is believed that they have the matter in hand, and the payment of the notes has been stopped.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
HOUSE OF LORDS.

The House met at the usual hour. THE POSITION OF GENERAL GORDON.—EarI GRANVILLE, replying to the Earl of Hardwick, said the Government was not prepared to send a military expedition into the heart of the Soudan. General Gordon did not think it necessary to be backed-up by British force. His latest advices were re- assnring.—ln reply to Lord Napier, Earl GRANVILLE said he thought the difficulties in the way, the expedition te Khartoum from Suakim or Cairo,were greater than was antici- pated.—The Marquis of SALISBURY regretted the Govern- ment's decision.—Earl Mamma:it admitted the difficulties of General Gordon's mission, but his position had now im- proved.—Replying to Lord Strathendon, Earl GRANVILLE denied that Mr. Gladstone's visit to Copenhagen had any political significance.—The House shortly afterwards ad- journed.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

The Speaker took the chair at 4 o'clock. NOTICES AND QUESTIONS.—Mr. GOURLEY asked whether the Government intended taking any steps for the defence of the Nile provinces in Upper and Lower Egypt. —Lord HARTINOTON said that the subject had occupied the attention of the Government and the military authorities, but it would not be desirable to state the course that was to be adopted.—Lord E. Frraxatratcx, replying to Mr. Samuelson, said that the terms of the accession of this country to the International Convention of Patents would be presented as soon as they were received.—Mr. DODSON, replying to Mr. James Howard, said that local authorities had been urged to take.vigorous action to prevent the spread of foal-and-mouth disease, but he was not prepared to advise the issuing of an order in Council directing the slaughter of all animals at present affected with the dis- ease.—Sir W. Ilanconav said that on Tuesday next, at two o'clock, he proposed asking for leave to introduce a Bill for the government of London.—The CHANCELLOR of the EXCHEQUER said he would take the Civil Service Estimates on the first day the House met after the holidays.—A dis- cussion took place as to when the adjournment of the House for the holidays was to be moved, Mr. BALFOUR saying that members might desire to iefer to the subject of Egypt, no decision was arrived at. IRISH MAGISTRATES.—Mr. JUSTIN MCCARTHY Called attention to the condition of the Irish magistracy. He insisted that the selection for office was made almost ex- clusively from Protestants, and eligible Roman Catholics were appointed, but in rare instances. He moved, that in the opinion of the House the present condition of the Irish magistracy, constituted as it was almost exclusively from one religious denomitation and one class, was offensive and injurious to the vast majority of the Irish people, and was calculated to destroy all confidence in the ordinary ad- ministration of justice in Ireland.—Mr. O'Baintz seconded the resolution.—Mr. C. RussaLL supported :the resolution, and said the change of present system of appointing Irish magistrates was urgently required.—Sir H. BRUCE opposed and Lord LTMINGTON supported the resolution.—The de- bate was continued by Messrs. T. D. Sullivan, M'Coan, Planket, Dickson, Ewalt, Nolan, Macfarlane, and Lord G. Hamilton.—Mr. TRIVILYAN admitted the present system of appointing Irish magistrates was not satisfactory, but said the Government could never consent to the appointt m cot of magistrates by popular election. The present Lord Chancellor of Ireland had intimated that no error- en his part should part should be wanting to redress in. equality and remove injustice. He had already appointed 61 magistrates without consulting the Lord Lieutenants of the countries, and he believed a better state of things would be the result. Me could not accept the resolution o Mr. McCarthy.
[Lirr strrirrce.]

itThe demand for napkin rings made of wood grown at Sir Walter Scott's home, Abbotsford, is proving a great drain on the forests of Maine. Mr. John Bright has been confined in London to his bed since Monday, front severe chill and slight attack of con- gestion of the lungs. He is now reported, however, to be progressing favourably. Mr. J. Jarrat has been appointed Chief Doorkeeper of the House of Commons, in succession to Mr. Hartley, who has retired after a service of thirty-five years. The Emperor of Germany, who has been ill for a few days, still keeps his bed by advice et his physicians, bat felt well enough on Thursday to receive a report from the , Minister of the Interior.

Mr. Brodrick on April 29 will call attention to the position of elementary school teachers appointed 1846-1851, and the detriment to the cause of education resulting therefrom, and will move a tesolution.

The sentence of two years' imprisonment, passed by the Court of First Instance on Dr. Julius Rosenberg, for having killed Count Stefan Battyany in a duel, has been reduced en appeal by the Court of Second Instance to six months' imprisonment. Nothing has yet been learnt by the officials in Liverpool with regard to the whereabouts of the absconded workhouse master, Mr. Anderson, on whose sureties the Guardians will make a claim for about £4OO. - -

The Standard says it is now arranged that the division on the second reading of the Franchise Bill shall take place on Monday next. A good many members will leave town on the following day, and it is not therefore likely that this arrangement will be departed from. Addressing the City of Dublin grand jury, on Thursday, Lord Chief Baron Pallas said it appeared the wave of crime which had lately swept over the district had subsided, and there was now every prospect of a continued state of peace and quietness.

Ati important capture of coiners has been made by the Birmingham police. Five men were apprehended on Thurs- day morning, and, on being searched, a large number of base florins and half-crow ns were found in their possession. SIR C. DILEE ON THE FRANCHISE BILL—Sir Charles Dilke, in the course of an address which he delivered to the Middlessex Liberal Association on Wednesday night, said the Government had confidence in the treatment of the question of redistribution by the present Legislature, and would ask it to deal with the subject next year. The re- distribution which the Government looked for " would give more weight not only to Yorkshire, to Lancashire, and to Scotland, but also to the Metropolis and the home counties." He ridiculed Sir R. Peel's assertion that the Franchise Bill would give votes to two millions of the most ignorant people in the country.

Miss Mary Needham, a lady of independent means. Dr. Barnard°, of London, was amongst the wedding guests. MURDER AT SWANSEA.—An inquest was held at Swansea, on Thursday, on the bodies of Josiah Padley and Jane fa" ley. The man murdered his wife with a crowbar, an afterwards hanged himself. It was stated that Padlsy ha been frequently charged with ill-using his wife, and Daa suffered imprisonment. He had left a letter in which 110 alleged that his wife had been unfaithful. The jury re- turned a verdict of wilful murder, and fel° cte se. Loss OF A SHIP AND FIFTEEN LlTHS.—lntelligence WEN received at Lerwick on Thursday evening from the island Of Whalsay, Shetland, that a terrible shipping disaster occorrill, on Tuesday during a gale. The Danish barque Alba/ '2' and from Copenhagen, with a general cargo. struck on tb• south shore of the island and was dashed to pieces. Fine* out of 19 souls on board perished. I FIRE AT AN INFIRMLEY.—A fire occurred on Tburedsl morning in the store of the Glasgow Royal Infirmary. Tb patients in the wards on each side became pinic-strickeat and were removed, but two women and a girl got upon O. roof of the front building, and would have jumped int°, the street if a cabman had not drawn his vehicle near OP thus enabled them to alight in safety. The store where tilt ; fire originated was gutted, and some windows of the firmary burned, but no one was injured. The-object of this Company is to -establish an institution in the North of England for the reception Of visitors and invalids. and those who may be advised to undergo the Continental system of treatment known as "The Mont Dore Cure," so highly approved of by the medical profession in rheumatic, gouty, tuberculous. and other morbid constitutional states; also In asthma, consumption' bronchitis, emphyeema. nano- pulmonary catarrh, and other affections of the throat, chest, rand mucous membranes. The West Kirby "Mont Bore" will be a reproduction of the Auvergne establishment with the important accessories of a ' first-class i eeidental hotel. picturesque pleasure-grounde, and mild yet bracing air. It will, unlike the Auvergne, be is availaole in winter as in summer. Auvergne is not easily reached, and can only be visited 'with advantage from June to September, " The Mont Dore Cure" has.lately been introduced into this country, and an establishment is now approaching completion at Bournemouth, under distinguished patronage, and largely supported by the medical profession. But as a number of invalids in the North of England have not the time to avail themselves of this treatment miler from home, it lathe opinion I or medical men that a similar institution might. with every prospect of success, be establithed at the beautiful watering- Otos of West Kirby, a recognised rising and popular health ; resort. The directors have entered into a p °visional contract for the pureham of a freehold site at ,West Kirby. The property is situated in one of the most charming and attractive spots in ' the neighbourhood, posse-sing unequalled natural features, and commanding uninterrupted"riews of the magnificent Welsh mountains and Hilbrs Island. -with the Irish Sea in the die- eitamisaiteisurraiestiairr4tclataotift for the purpose of such an The batimswill form an important feature of the ucdertaking, and will be of the most complete description, for the cure of rheumatism, asthma, and other diseases, will be adopted, like to that-known a• the •• Mont Dore" cure. Accommodation will be provided for over 150 residents, and will include suites of apartments, private sitting and bed- rooms, general drawing-room, ladies' morning room. dining, , reading, billiard, smoking, and recreation rooms. I Experience has ehown that such institations and bathing establishments,as the'llont Dore (Auvergne) Bathe which were I visited by upwards of 6,000 persons in 1880, make large re- turns even during short seasons, and it Is confidently expected that the• West Kirby Mont Dare, which will be open for in- valids and Msitors during the whole year, will prove a most profitable investment. It is anticipated that under proper management. and after Iproviding for all interest on mortgage and debentures, a profit I of from • £lO to £l2 10s, per oent: en the share capital will be istallsed. The only agreement entered into is one dated the 18th day I or December. 1888, between the Revaohn Cumming Macdona, I the vendor, and George Frederick Clarke. /Seq., on behalf of the Company, for the purchase of the freehold. Notice may also be drawn to the fact that it has been decided that all holders of the Company's shares to the extent of £5O will derive a ;benefit of 10 per cent. reduction in the tariff of tbe establishment. . troops in the city. A meeting of the leading citizens has been held, in order to organise a special pollee force. It is generally believed that the troubles are over. A number of records in the Court House were saved. NEW YOUli, TUESDAY—Although a number of troops en roatt for Cincinnati have been ordered back, those who are at present there will remain. The city is at present quiet, but further disorders are considered possible. It has been been ascertained that 41 persons were killed during thei rioting and 120 wounded, and it is known that several other persons were wounded. TERRIBLE Ct CLONE IN AMERICA.-30 LIVES I LOST. NEW Yonx, THURSDAY.—Despatches received here report 11,741MT11M VI Cylinvuo the last two days near Huntsville, Alabama, Chattanooga, Teatlessee, Columbus, Ohio, Pittsburg, and in various districts of Ohio, and Indiana. The aggregate damage to property is enormoue, while 30 persons are believed to have been killed, and over 100 injured. Whole forests are stated to have been up- rooted, and in Tennessee a train was blown from the line into a ditch, two persons being killed. THE TONQUIN EXPEDITION. Paws, MONDAY—The Paris publishes a telegram from General Millot, announcing the commencement Of the rainy season in Tonquin. It adds that Hong Hoa will probably be taken on the 7th or Bth April, and that troops will then commence returning to Franca. In view of their approach- jog departure, General Millot is organising auxiliary native regiments, who will be entrusted with the defence of Tonquin. SPAIN.—GENERAL ELECTIONS. MADRID, MONDAY EVENING.—The King to-day signed a Royal decree, which will be gazetted to-morrow, dissolving the Cortes, and fixing the General Ecction. It is st.:tcd that the elections for members of the Chamber of Deputies will take place on April 27th, and for Senators ten days later. The new Cortes will assemble on May 20th. A PAPAL ALLOCUTION. Roo, SATURDAY.—The Pope, in his last Allocution to the Cardinals, denounced in vigorous terms recent violations of the rights of the Church, demanded the restitution Of the Temporal Power, and protested with marked warmth against the judgment given by the Italian Courts concern- ing the property of the Propaganda. His Holiness said he foresaw fresh attacks upon the Papacy, but he would ever uphold with firmness the rights of the Holy See. EARTHQUAKE IN ISCHIA. ROMB, SATURDAY.—A despatch from Casamieciola states that a rather violent earthquake occarred in the island of Ischia yesterday, the slunk being especially noticeable at Serrara, Fontana, and Forio. Ns damage was done.
